questions.title: What makes a similarity function a valid SVM kernel?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the positive-semidefinite condition for a kernel and why an arbitrary similarity score may not satisfy it.
questions.tldrAnswer: A valid inner-product kernel is symmetric and produces positive-semidefinite Gram matrices for every finite input set.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A kernel represents an inner product $k(x,z)=\langle\phi(x),\phi(z)\rangle$ in some feature space. Therefore its Gram matrix $K$, with entries $K_{ij}=k(x_i,x_j)$, must satisfy $a^\top Ka\geq0$ for every vector $a$ and every finite collection of inputs. Symmetry is also required.

This condition permits the usual convex SVM dual formulation and an implicit feature-space interpretation. A function that merely assigns larger values to similar objects need not meet it. Likewise, applying an arbitrary transformation to a distance does not automatically produce a valid kernel.

### Assumptions

The condition applies on the specified input domain. Testing eigenvalues on one observed Gram matrix can detect a problem but cannot prove validity for every possible input set.

### Common mistake

Floating-point round-off can create tiny negative computed eigenvalues. Distinguish numerical tolerance from a materially indefinite matrix, and use established kernel constructions or a mathematical proof.
keyTakeaways: State the Gram-matrix quadratic-form condition.
Explain its connection to feature-space inner products.
Distinguish finite-sample numerical checks from a domain-wide proof.

questions.title: How do C and gamma change an RBF SVM?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why increasing C is different from increasing the RBF kernel parameter gamma.
questions.tldrAnswer: C changes the cost of margin violations relative to regularisation; gamma changes how quickly similarity decays with squared distance.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The RBF kernel is $k(x,z)=\exp(-\gamma\|x-z\|^2)$. A large $\gamma$ makes similarity fall rapidly, allowing highly local distinctions. A small value makes many observations appear similar and can produce a smoother, less expressive boundary over the observed region.

The parameter $C$ weights margin violations relative to the norm penalty. Larger values place more emphasis on fitting training labels; smaller values permit more violations in exchange for stronger regularisation. Their effects interact, so tuning one while fixing an unsuitable value of the other can be misleading.

### Assumptions

Features have meaningful scales and distances. Rescaling inputs changes squared distances and therefore the effective kernel width. Class or sample weighting also changes the effective penalties on observations.

### Common mistake

Neither parameter alone guarantees a particular generalisation error. A highly local kernel can fit noisy labels, while an overly broad kernel can underfit. Tune both inside validation with preprocessing fitted in each training fold.
keyTakeaways: Separate the violation penalty from the kernel width.
Explain gamma through the RBF distance equation.
Account for feature scale and joint validation.

questions.title: How do Gini impurity and entropy choose a tree split?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how class proportions in child nodes determine split quality and why child size matters.
questions.tldrAnswer: Both measure class mixing, and candidate splits are compared using the sample-weighted impurity of their children.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For class proportions $p_k$ in a node, Gini impurity is $1-\sum_kp_k^2$ and entropy is $-\sum_kp_k\log p_k$, with zero-probability terms taken as zero. Both are zero for a pure node and higher when classes are mixed.

A candidate split is evaluated by the parent impurity minus the weighted average child impurity. A large child contributes more than a tiny one because it contains more observations or sample weight. Looking only at the purest child can therefore select a poor split.

### Assumptions

Class proportions are estimated from the node's training data. The criterion is a local training objective, while depth, minimum leaf size and pruning control the resulting tree.

### Common mistake

Entropy and Gini are not rival definitions of prediction accuracy. They often choose the same split but can rank close alternatives differently. Neither guarantees the best complete tree or reliable probabilities in tiny leaves.
keyTakeaways: Define both impurity measures.
Weight child impurities by their observations or sample weights.
Separate local split quality from whole-tree generalisation.

questions.title: Why can a good local split miss a useful interaction?
questions.questionMarkdown: Use an XOR-style problem to explain a limitation of greedy decision-tree construction.
questions.tldrAnswer: A split can reveal little on its own even when a sequence of splits predicts perfectly, so local improvement is not a guarantee of a good full tree.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A typical tree chooses the split with the largest immediate impurity decrease and then repeats the process within each child. It does not search all possible complete trees before deciding the root.

For two balanced binary features with an XOR label, each individual feature is marginally uninformative: both its values contain equal proportions of both classes. After splitting on either feature, however, the other feature perfectly separates the labels within each child. A rule requiring strictly positive immediate improvement can stop before discovering that interaction.

### Assumptions

The exact XOR example assumes a balanced noiseless population. Finite-sample imbalance may create a small apparent improvement, so implementation choices and stopping thresholds determine what happens in practice.

### Common mistake

Greater permitted depth alone does not guarantee discovery if the first split is blocked. Conversely, allowing every weak split can overfit noise. Validate the full construction procedure and consider models or features that represent relevant interactions.
keyTakeaways: Explain greedy rather than global tree search.
Describe the marginally uninformative XOR first split.
Connect stopping rules to missed interactions and overfitting.

questions.title: How does cost-complexity pruning select a smaller tree?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare post-pruning with stopping growth at a fixed maximum depth.
questions.tldrAnswer: Post-pruning trades fitted loss against the number of leaves along a sequence of subtrees; a depth limit restricts growth before that sequence is considered.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Cost-complexity pruning evaluates a tree with an objective such as $R(T)+\alpha|L(T)|$, where $R(T)$ is its training loss or impurity and $|L(T)|$ is the number of terminal nodes. Larger $\alpha$ makes additional leaves more expensive.

A fitted tree can be reduced by replacing branches with leaves, yielding candidate subtrees at increasing pruning strengths. Validation chooses among these candidates. This differs from a maximum-depth rule, which prevents some branches from being grown at all and imposes the same depth ceiling regardless of local usefulness.

### Assumptions

The loss definition and its scaling determine the numerical interpretation of $\alpha$. Pruning candidates must be generated within each training fold when evaluating the complete procedure.

### Common mistake

Selecting pruning strength from test performance uses the test set for model choice. A smaller tree may be easier to inspect, but pruning does not automatically make its splits stable or causally meaningful.
keyTakeaways: Explain the loss-plus-leaf-count objective.
Distinguish post-pruning from growth restrictions.
Select pruning strength within validation.

questions.title: Why does a squared-error tree predict a leaf mean?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the best constant prediction inside a regression-tree leaf and contrast absolute-error fitting.
questions.tldrAnswer: The mean minimises summed squared residuals; a median minimises summed absolute residuals.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Suppose a leaf contains outcomes $y_1,\ldots,y_m$ and predicts one constant $c$. Squared loss is $\sum_i(y_i-c)^2$. Differentiating gives $2mc-2\sum_i y_i$, so the minimiser is the sample mean. With observation weights, the same calculation gives the weighted mean.

For absolute loss, the optimum is a median because moving the prediction changes the number of positive and negative residual contributions. With an even number of outcomes there may be an interval of minimising medians.

### Assumptions

The statement concerns the constant prediction after leaf membership is fixed. The chosen loss also affects which splits the algorithm selects, not only the final leaf value.

### Common mistake

Changing the reported leaf statistic after training does not reproduce a tree fitted under a different loss. Small leaves also estimate their target noisily, even when their training residuals are tiny.
keyTakeaways: Derive the mean from the squared-loss derivative.
Identify a median as an absolute-loss minimiser.
Distinguish fixed-leaf estimation from split selection.

questions.title: Why do regression trees struggle to extrapolate a trend?
questions.questionMarkdown: A target rises steadily with income, but new incomes exceed every training value. Explain an ordinary tree's prediction behaviour.
questions.tldrAnswer: An ordinary regression tree sends the new observation to an existing leaf and returns its constant value, rather than continuing a fitted slope.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A regression tree partitions feature space using threshold rules. Each terminal region receives a fixed prediction, commonly the mean of its training outcomes. An input beyond the largest observed value still follows the thresholds into an existing outer region.

Consequently the model extends a constant surface into that region. It cannot infer that a linear or exponential trend should continue simply because the training values appeared to follow one. An average of ordinary regression trees remains piecewise constant, although many thresholds can make its changes look smooth within the observed range.

### Assumptions

This describes constant-leaf trees. Trees with local linear models, hybrid models or specially constrained extrapolation rules have different behaviour. Other features may still send an extreme input to different leaves.

### Common mistake

Excellent random-split validation may hide an extrapolation problem when train and validation ranges overlap. Use evaluation periods or ranges matching intended deployment, and compare with a model whose structural assumptions support the required extrapolation.
keyTakeaways: Trace an out-of-range input to an existing leaf.
Explain constant extension rather than continuation of a slope.
Match validation to the deployment range.

questions.title: Why can a random identifier look important to a forest?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why impurity-based feature importance can favour a feature with many possible split points.
questions.tldrAnswer: More candidate splits create more chances to fit accidental training patterns, which can inflate accumulated impurity reduction.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Impurity importance sums the training impurity reductions credited to splits on each feature, usually with node-size weighting. A numeric identifier with many distinct values offers many candidate thresholds. Even without a stable relationship to the target, searching those thresholds can find apparently useful partitions by chance.

A low-cardinality feature has fewer such opportunities. Comparing the resulting importances can therefore reward the search space rather than useful predictive information, especially in deep trees that fit noise.

### Assumptions

The bias concerns the split-selection and training-importance procedure. Its size depends on tree settings, sample size and the available feature distributions; high cardinality is not proof that a genuinely informative feature is unimportant.

### Common mistake

An importance ranking is not a causal ranking. Compare with held-out permutation importance and repeated fits. Permutation methods have their own limitations, including correlated predictors and unrealistic shuffled combinations, so a different importance method is not an automatic explanation of the data-generating process.
keyTakeaways: Connect split-search opportunity to training impurity reduction.
Explain why held-out evaluation can expose noise fitting.
Distinguish predictive importance from causal influence.

questions.title: Why restrict candidate features at each forest split?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain what changes when every tree split sees only a random subset of predictors.
questions.tldrAnswer: Feature sampling can prevent the same dominant predictors from controlling every tree, reducing dependence at the possible cost of weaker individual trees.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If every tree considers every feature at every split, a particularly strong predictor may repeatedly define the upper branches. Bootstrap samples can then produce similar trees despite their different observations.

Sampling a subset of candidate features forces some splits to consider alternatives. This can diversify prediction errors across trees, so averaging cancels more variation. However, excluding strong predictors can also make individual trees less accurate. The ensemble result depends on both effects.

### Assumptions

The feature-subset size is a tuning choice, and the appropriate value depends on signal distribution, redundant predictors and the number of features. Sampling features at each split differs from selecting one fixed subset for an entire tree.

### Common mistake

Lower correlation alone does not guarantee a better forest. Completely uninformative trees can be diverse and still predict poorly. Compare validation performance as candidate-feature count changes, and inspect whether rare but important features receive enough opportunities.
keyTakeaways: Describe feature sampling at each split.
Explain the dependence-versus-tree-strength trade-off.
Use validation rather than assuming more randomness is better.

questions.title: How does out-of-bag evaluation work?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the approximate fraction of omitted observations per bootstrap tree and explain how their predictions are combined.
questions.tldrAnswer: An observation is omitted with probability approaching 1/e; its out-of-bag prediction uses only trees trained without that observation.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
When a bootstrap sample makes $n$ independent draws from $n$ observations, a particular observation is absent with probability $(1-1/n)^n$, approaching $e^{-1}\approx0.368$.

For each training observation, out-of-bag evaluation aggregates predictions from only the trees whose bootstrap samples omitted it. Comparing those predictions with its outcome gives an internal error estimate without reserving one common validation subset. Different observations can receive predictions from different numbers of trees.

### Assumptions

Observation-level bootstrapping should match the sampling problem. Repeated records from the same person can leak information if only one record is omitted while related records remain in a tree's training sample. Any globally fitted supervised preprocessing can create similar leakage.

### Common mistake

Repeatedly selecting forest settings using out-of-bag performance makes that estimate part of model selection. It is then no longer an untouched final evaluation. Enough trees are also needed for stable out-of-bag predictions.
keyTakeaways: Derive the omission probability.
Aggregate only predictions from trees that omitted the observation.
Identify grouped-data leakage and repeated-tuning limitations.

questions.title: Why does gradient boosting fit negative gradients?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the update target for general differentiable loss and why ordinary residuals appear for squared error.
questions.tldrAnswer: Each new learner approximates the direction that locally decreases the loss. That direction equals outcome-minus-prediction residuals only for suitable squared loss.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let $F(x_i)$ be the current prediction and $\ell(y_i,F(x_i))$ the loss. Gradient boosting computes pseudo-responses $r_i=-\partial\ell(y_i,F(x_i))/\partial F(x_i)$, then fits a weak learner to approximate them.

For half squared error, the derivative is $F(x_i)-y_i$, so the negative gradient is the ordinary residual. Other losses produce different targets. The fitted learner is added with a step size, and some implementations additionally optimise leaf values or a line-search coefficient.

### Assumptions

The gradient is taken with respect to the prediction scale used by the loss. In binary logistic boosting that scale is commonly a log-odds score, not the final probability.

### Common mistake

“Every boosting algorithm fits residuals” hides the essential loss dependence. Also, a weak learner cannot usually reproduce the exact gradient vector, and a large step can overshoot. Validate learning rate, tree structure and number of rounds together.
keyTakeaways: Define pseudo-responses as negative prediction gradients.
Derive ordinary residuals for half squared error.
Track the prediction scale and learning-rate role.

questions.title: Why does AdaBoost increase weights on mistakes?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain a binary AdaBoost round and the risk posed by mislabelled observations.
questions.tldrAnswer: Reweighting makes the next weak classifier focus more on previously misclassified examples, consistent with reducing an exponential margin loss.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
In binary AdaBoost, a weak classifier is fitted to weighted observations. Its weighted error determines a contribution coefficient, commonly $\alpha_t=\tfrac12\log((1-\epsilon_t)/\epsilon_t)$ when $0<\epsilon_t<1/2$. Observation weights are then multiplied by $\exp(-\alpha_t y_i h_t(x_i))$ and normalised.

Correct classifications receive a smaller multiplier than mistakes. The final prediction combines the classifiers' weighted votes. This can be derived from stagewise minimisation of exponential loss on the accumulated classification margin.

### Assumptions

These equations describe the standard binary formulation with labels and weak predictions in $\{-1,1\}$. Perfect or ineffective weak classifiers require boundary handling, and multiclass variants use different details.

### Common mistake

High weight does not prove an observation is especially valuable. A corrupted label can remain difficult forever and attract increasing attention. AdaBoost may therefore be sensitive to label noise; inspect difficult cases and validate rather than interpreting reweighting as error correction.
keyTakeaways: Describe weighted fitting, contribution weight and renormalisation.
Connect updates to exponential margin loss.
Explain why persistent noisy labels can dominate attention.

questions.title: How do learning rate, depth and rounds interact?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why reducing a boosting learning rate without increasing rounds can worsen performance. Is boosting inherently more stable than bagging?
questions.tldrAnswer: Learning rate controls each update's size, rounds control how many updates accumulate, and tree depth controls the interactions each update can represent.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Boosting builds a prediction function by adding learners sequentially. A smaller learning rate makes each addition less influential, so more rounds are often needed to reach a comparable fit. Holding rounds fixed while reducing the rate can simply leave the model underfitted.

Tree depth controls the structure available to each addition. A stump represents one split at a time, whereas deeper trees can directly capture combinations of several conditions. More depth also increases the opportunity to fit noise and can change the useful learning-rate range.

### Assumptions

These controls depend on the loss, data size and base-learner implementation. Their effects cannot be reduced to one universal complexity number.

### Common mistake

A very small rate is not a guarantee against overfitting. Evaluate combinations and use an appropriate validation stopping rule. Keep the final test set separate from choosing the round with the best observed score.

### Stability is not guaranteed

Boosting is not inherently more stable than bagging. Sequential corrections can focus on difficult observations, including noisy labels or outliers, and flexible base learners can overfit. Bagging often reduces variance by averaging resampled learners, but its effect depends on their correlation and the base learner. Compare sensitivity to data perturbations and held-out performance under explicit settings. Shrinkage, depth limits, subsampling and stopping are controls to assess, not a proof of universal stability.
keyTakeaways: Explain update size versus number of updates.
Relate depth to representable interactions.
Tune the controls jointly using validation.
Reject a universal stability ranking between boosting and bagging.

questions.title: Why must a stacking model use out-of-fold predictions?
questions.questionMarkdown: Describe how to train a meta-model without letting base models expose their training overfit.
questions.tldrAnswer: Train each meta-feature from a base model that did not fit the corresponding observation, then refit base models on all available training data for deployment.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A stacking model learns how to combine predictions from several base learners. If those predictions are generated on the same observations used to fit each base learner, a flexible learner may look nearly perfect to the meta-model. Its deployment predictions will not have that artificial advantage.

Create folds within the training data. For each fold, fit base learners on the other folds and predict the held-out fold. Concatenating these predictions produces out-of-fold meta-features, each paired with an outcome absent from the corresponding base fit. Fit the meta-model on these features, then refit base learners on the full training set.

### Assumptions

All base preprocessing and tuning must respect the fold boundary. Grouped or temporal data require suitable folds rather than arbitrary random partitions.

### Common mistake

Out-of-fold meta-training does not itself provide an untouched evaluation of the stack. Assess the complete stacking procedure on separate data or an outer cross-validation loop.
keyTakeaways: Explain why in-sample base predictions mislead the meta-model.
Describe fold-wise prediction and final base-model refitting.
Evaluate the complete stack outside its training procedure.

questions.title: When is probability averaging useful?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare majority voting with averaging class probabilities, including the conditions needed for sensible soft voting.
questions.tldrAnswer: Soft voting retains confidence information that hard labels discard, but requires aligned classes and useful probability estimates.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Hard voting counts predicted labels. Soft voting averages predicted probabilities, possibly using validation-selected weights, then chooses the class with the largest average. A model assigning 0.51 and one assigning 0.99 both cast the same hard vote, but contribute differently to a probability average.

This additional information can help when probabilities are meaningful and errors differ across models. It can hurt when one model is confidently wrong or its output scale is incompatible with the others.

### Assumptions

Every probability column must refer to the same class, and weights should be selected without inspecting the final test set. Models trained on different sampling prevalences may require adjustment before their probabilities describe the same population.

### Common mistake

Averaging probabilities does not automatically produce a calibrated result, even if each component looks reasonable in aggregate. Measure the combined model's discrimination, calibration and task-specific decisions rather than assuming the ensemble inherits every favourable property.
keyTakeaways: Contrast label votes with probability averages.
Require aligned class mappings and appropriate population probabilities.
Evaluate the combined model rather than assuming calibration.

questions.title: How does balanced accuracy change a majority-class baseline?
questions.questionMarkdown: In a binary population with 2% positives, an all-negative classifier achieves 98% accuracy. Calculate its balanced accuracy and explain what the different weighting reveals.
questions.tldrAnswer: Its balanced accuracy is 50%: positive-class recall is zero and negative-class recall is one. Equal class weighting exposes failure that prevalence-weighted ordinary accuracy hides.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Binary balanced accuracy is the mean of the two class recalls: $(\mathrm{TPR}+\mathrm{TNR})/2$. An all-negative classifier has positive recall zero and negative recall one, so its balanced accuracy is 0.5 regardless of the 2% positive prevalence.

Ordinary accuracy instead weights these recalls by prevalence: $\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}+(1-\pi)\,\mathrm{TNR}$. With $\pi=0.02$, the same classifier scores 0.98. The difference reflects which classes receive weight, not a change in the underlying predictions.

### Assumptions

Both classes must be represented well enough to estimate their recalls. Equal class weighting is a deliberate evaluation choice; it does not mean each error has the same operational consequence. Rare-class recall may have substantial uncertainty.

### Common mistake

Balanced accuracy does not include alert precision or encode monetary costs. A model can improve it while producing more alerts than a team can review. Report class recalls and uncertainty, then connect threshold selection to the actual decision and population.
keyTakeaways: Calculate ordinary accuracy as prevalence-weighted class recalls.
Calculate balanced accuracy as their equal-weight mean.
Distinguish class weighting from error costs and alert precision.

questions.title: What does F1 leave out?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the F1 formula and identify a decision problem where it can be misleading.
questions.tldrAnswer: F1 balances precision and recall at a chosen threshold but ignores true negatives and does not encode actual error costs.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: $F_1=2PR/(P+R)$. Equivalently, $F_1=2TP/(2TP+FP+FN)$ when the denominator is non-zero. The harmonic mean is low when either precision or recall is low, so a high value requires both to be reasonably strong.

True negatives do not appear in this expression. Consequently F1 does not summarise all decisions and cannot directly represent a cost calculation in which correctly rejecting a large negative population or unequal error costs matter.

### Assumptions

F1 depends on the chosen positive class, decision threshold and population prevalence. Zero denominators require an explicit reporting convention. Comparing models requires consistent evaluation populations.

### Common mistake

Maximising F1 is not equivalent to maximising profit or minimising harm. Its implicit trade-off may be unsuitable for medical screening, fraud review or capacity-limited intervention. Choose a metric and threshold from the actual decision objective.
keyTakeaways: Write F1 using confusion-matrix counts.
Identify the omitted true negatives.
Distinguish F1 optimisation from cost-based decisions.

questions.title: What does ROC AUC mean as a ranking probability?
questions.questionMarkdown: Interpret a binary classifier's ROC AUC and explain what a value of 0.9 does not tell you.
questions.tldrAnswer: AUC is the chance that a random positive receives a higher score than a random negative, with half credit for ties. It does not identify a useful operating threshold.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Draw one positive and one negative independently from their respective class distributions. ROC AUC equals $\Pr(S_+>S_-)+\tfrac12\Pr(S_+=S_-)$. This connects the area under the true-positive-rate versus false-positive-rate curve to pairwise ordering.

An AUC of 0.9 therefore indicates strong average ranking, not that 90% of individual classifications are correct. A strictly increasing score transformation preserves the ordering and AUC while potentially changing probability interpretation completely.

### Assumptions

The evaluation sample should represent the class-conditional distributions relevant to deployment. Dependence between repeated observations and uncertainty from a small positive class require appropriate treatment.

### Common mistake

A good average across the whole ROC curve may hide poor performance in the narrow false-positive range the application can tolerate. Inspect that operating region, precision under deployment prevalence and the selected threshold. AUC does not measure calibration or establish that any particular decision policy is useful.
keyTakeaways: Give the pairwise probability interpretation including ties.
Separate ranking from accuracy and calibration.
Evaluate the relevant threshold region.

questions.title: Why does precision change when prevalence changes?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive precision from prevalence, sensitivity and false-positive rate, then explain the effect of deploying in a rarer-positive population.
questions.tldrAnswer: Even unchanged class-conditional error rates yield lower precision when positive prevalence falls.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let $\pi=\Pr(Y=1)$, let TPR be sensitivity and let FPR be the false-positive rate. Bayes' rule gives

$$
\Pr(Y=1\mid\hat Y=1)=
\frac{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}}
{\pi\,\mathrm{TPR}+(1-\pi)\,\mathrm{FPR}}.
$$

When positives become rarer, fewer true alerts compete with false alerts from the larger negative population. Precision therefore falls if TPR and a non-zero FPR remain fixed. For example, TPR 0.8 and FPR 0.1 give precision about 0.47 at prevalence 0.1 but only about 0.075 at prevalence 0.01. A precision-recall curve can change even when the class-conditional score distributions, and hence the ROC curve, do not.

### Assumptions

This comparison assumes only prevalence changes, with stable class-conditional score distributions and the same threshold. Real deployment changes may also alter those distributions.

### Common mistake

Precision measured on a balanced case-control dataset is not automatically the expected fraction of useful production alerts. Reconstruct the relevant prevalence or evaluate on representative data, and quantify uncertainty when positive cases are scarce.
keyTakeaways: Derive precision with Bayes' rule.
State the stable class-conditional distribution assumption.
Avoid transferring balanced-sample precision directly to deployment.

questions.title: Why does log loss punish confident mistakes strongly?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare predicting 0.6 and 0.001 for an outcome that turns out positive.
questions.tldrAnswer: The positive-outcome loss is minus the logarithm of its predicted probability, so assigning probability near zero makes the penalty large.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Binary log loss is $-[y\log p+(1-y)\log(1-p)]$. For a positive outcome, it reduces to $-\log p$. Predicting 0.6 incurs about 0.51 natural-log units, while predicting 0.001 incurs about 6.91. Declaring an observed event almost impossible is therefore much worse than expressing moderate uncertainty.

Expected log loss is minimised by reporting the true conditional event probability when the model can represent it. This makes it useful for assessing probability predictions rather than only thresholded decisions.

### Assumptions

Probabilities must refer to the event and population being evaluated. Dataset shift, label errors and sampling weights can affect the appropriate interpretation.

### Common mistake

Implementations clip probabilities away from zero and one to avoid numerical infinities. Clipping is computational protection; it does not mean exact certainty is harmless under the ideal score. Compare scores using consistent clipping, averaging and logarithm conventions.
keyTakeaways: Write binary log loss and calculate the positive-event case.
Explain why nearly impossible observed events receive large penalties.
Distinguish numerical clipping from the ideal scoring objective.

questions.title: Why is truthful probability reporting optimal under Brier score?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the expected binary Brier loss when the true event probability is q and a forecaster reports p.
questions.tldrAnswer: Expected squared probability error equals an irreducible term plus the squared difference between the reported and true probabilities.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For binary outcome $Y$, Brier loss is $(p-Y)^2$. If $\Pr(Y=1)=q$, its expectation is $q(1-p)^2+(1-q)p^2=(p-q)^2+q(1-q)$. The second term does not depend on the report, so the unique optimum is $p=q$.

This establishes properness for the binary score. It also explains why confident wrong predictions receive a large penalty, although the penalty remains bounded between zero and one rather than diverging as log loss can.

### Assumptions

The derivation concerns a fixed information set and its conditional event probability. Multiclass implementations and scaling conventions can differ, so compare like with like.

### Common mistake

A lower Brier score is not proof that calibration alone improved. Resolution, or the ability to distinguish observations with different event probabilities, also affects the overall score. Use calibration plots and decision-focused evaluation alongside the aggregate value.
keyTakeaways: Derive the squared-distance decomposition.
Identify the truthful probability as the minimiser.
Separate overall probability accuracy from calibration alone.

questions.title: When would MAE and RMSE favour different models?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how two models can be ranked differently by mean absolute error and root mean squared error.
questions.tldrAnswer: RMSE gives large residuals more influence through squaring; MAE grows linearly and targets a different optimal prediction.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
MAE averages absolute residuals, while RMSE takes the square root of their mean square. Squaring gives a few large errors much more weight. A model with many small errors and one severe failure can therefore beat another on MAE while losing on RMSE.

Both scores are expressed in the target's units. The square root changes interpretability, but minimising population RMSE has the same minimiser as mean squared error: the conditional mean. Absolute-error risk is minimised by a conditional median.

### Assumptions

Select a score whose error weighting reflects the decision. Outcome units and evaluation populations must match when comparing values. Weighted versions require an explanation of whose errors receive more influence.

### Common mistake

Calling MAE universally robust or RMSE universally better avoids the actual cost question. Large failures may be precisely what matters operationally. Inspect the residual distribution and relevant subgroups instead of relying on one number to describe every error.
keyTakeaways: Explain linear versus squared residual weighting.
Identify the conditional median and mean targets.
Choose the score from consequences of errors.

questions.title: How can R squared be negative?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain a negative R-squared score on held-out data and identify its reference prediction.
questions.tldrAnswer: The model's squared error exceeds that of predicting the held-out outcome mean for every observation.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For non-constant evaluation outcomes, $R^2=1-\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2/\sum_i(y_i-\bar y)^2$. The denominator is the error of the constant prediction equal to that evaluation set's mean. If model error is larger, the ratio exceeds one and $R^2$ is negative.

Ordinary least squares with an intercept cannot do worse than its mean-only fit on the same training data, but this argument does not apply to held-out observations. It also need not apply to a model fitted without an intercept or using a different objective.

### Assumptions

The denominator must be non-zero. Constant outcomes produce undefined or implementation-specific results, and very little outcome variation can make the score unstable.

### Common mistake

The reference mean in the score is calculated from evaluation outcomes and is not necessarily a deployable forecast known in advance. A negative result signals poor performance against this mathematical reference, not a universal lower bound or a percentage of correctly predicted outcomes.
keyTakeaways: Write the squared-error ratio.
Identify the evaluation-set mean reference.
Explain held-out, intercept and constant-target qualifications.

questions.title: Why can percentage error be misleading near zero?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain what happens when mean absolute percentage error is applied to outcomes containing small values or zeros.
questions.tldrAnswer: Dividing by the actual outcome makes small denominators dominate, and exact zeros leave the ideal percentage error undefined.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A common percentage-error term is $|y-\hat y|/|y|$. An absolute error of one unit means 1% when the actual value is 100 but 100% when it is one. As the actual value approaches zero, even a small error can dominate the average.

At zero the ratio is undefined. Some software replaces the denominator with a tiny positive value, producing a very large finite number rather than resolving the conceptual problem. Signed outcomes also complicate the business meaning of percentage error.

### Assumptions

Relative error is meaningful only if the outcome scale supports ratio comparisons and denominators are sufficiently far from zero. A metric appropriate for large positive revenue may be unsuitable for net profit that crosses zero.

### Common mistake

Removing all zero outcomes after inspecting results changes the evaluation population. Choose a justified absolute, scaled or distribution-based alternative before comparison, and document how small denominators are handled.
keyTakeaways: Explain denominator-driven weighting.
Distinguish undefined percentages from numerical safeguards.
Choose an evaluation population and alternative metric deliberately.

questions.title: How do macro, micro and weighted averages differ?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain three ways to summarise class-specific precision, recall or F1 in a multiclass problem.
questions.tldrAnswer: Macro gives each class equal weight, weighted averages use class support, and micro combines decision counts before computing the score.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Macro averaging first calculates a score per class, treating that class as positive, then averages the scores equally. A rare class can therefore influence the summary as much as a common one.

A support-weighted average gives each class weight proportional to its number of true examples. Micro averaging instead adds the true-positive, false-positive and false-negative counts across classes before calculating the metric. In complete single-label multiclass classification, micro precision, recall and F1 coincide with accuracy.

### Assumptions

The equivalence with accuracy requires the stated single-label setting and inclusion of every class. Multilabel problems, excluded labels and zero-denominator conventions change the interpretation.

### Common mistake

A weighted average does not guarantee strong rare-class performance, while a macro score can be noisy when some classes have very few examples. Show class supports and important class-specific scores rather than treating one aggregation as universally fair.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish averaging scores from aggregating counts.
State when micro scores equal accuracy.
Report support and class-specific limitations.

questions.title: How do error costs determine a classification threshold?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the optimal positive-decision threshold using false-positive cost and false-negative cost, assuming correct decisions cost zero.
questions.tldrAnswer: Predict positive when the calibrated event probability exceeds false-positive cost divided by the sum of the two error costs.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let $p=\Pr(Y=1\mid x)$, false-positive cost be $C_{\mathrm{FP}}>0$ and false-negative cost be $C_{\mathrm{FN}}>0$. The expected cost of a positive decision is $C_{\mathrm{FP}}(1-p)$; the expected cost of a negative decision is $C_{\mathrm{FN}}p$.

Choose positive when the first is smaller, giving $p>C_{\mathrm{FP}}/(C_{\mathrm{FP}}+C_{\mathrm{FN}})$. At equality either action has the same expected cost under this model. Higher missed-positive cost lowers the threshold.

### Assumptions

The probability must describe the deployment population and available information. Costs are fixed, correct decisions have zero cost, and there are no capacity constraints or interactions between decisions.

### Common mistake

Applying this formula to an uncalibrated score does not implement the derived policy. If review capacity is limited, intervention changes outcomes, or costs vary by person, formulate those additional choices explicitly rather than forcing them into one constant threshold.
keyTakeaways: Compare expected costs of both actions.
Derive the threshold algebraically.
State calibration, cost and capacity assumptions.

questions.title: When must validation keep whole entities together?
questions.questionMarkdown: You have repeated measurements from each patient and want to predict for new patients. Explain the correct fold boundary.
questions.tldrAnswer: All observations from one patient should stay in one fold so validation measures transfer to unseen patients rather than recognition of familiar patients.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Records from the same entity can share stable characteristics, measurement conditions or labels. If some enter training and others validation, a model may exploit patient-specific patterns that will be unavailable for a new patient.

Assign each patient to one fold and keep every associated record together. Fit preprocessing within the training patients. Evaluate at the unit relevant to the decision, because a patient with many records should not automatically dominate a patient-level performance claim.

### Assumptions

The grouping unit should match the intended unseen entity. Predicting new visits for known patients is a different task and may require a temporal rather than purely patient-disjoint evaluation. Hospital-level variation may require an additional grouping boundary.

### Common mistake

A group split does not guarantee balanced labels or equal fold sizes. Large or unusual groups can make results variable. Report group counts and fold variation, and avoid choosing the split that happens to give the most favourable score.
keyTakeaways: Match the group boundary to the deployment entity.
Keep preprocessing inside group-disjoint training folds.
Address unequal group sizes and higher-level grouping.

questions.title: Why should forecasting validation respect time?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain a rolling or expanding-window evaluation and when a gap between training and validation is needed.
questions.tldrAnswer: Train only on information available before the forecast origin and evaluate on later periods; use gaps where labels or feature windows would otherwise overlap improperly.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
An expanding-window design trains on all eligible history before each forecast origin and evaluates a later block. A rolling window uses only a fixed recent portion of that history. Repeating this over several origins reveals how the procedure behaves across different periods.

The split must account for information availability, not only row timestamps. A label based on the following month may not be known at the training cutoff. Overlapping outcome windows or delayed features can require an exclusion gap.

### Assumptions

The evaluation horizon and retraining schedule should resemble deployment. Future periods need not follow the same distribution, so historical performance is evidence about observed shifts rather than a guarantee of stationarity.

### Common mistake

Sorting rows by time after randomly fitting preprocessing does not remove future information from that preprocessing. Fit all learned transformations using eligible history, and construct features as they would actually have been available at each prediction time.
keyTakeaways: Describe rolling and expanding training windows.
Apply information-availability rather than row-time boundaries.
Explain gaps and deployment-matched horizons.

questions.title: What does nested cross-validation estimate?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the distinct roles of the inner and outer loops and how the final deployment model is fitted.
questions.tldrAnswer: The outer loop evaluates the whole model-selection procedure; the inner loop chooses its settings using only the outer training data.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
In each outer split, reserve one part for assessment. Within the remaining data, run inner cross-validation to select hyperparameters, features or model families. Refit the selected procedure on that outer training portion and evaluate it once on the outer held-out portion.

Aggregating outer results estimates how the specified selection procedure performs when trained on datasets of that size. After assessment, a deployment model can be selected using the planned tuning procedure on all available training data and then refitted.

### Assumptions

Both loops must respect grouping, time and preprocessing boundaries. The outer scores evaluate a procedure, not one immutable coefficient vector, because each outer split may select different settings.

### Common mistake

Choosing a new search strategy after repeatedly inspecting outer scores makes the outer loop part of selection too. Nested validation reduces selection bias only for decisions actually contained inside its boundary; it is also computationally expensive and does not eliminate distribution shift.
keyTakeaways: Separate inner selection from outer assessment.
Explain final fitting after procedure evaluation.
Keep adaptive choices within the appropriate evaluation boundary.

questions.title: What does stratifying validation folds achieve?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why preserving class proportions can help evaluation and why it does not solve every split problem.
questions.tldrAnswer: Stratification reduces accidental class imbalance across folds, but it does not remove entity overlap, future information or distribution mismatch.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A class-stratified split aims to keep each fold's class proportions close to those of the full dataset. This can prevent a rare class from disappearing from a fold and make class-based metrics less erratic.

The method addresses allocation of labels, not the origin of observations. Repeated measurements from one customer can still appear on both sides, and later events can still inform earlier predictions if the split is otherwise random.

### Assumptions

Each class needs enough independent examples to support the requested number of folds. Grouping or time restrictions may prevent exact proportional balance and should take priority when they define the deployment task.

### Common mistake

A balanced validation set is not necessarily a representative one. Deliberately changing prevalence affects accuracy, precision and probability evaluation. Record the sampling design and distinguish proportional stratification from oversampling or constructing an artificial equal-class test set.
keyTakeaways: Explain proportional allocation rather than synthetic balancing.
Recognise rare-class limits on fold count.
Prioritise dependence and time boundaries where required.

questions.title: What can training and validation learning curves suggest?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain what you infer when training performance is strong but validation performance improves as more data are added.
questions.tldrAnswer: A shrinking training-validation gap can suggest sensitivity to sample size, but learning curves diagnose patterns rather than prove one particular cause.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A learning curve compares performance after fitting the same procedure to different amounts of training data. Strong training scores with weaker validation scores suggest that fitting the available examples is easier than transferring to new ones. If validation improves as sample size grows, additional comparable data may help.

When both scores remain poor, the bottleneck could be limited representation, excessive regularisation, poor features or optimisation failure. These alternatives require further investigation; the curve alone cannot distinguish them.

### Assumptions

Use a consistent metric, representative subsets and evaluation boundaries. Time-ordered data may not permit randomly increasing sample size without changing the period being represented.

### Common mistake

Extrapolating a visually improving curve far beyond observed sample sizes can overstate the value of collecting data. New labels may differ in quality or distribution. Include uncertainty across suitable resamples and compare targeted changes rather than assigning a definitive bias or variance diagnosis from one plot.
keyTakeaways: Interpret performance gaps and changes with sample size.
Name alternative explanations for poor scores.
Avoid unsupported extrapolation and report variability.

questions.title: Why are cross-validation fold scores dependent?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why dividing the standard deviation of fold scores by the square root of the fold count can give a misleading standard error.
questions.tldrAnswer: Fold models share many training observations, so their errors are not independent replicate measurements.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
In ordinary k-fold cross-validation, each observation is held out once, but each fitted model trains on most of the same observations as the other models. An influential training example can affect several fitted models and their validation errors together.

The usual standard-error formula based on independent replicates therefore does not follow simply from having k reported scores. Fold-to-fold variation describes sensitivity to that partition, not all uncertainty from drawing a new dataset and repeating model selection.

### Assumptions

Dependence varies with the estimator, split design and data. Repeated cross-validation adds partitions but still reuses the same observations, so it does not create fully independent experiments.

### Common mistake

A narrow interval based on hundreds of reused fold scores can suggest far more certainty than the data support. Use uncertainty methods justified for the design, preserve independent groups in resampling, and state whether uncertainty concerns a fitted model, a training procedure or a population performance estimate.
keyTakeaways: Explain overlap in training sets.
Distinguish fold variability from sampling uncertainty.
Avoid treating repeated partitions as independent datasets.

questions.title: When can importance weighting correct covariate shift?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the weighting identity for target-population prediction loss and state its essential assumptions.
questions.tldrAnswer: Weight source examples by the target-to-source feature density ratio when the conditional outcome distribution is unchanged and the target has source support.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let source and target feature densities be $p_s(x)$ and $p_t(x)$. If $p_t(y\mid x)=p_s(y\mid x)$ and target support is contained in source support, then target risk can be written as

$$
\mathbb{E}_t[\ell(Y,f(X))]
=\mathbb{E}_s\!\left[\frac{p_t(X)}{p_s(X)}\ell(Y,f(X))\right].
$$

The ratio makes source observations representative of the target feature distribution. It may be estimated using unlabelled target features, but estimation introduces additional uncertainty.

### Assumptions

The stable conditional-outcome assumption is stronger than observing different feature histograms. Positive source density is needed wherever the target has probability mass, and the weighted loss must have suitable moments.

### Common mistake

Weighting cannot invent labels in unsupported regions or repair a changing conditional relationship. Very large ratios make estimates unstable. Clipping weights trades variance for bias, so it should be evaluated and disclosed rather than described as an exact correction.
keyTakeaways: Derive target risk by a feature-density ratio.
State stable conditional outcomes and support overlap.
Explain weight-estimation uncertainty and clipping bias.

questions.title: Why does feature scale matter to a distance-based model?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how measuring one feature in metres rather than kilometres can change nearest-neighbour or regularised linear predictions.
questions.tldrAnswer: Numerical scale changes distances and the coefficient magnitudes needed for a relationship, so it changes the model's geometry or penalty.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Euclidean distance sums squared coordinate differences. A feature with a much larger numerical range can dominate that sum even if its units are arbitrary. Changing metres to kilometres therefore changes nearest-neighbour ordering unless the distance calculation compensates.

Scale also matters to coefficient penalties. A rescaled feature requires an inversely rescaled coefficient for the same prediction, changing its L1 or L2 cost. Standardisation centres and scales features to a chosen reference, often the training mean and standard deviation.

### Assumptions

Comparable numerical variation does not necessarily mean equal domain importance. Constant features and extreme tails require deliberate handling. Fit transformation statistics only on training observations.

### Common mistake

Scaling is not universally needed. Ordinary axis-aligned trees are generally unaffected by positive affine unit changes, apart from numerical details. Nonlinear monotone transforms preserve training order but can move inverse-transformed midpoint thresholds, changing predictions for unseen values. Standardisation also does not remove irrelevant dimensions or guarantee a meaningful distance.
keyTakeaways: Explain scale through squared coordinate distances.
Connect feature scaling to coefficient penalties.
Fit transformations on training data and distinguish tree behaviour.

questions.title: Why use one-hot encoding for nominal categories?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the representation and why a linear model with an intercept may drop one category.
questions.tldrAnswer: Indicator columns avoid imposing an arbitrary numeric order. Dropping one level removes exact collinearity with the intercept in an unpenalised linear model.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
One-hot encoding assigns an indicator column to each category. For an observation in a given category, its corresponding indicator is one and the others are zero. A linear model can then learn a separate contribution for each level without assuming that category labels form a numeric scale.

If all category indicators are included with an intercept, their sum equals the intercept column. Dropping one category creates a reference level: the remaining coefficients represent differences from that reference, conditional on the other model terms.

### Assumptions

The vocabulary must be learned from training data or a justified pre-defined domain. Prediction-time unseen categories need an explicit policy. Regularised or constrained models can use full encodings with different identifiability conventions.

### Common mistake

Dropping a level is not always an innocuous choice under penalties because it can treat the baseline asymmetrically. State the coding and penalty scheme when interpreting coefficients.
keyTakeaways: Explain indicator columns without ordinal assumptions.
Identify the intercept-related linear dependence.
State the reference and unseen-category conventions.

questions.title: When do integer category codes create false structure?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why coding red, blue and green as 0, 1 and 2 can mislead some models.
questions.tldrAnswer: Numeric codes can imply order and spacing that nominal categories do not possess, and different model families use those implications differently.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A linear model given codes 0, 1 and 2 assigns evenly spaced contributions through one coefficient. A distance-based model treats 0 as closer to 1 than to 2. Neither relationship follows from the names of colours.

A threshold tree also sees an order: a single split can separate contiguous code ranges, but arbitrary category subsets may need several splits. A model with native categorical handling may instead use a representation designed for unordered levels.

### Assumptions

An ordinal feature such as low, medium and high has a real order, but that does not automatically establish equal spacing. The measurement scale and learner's treatment of numbers must both be considered.

### Common mistake

Replacing strings with integers is not merely a storage change once a model consumes those integers as quantities. Validate alternative encodings and document how unknown or missing values are represented without accidentally assigning them a meaningful rank.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish nominal order from numerical spacing.
Explain different implications for linear, distance and threshold models.
Specify unknown and missing-category treatment.

questions.title: What should happen when a new category appears at prediction time?
questions.questionMarkdown: Design a policy for a categorical value absent from training and explain a potential ambiguity in one-hot encoding.
questions.tldrAnswer: Choose an explicit unknown-category policy before deployment; an all-zero vector can be ambiguous when the reference category is also dropped.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
An encoder may reject unknown values, map them to a dedicated unknown level, or ignore them by returning all zeros. Each choice has consequences. Rejection makes the problem visible but can interrupt predictions; a dedicated level preserves the distinction if the model has a sensible fallback; ignoring allows prediction but discards the new category's identity.

When one training category was dropped as a baseline, that baseline also has all-zero indicators. Ignoring unknown values then makes them indistinguishable from the baseline to the model.

### Assumptions

The production vocabulary and rate of new categories should be understood. Rare-level grouping can supply a useful fallback only if grouped examples are relevant to future unknowns.

### Common mistake

Adding a new indicator column at prediction time without retraining changes the feature contract. Keep the fitted schema stable, monitor unknown rates and update the complete training procedure when the vocabulary changes materially.
keyTakeaways: Compare rejection, explicit unknown and all-zero policies.
Identify collision with a dropped reference category.
Preserve the fitted feature schema and monitor new levels.

questions.title: Why should target encoding be cross-fitted?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the leakage created by encoding a category with its own observations' average outcome.
questions.tldrAnswer: An observation must not directly contribute its label to the encoding used to train its prediction; out-of-fold encodings reduce that leakage.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Target encoding replaces a category with a statistic of its outcomes, often a smoothed mean. For a category occurring once, an unsmoothed training encoding equals that observation's label. A downstream model can therefore appear to predict exceptionally well while learning information unavailable for a new case.

Cross-fitting divides training data into folds and computes each fold's encodings from the other folds. After model training, a mapping based on the complete training set can encode validation or deployment observations. Smoothing rare categories towards an overall mean reduces estimation noise.

### Assumptions

The folds must respect groups and time. All encoding choices, including smoothing strength, belong inside model selection. Unknown categories require a pre-defined fallback.

### Common mistake

Merely separating a final test set does not prevent leakage within the model's training features. Cross-fitting addresses self-label use; it does not guarantee useful encoding when categories change meaning or have too little independent information.
keyTakeaways: Explain the singleton-category leakage example.
Describe out-of-fold training encodings and the deployment mapping.
Combine smoothing with appropriate grouping and unknown handling.

questions.title: When can a missing-value indicator help prediction?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why a model might benefit from knowing that a value was absent even after imputation.
questions.tldrAnswer: The fact of missingness can carry information distinct from the imputed numerical value, but that information may depend on collection practices.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Imputing a missing measurement with a median makes it numerically resemble a genuinely observed median value. A separate indicator allows the model to distinguish those cases. This can help when measurement availability is related to the outcome, such as a test being ordered more often for particular patients.

The indicator does not recover the missing value. It gives the model another predictor describing the observation process. Some learners handle missingness internally, so the value of an explicit flag depends on the learner and representation.

### Assumptions

The relationship between missingness and the outcome must remain relevant at deployment. Changes in forms, sensors or clinical procedures can break it. Imputation and indicator construction must be fitted consistently within training boundaries.

### Common mistake

Predictive improvement does not establish unbiased statistical inference or solve missing-data uncertainty. A collection-practice shortcut may work locally while failing elsewhere, so evaluate across periods or sites where that process could differ.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish absent measurements from observed imputation values.
Explain missingness as information about collection.
Check deployment stability and avoid inference claims.

questions.title: What does median-and-IQR scaling protect against?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare robust scaling with mean-and-standard-deviation scaling and explain what remains unchanged.
questions.tldrAnswer: Median and interquartile range are less sensitive to extreme observations, but scaling does not remove those observations or make every model robust.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A common robust transform subtracts the training median and divides by the interquartile range. Because these summaries depend on central order statistics, a few extremely large values have less influence on the centre and scale than they have on the mean and standard deviation.

The transformed extreme values remain extreme. Their magnitude may still dominate a squared loss or distance calculation. The transform changes the reference units; it does not trim observations, cap tails or correct data errors.

### Assumptions

There must be sufficient spread in the central portion of the feature. A zero interquartile range needs special handling, and sparse data may become dense if centred.

### Common mistake

The word robust does not guarantee that the downstream estimator resists high-leverage points or distribution shift. Fit the transform on training data, inspect tail behaviour and choose the loss and model separately.
keyTakeaways: State the median and interquartile transform.
Distinguish robust summaries from removal of outliers.
Handle zero spread and downstream sensitivity.

questions.title: How does unit-length normalisation change similarity?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the connection between Euclidean distance and cosine similarity for unit vectors, including what information is lost.
questions.tldrAnswer: For unit vectors, squared Euclidean distance equals two minus twice their cosine similarity. Normalisation discards vector magnitude.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For non-zero vectors $x$ and $z$, define $u=x/\|x\|_2$ and $v=z/\|z\|_2$. Then $\|u-v\|_2^2=2-2u^\top v$. Since $u^\top v$ is cosine similarity, nearest neighbours under Euclidean distance on these unit vectors have the same ranking as largest cosine similarity.

This is useful when direction captures composition while length mostly reflects document size or activity volume. It is inappropriate when magnitude carries essential information, such as total demand or measurement intensity.

### Assumptions

The representation and feature weighting should make angles meaningful. Zero vectors have no defined direction and need a stated handling rule. Row normalisation is different from scaling each feature column.

### Common mistake

Unit length does not make all features equally important or remove irrelevant coordinates. A large set of noisy dimensions can still distort angles, and positive rescalings of individual features can change the geometry before normalisation.
keyTakeaways: Derive the unit-vector distance identity.
Distinguish row normalisation from column scaling.
Explain lost magnitude and zero-vector handling.

questions.title: What structure does k-means favour?
questions.questionMarkdown: State the k-means objective and explain why it may fail to match meaningful groups.
questions.tldrAnswer: K-means minimises within-cluster squared Euclidean distance to centroids, favouring compact groups under the chosen feature geometry.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
K-means chooses assignments and centres to minimise $\sum_i\|x_i-\mu_{c_i}\|_2^2$. For fixed assignments, each centre is the mean of its assigned observations. For fixed centres, assigning a point to its nearest centre minimises its contribution.

This objective favours compact Euclidean groups. It can divide a long curved group into several pieces or merge portions of groups with unequal spread. Large-scale features and extreme observations can dominate squared distances.

### Assumptions

The selected features and their scaling define what closeness means. The number of clusters is specified, and numeric means should be meaningful for the representation. Ordinary k-means is not naturally a model for arbitrary categorical codes.

### Common mistake

A low training inertia does not prove that clusters correspond to real classes or useful customer segments. The best achievable inertia cannot increase as more centres are allowed, although separately fitted local solutions need not follow that ordering. Assess stability, geometry and intended use instead of selecting the count solely from training fit.
keyTakeaways: State the squared-distance objective and alternating minimisers.
Explain the geometry and scaling assumptions.
Distinguish compact partitions from meaningful classes.

questions.title: Why can k-means give different results on repeated runs?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the role of initial centres and what k-means++ does and does not guarantee.
questions.tldrAnswer: Alternating assignment and centre updates can reach different local solutions; distance-aware initialisation improves starting centres without guaranteeing the global optimum.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The joint optimisation over assignments and centres is not convex. Each assignment step and centre-update step improves or preserves the objective, but the sequence can settle into a solution that depends on the initial centres.

K-means++ spreads starting centres using probabilities related to squared distance from centres already chosen. This discourages starting all centres in one dense region. Repeating the procedure with several starts and retaining the best objective can reduce the chance of a poor local result.

### Assumptions

The metric and feature scaling remain fixed across runs. Empty clusters, duplicate points and stopping tolerances need consistent implementation handling. Random seeds aid reproducibility but do not establish quality.

### Common mistake

Convergence means the chosen update scheme stopped improving, not that the best possible partition was found. Compare stability across starts and relevant data perturbations; unstable partitions may indicate weak structure rather than merely an unlucky seed.
keyTakeaways: Explain local convergence in a non-convex joint problem.
Describe distance-aware initialisation.
Distinguish reproducibility, objective quality and cluster stability.

questions.title: How does DBSCAN separate clusters from noise?
questions.questionMarkdown: Define core, border and noise points and explain a limitation when densities vary.
questions.tldrAnswer: DBSCAN connects sufficiently dense neighbourhoods; one global distance threshold can struggle when valid groups have very different densities.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A core point has enough observations within a specified neighbourhood radius, according to the minimum-sample convention. Connected core points form dense regions. A border point lies near a core region but is not itself dense enough to extend it. Points not assigned through these relationships are labelled noise.

Unlike k-means, DBSCAN does not require a chosen number of clusters and can follow non-convex shapes. Its distance threshold, however, is expressed in the feature space's units and strongly depends on scaling.

### Assumptions

Density in the chosen metric should reflect the desired grouping. A radius large enough to connect a sparse group may merge nearby dense groups; a small radius may fragment sparse groups. High-dimensional distances can make neighbourhood choices difficult.

### Common mistake

Noise labels are not proof of erroneous or fraudulent observations. They mean low density under this representation and parameter choice. Border assignments can also be ambiguous when a point neighbours more than one core region.
keyTakeaways: Define core, border and noise roles.
Explain scale and varying-density limitations.
Avoid treating a noise label as an external truth.

questions.title: What does a silhouette score compare?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain a point's silhouette value and why a high average does not establish the right clustering.
questions.tldrAnswer: It compares average distance within the assigned cluster with distance to the nearest competing cluster, under a chosen metric.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a point, let $a$ be its average distance to other points in its cluster and $b$ the smallest average distance to any other cluster. Its silhouette is $(b-a)/\max(a,b)$. Values near one indicate much closer neighbours within the assigned cluster; values near zero suggest a boundary; negative values suggest another cluster is closer on average.

Averaging gives a compactness-and-separation summary, not a measure of agreement with an external purpose. The chosen distance and representation directly affect it.

### Assumptions

The calculation needs a valid number of cluster labels, ordinarily at least two and fewer than the number of observations. Singleton clusters require a convention, commonly zero silhouette.

### Common mistake

A high score can favour separated, roughly convex groups over a meaningful curved or variable-density structure. Use it alongside stability, domain checks and downstream usefulness, and report how noise points from density clustering were handled.
keyTakeaways: Define within-cluster and nearest-other-cluster distances.
Interpret positive, zero and negative values.
State metric, singleton and shape limitations.

questions.title: How does linkage change hierarchical clustering?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare single, complete and average linkage and explain the chaining effect.
questions.tldrAnswer: Linkage defines the distance between groups: nearest pair, farthest pair or average pair distance, respectively.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Agglomerative clustering begins with separate observations and repeatedly merges the closest groups. Single linkage uses the smallest cross-group distance, so one nearby pair can join otherwise distant sets. A sequence of intermediate observations can therefore form a long chain.

Complete linkage uses the largest cross-group distance and favours bounded diameters. Average linkage uses the mean cross-group distance, balancing many pairwise relationships rather than one extreme pair. These definitions can produce different merge sequences on the same observations.

### Assumptions

The point-level distance and feature scaling are fixed and meaningful. Tie handling can affect results, and large datasets can make the distance calculations expensive.

### Common mistake

A dendrogram does not reveal one objectively correct number of groups. Cutting at a height or cluster count is an additional decision, and its interpretation depends on linkage. Do not read merge heights from different linkage methods as interchangeable measures of substantive similarity.
keyTakeaways: Define the three cross-group distances.
Explain single-linkage chaining.
Treat dendrogram cutting as a separate modelling choice.

questions.title: How does EM fit a Gaussian mixture?
questions.questionMarkdown: Describe the expectation and maximisation steps and explain two reasons the fitted solution can be problematic.
questions.tldrAnswer: EM alternates soft component responsibilities with weighted parameter updates, but can reach local optima or near-singular components.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
In the expectation step, the current mixture weights, means and covariances determine each observation's posterior responsibility for every component. In the maximisation step, these responsibilities become weights for updating the component proportions, means and covariance matrices.

For exact steps, the observed-data likelihood does not decrease. That property does not imply convergence to the global maximum. Different initialisations can lead to different component arrangements.

### Assumptions

The mixture's covariance structure and component count should be appropriate for the data. Unconstrained Gaussian-mixture likelihood can become unbounded when a component collapses around an observation, so covariance regularisation or constraints are important.

### Common mistake

Soft responsibilities are model-based probabilities, not verified membership in real categories. Components can overlap or divide one substantive group to approximate a non-Gaussian shape. Inspect fit, numerical warnings and stability rather than interpreting every fitted component as a distinct population.
keyTakeaways: Describe responsibilities and weighted parameter updates.
Distinguish non-decreasing likelihood from global optimisation.
Explain covariance collapse and limits of component interpretation.

questions.title: Why can cluster-count criteria disagree?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare inertia, silhouette, mixture-model criteria and downstream usefulness when selecting the number of groups.
questions.tldrAnswer: Each criterion answers a different question about fit, geometry, complexity or use, so there need not be one universally correct count.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The best achievable k-means inertia cannot increase as more centres are allowed, so an elbow is a judgement about diminishing returns. Separately fitted local solutions can depart from that ordering. Silhouette balances within-group compactness against separation under a chosen distance. For a probabilistic mixture, information criteria such as BIC trade likelihood against parameter count under their modelling assumptions.

A downstream task may prefer a smaller set of stable, interpretable segments even when a geometric or likelihood criterion favours more groups.

### Assumptions

Compare criteria within appropriate model families and representations. A BIC comparison depends on the fitted likelihood and parameterisation, while a silhouette comparison depends on distance and assignments.

### Common mistake

Trying many representations and reporting only the count with the most appealing plot hides uncertainty. Examine stability under data perturbations and whether groups support the intended decisions. If the data form a continuum, forcing discrete categories may be less useful than retaining continuous scores.
keyTakeaways: Explain the distinct objectives of common criteria.
Check stability and intended downstream use.
Allow that useful discrete groups may not exist.

questions.title: Why can many weak features harm nearest neighbours?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how irrelevant dimensions can change nearest-neighbour decisions even after standardisation.
questions.tldrAnswer: Noisy coordinates add distance variation unrelated to the target and can make local neighbourhoods less informative; standardisation does not remove that noise.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Nearest-neighbour methods rely on nearby observations having useful outcome similarity. When many irrelevant coordinates are added, distance increasingly reflects those coordinates rather than the few meaningful ones. Under some high-dimensional distributions, nearest and farthest distances also become relatively similar, weakening the contrast that neighbourhood methods exploit.

Standardisation prevents one coordinate's units from dominating, but equalising the scale of many irrelevant features can still leave them collectively dominant. Feature selection, a justified metric or dimensionality reduction may help.

### Assumptions

Distance concentration is distribution-dependent, not an inevitable consequence of any large column count. Data can lie near a lower-dimensional structure, and correlated features change the effective geometry.

### Common mistake

Reducing dimension is not automatically safe either: an unsupervised projection can discard a low-variance predictive direction. Evaluate the entire representation and neighbour-selection procedure on held-out data, including preprocessing within the training boundary.
keyTakeaways: Explain accumulation of irrelevant-coordinate distance.
Qualify concentration by the data distribution.
Evaluate feature reduction without assuming it preserves target information.
