questions.title: Why do neural networks need nonlinear activations?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain what happens when several affine layers are composed without any intervening nonlinearity. Compare sigmoid, tanh and ReLU as hidden activations.
questions.tldrAnswer: Their composition is still one affine map, so depth alone does not create a nonlinear input-output relationship.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For two affine layers, $h=W_1x+b_1$ and $y=W_2h+b_2$, substitution gives $y=(W_2W_1)x+(W_2b_1+b_2)$. Repeating this argument collapses any such stack into a single affine map.

A nonlinear activation between layers prevents that algebraic collapse. The network can then construct features whose effects depend on the input region, allowing curved boundaries and interactions that one affine map cannot represent.

### Assumptions

The argument concerns the function represented, not the optimisation path. Factoring a linear map across layers can still affect optimisation and implicit constraints. Restricted intermediate widths can also impose a rank limit.

### Common mistake

Adding a nonlinear activation is not a guarantee that training finds the desired function or generalises. Activation choice affects gradients, saturation and representation. A nonlinear output alone still leaves the preceding stack equivalent to one affine score transformation.

### Comparing three activations

Sigmoid maps to $(0,1)$ and tanh to $(-1,1)$; both saturate for sufficiently large-magnitude inputs, giving small derivatives. Tanh is zero-centred, but this does not prevent saturation. ReLU is $\max(0,x)$: its derivative is one on the positive side and zero on the negative side, with an implementation-defined subgradient at zero. ReLU can leave a unit inactive if its inputs remain negative. These trade-offs affect hidden-layer optimisation; sigmoid remains useful for a binary-probability output and softmax for mutually exclusive classes.
keyTakeaways: Collapse a two-layer affine composition algebraically.
Explain how intermediate nonlinearity changes the function class.
Distinguish representation from optimisation and generalisation.
Compare sigmoid, tanh and ReLU ranges, saturation and inactive-unit behaviour.

questions.title: What does backpropagation compute?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how reverse-mode differentiation computes parameter gradients and distinguish it from the optimiser.
questions.tldrAnswer: Backpropagation applies the chain rule backwards through the computation graph; an optimiser then uses those derivatives to update parameters.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A network's loss depends on intermediate values, which depend on earlier values and parameters. Backpropagation starts with the loss derivative and propagates sensitivities backwards. At each operation, it combines the incoming derivative with that operation's local derivative and accumulates contributions when a value affects the loss through several paths.

This reuses intermediate computations efficiently when a scalar loss depends on many parameters. The resulting gradients describe how small parameter changes affect the current loss locally.

### Assumptions

Operations need derivatives or a defined treatment at non-differentiable points. Stored activations, recomputation and numerical precision affect practical memory and accuracy. Loss reductions and batch scaling also change gradient magnitude.

### Common mistake

Backpropagation is not gradient descent itself and does not choose a learning rate. The optimiser performs updates using the computed gradients. Correct derivatives do not guarantee a global optimum, good conditioning or useful predictions on new data.
keyTakeaways: Describe reverse chain-rule propagation and path accumulation.
Separate gradient computation from parameter updates.
State local-derivative and numerical limitations.

questions.title: Why can gradients vanish or explode in deep networks?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the role of repeated Jacobian products and why gradient clipping is only a partial remedy.
questions.tldrAnswer: Backpropagated derivatives multiply local transformations; repeated contraction can erase a signal while repeated amplification can make it unstable.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A gradient reaching an early layer passes through products of later-layer Jacobians. If relevant directions are repeatedly contracted, the early gradient can become too small to support learning. If they are amplified, its magnitude can grow rapidly and destabilise updates.

Activation derivatives, weight scales and alignment of directions all matter. Saturating activations can strongly contract derivatives; poor initialisation can amplify them. Residual connections, suitable initialisation and normalisation can improve propagation, but no one intervention guarantees stable training.

### Assumptions

A bound based on the product of Jacobian norms describes possible growth, not the exact gradient along every input and direction. The loss, sequence length and data also affect the observed behaviour.

### Common mistake

Clipping limits large update gradients but does not restore information already lost through vanishing derivatives. It can also change the update direction or magnitude. Monitor layer-wise gradients and diagnose the source rather than treating clipping as a complete solution.
keyTakeaways: Connect gradient propagation to Jacobian products.
Explain both contraction and amplification.
Identify clipping's inability to recover vanished information.

questions.title: Why is dropout usually disabled during evaluation?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain inverted dropout and why leaving it active changes ordinary prediction behaviour.
questions.tldrAnswer: Inverted dropout randomly removes activations and rescales survivors during training; ordinary evaluation uses all activations without that randomness.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
With keep probability $q$, inverted dropout replaces activation $h$ by $mh/q$, where $m$ is a Bernoulli variable with mean $q$. Conditional on $h$, the dropped activation has expectation $h$. Training therefore exposes later layers to randomly perturbed representations while preserving this local expected scale.

During ordinary evaluation, the mask is removed and no extra scaling is needed under this convention. Another convention rescales at evaluation instead, so implementation details must match.

### Assumptions

The expectation identity applies to the local activation, not to the entire nonlinear network's output. Dropout rate and placement are modelling choices that require validation.

### Common mistake

The evaluation network is not generally the exact average prediction of every possible masked network. Keeping dropout active intentionally can produce stochastic uncertainty estimates in a specific procedure, but that is different from forgetting to switch to evaluation mode and does not automatically yield calibrated uncertainty.
keyTakeaways: Derive the local expectation under inverted dropout.
State the normal training and evaluation behaviour.
Distinguish local scaling from exact model averaging.

questions.title: Why does batch normalisation behave differently at inference?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain minibatch statistics, running estimates and a failure mode with small batches.
questions.tldrAnswer: Training commonly normalises using current-batch statistics, while evaluation uses accumulated estimates so one prediction does not depend on the other cases in its batch.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Batch normalisation centres an activation using an estimated mean and scales it by an estimated standard deviation with a small numerical stabiliser. Learned scale and shift parameters allow the model to adjust the transformed values.

During training, statistics are usually computed from the current minibatch and running estimates are updated. At evaluation, those running estimates are used instead. Otherwise the prediction for one observation could change when unrelated observations are placed beside it in a batch.

### Assumptions

The running statistics should represent the activations encountered at inference. Small batches can make training estimates noisy, and a shift in deployment data can make stored statistics inappropriate. The dimensions over which statistics are computed depend on the layer implementation.

### Common mistake

Leaving a model in training mode during evaluation changes both normalisation and, often, dropout. Also, improved optimisation from batch normalisation should not be attributed solely to one claimed mechanism; its effects extend beyond the original internal-distribution-shift explanation.

questions.title: How can stopping early act as regularisation?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how validation-based early stopping selects a training duration and how to evaluate that choice honestly.
questions.tldrAnswer: Stopping limits how far the optimiser fits the training sample, while the validation rule makes training duration another selected model setting.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Training loss can continue falling after performance on new data stops improving. Early stopping monitors a chosen validation metric and retains a checkpoint according to a pre-defined rule, such as the best score with a patience period before termination.

Restricting the number of updates can limit fitting to noise, so stopping time can act as a form of regularisation. The effect depends on the optimisation path, learning rate and model; it is not equivalent to one universal penalty.

### Assumptions

The validation set represents the intended use and is not used for fitting gradients. The metric, improvement tolerance, patience and checkpoint restoration behaviour should be specified. Noisy validation curves can select an unstable stopping time.

### Common mistake

Repeatedly choosing the best test checkpoint turns the test set into validation. Report final performance on separate data or an outer evaluation loop, and make clear whether the selected checkpoint or the final training checkpoint is deployed.

questions.title: How does momentum differ from a larger learning rate?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why accumulated gradients can speed movement in one direction while reducing oscillation in another.
questions.tldrAnswer: Momentum carries a decaying history of gradients, so the update depends on previous directions rather than only the current gradient.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
One convention uses $v_t=\mu v_{t-1}+g_t$ and $\theta_{t+1}=\theta_t-\eta v_t$, with $0\leq\mu<1$. Consistent gradient directions accumulate in the velocity. Alternating directions can partly cancel.

In a narrow curved valley, this can damp oscillation across the steep direction while maintaining progress along a direction with persistent gradients. A larger fixed learning rate multiplies only the current gradient and does not contain this directional memory.

### Assumptions

Other implementations include a factor of $1-\mu$ or use Nesterov look-ahead, so numerical settings are not interchangeable without checking the convention. Momentum and learning rate interact.

### Common mistake

Momentum is not guaranteed to improve every objective or schedule. A large stored velocity can overshoot when curvature or gradient direction changes. Inspect convergence and tune the update rule rather than interpreting momentum as a universally safe acceleration.
keyTakeaways: Describe the velocity recurrence.
Explain accumulation and cancellation across directions.

questions.title: Why does Adam divide its moving moments by correction factors?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the zero-initialisation bias in Adam's moment estimates and the role of the second moment.
questions.tldrAnswer: Moving averages initialised at zero are initially biased towards zero; the correction removes that initialisation effect under the simple stationary argument.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Adam maintains $m_t=\beta_1m_{t-1}+(1-\beta_1)g_t$ and $v_t=\beta_2v_{t-1}+(1-\beta_2)g_t^2$, with elementwise squares and zero initial values. If gradient moments are stationary, their expectations are multiplied by $1-\beta_1^t$ and $1-\beta_2^t$.

The corrected estimates divide by these factors. Updates then use the corrected first moment divided by the square root of the corrected second moment plus a stabilising term. The second moment is an uncentred squared-gradient average, not the variance after subtracting a mean.

### Assumptions

The stationary calculation explains initialisation bias; actual training gradients change with parameters and data. Hyperparameters and the placement of the numerical stabiliser affect the implemented update.

### Common mistake

Bias correction does not make gradients unbiased estimators of a global optimum or guarantee convergence and generalisation. It addresses a particular moving-average initialisation issue, while adaptive coordinate scaling introduces separate optimisation behaviour.
keyTakeaways: Write both moving-moment recurrences.
Derive the zero-initialisation correction factors.
Distinguish an uncentred second moment from variance and convergence guarantees.

questions.title: Why is L2 regularisation not generally Adam weight decay?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how adding a squared-parameter penalty differs from directly shrinking parameters under an adaptive optimiser.
questions.tldrAnswer: An L2 penalty enters the gradient and is transformed by adaptive scaling; decoupled decay shrinks weights separately from that transformation.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Adding $\lambda\|\theta\|^2/2$ to the loss adds $\lambda\theta$ to its gradient. With ordinary SGD, the update becomes $(1-\eta\lambda)\theta-\eta g$, which is direct weight shrinkage with matching scaling.

In Adam, the penalty contribution also enters moving moments and coordinate-wise normalisation. Its effect therefore depends on gradient history and varies across coordinates. AdamW applies decay separately from the adaptive gradient update, avoiding that coupling.

### Assumptions

The numerical meaning of the decay coefficient depends on learning rate and implementation conventions. Biases and normalisation parameters are often excluded from decay by deliberate parameter-group choices.

### Common mistake

Switching an optimiser name while keeping every coefficient unchanged does not preserve an equivalent regularisation strength. Tune the decay and schedule together. Decoupling does not prove that all parameters should shrink or that the resulting model will generalise better on every task.
keyTakeaways: Derive the SGD equivalence with matched scaling.
Explain how adaptive moments break that equivalence.
State parameter-group and coefficient conventions.

questions.title: What does convolutional weight sharing buy?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how a shared image filter reduces parameter count and distinguish translation equivariance from invariance.
questions.tldrAnswer: One filter is reused across spatial locations, reducing separate parameters and making feature responses move with the input under suitable boundary conditions.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A convolutional layer applies the same learned local kernel at many positions. For a kernel of height $h$, width $w$, $c_{\mathrm{in}}$ input channels and $c_{\mathrm{out}}$ output channels, the weight count is $hwc_{\mathrm{in}}c_{\mathrm{out}}$, plus optional biases, rather than a separate set for every image position.

Reusing a detector means a translated local pattern can produce a translated feature response. This is equivariance: the output changes in a corresponding way. Invariance would mean the output stays unchanged, often an aim of later pooling or aggregation.

### Assumptions

Exact translation behaviour is qualified by padding, image boundaries, stride and sampling. Weight sharing is useful when similar local patterns can occur across locations.

### Common mistake

Convolution alone does not make a whole classifier invariant to arbitrary translations, rotations or scale changes. Nor does local sharing guarantee that every task should ignore position; some applications require explicit location information.
keyTakeaways: Calculate shared-kernel parameter count.
Distinguish equivariance from invariance.
State boundary, stride and task-location qualifications.

questions.title: What information does a recurrent hidden state contain?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how a recurrent network processes a sequence and why its state is not a complete record of the past.
questions.tldrAnswer: The state is a learned, fixed-size summary updated at each step; it can retain useful past information without preserving every detail.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A simple recurrent network updates $h_t=\phi(W_xx_t+W_hh_{t-1}+b)$. The same parameters are reused across time, so the new state combines the current input with a transformed previous summary. An output can depend on each state or only on the final state.

Training unfolds this computation over time and propagates gradients through the repeated transitions. Long sequences can make useful long-range credit assignment difficult. Gated variants change the update mechanism to help control what is retained or forgotten.

### Assumptions

Sequence order and reset boundaries must be correct. Carrying state between unrelated examples accidentally mixes their information. Truncating gradient propagation changes which dependencies training can directly reinforce.

### Common mistake

A hidden vector is not an exact history buffer. Its finite representation may discard relevant details. It also differs from an attention key-value cache, which ordinarily retains separate representations for many earlier positions rather than only one recurrent summary.
keyTakeaways: Explain the shared recurrent update.
Identify state-reset and truncated-training boundaries.
Distinguish a compressed summary from an attention cache.

questions.title: Which independence assumption does naive Bayes make?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the factorisation used for classification and why features can still be correlated overall.
questions.tldrAnswer: Features are assumed independent conditional on the class, not necessarily independent across the whole population.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Bayes' rule gives a class posterior proportional to the prior times the feature likelihood. Naive Bayes approximates the latter by $\Pr(x\mid y)=\prod_j\Pr(x_j\mid y)$. Classification compares these products multiplied by the class priors, usually using logarithms for numerical stability.

Two features may be marginally correlated because both vary across classes, even if they are independent within each class. The assumption therefore concerns a conditional relationship.

### Assumptions

The feature-likelihood family must suit the representation, such as counts or continuous measurements. Smoothing is important when estimated zero probabilities would erase an entire class likelihood.

### Common mistake

Useful classification does not prove that the independence assumption is true. Correlated evidence can be effectively counted more than once, producing overconfident posterior estimates even when the winning class is often correct. Assess calibration separately if probabilities drive decisions.
keyTakeaways: Write the class-conditional factorisation.
Distinguish conditional from marginal independence.
Discuss smoothing and overconfident probabilities.

questions.title: How does neighbour count change a nearest-neighbour model?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare a one-neighbour rule with a much larger neighbourhood for classification or regression.
questions.tldrAnswer: Small neighbourhoods follow local detail and noise; larger ones smooth more strongly and can blur meaningful boundaries.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A one-neighbour classifier copies the label of the closest training observation, so an isolated mislabelled example can determine a region's prediction. A larger neighbourhood combines more examples, reducing the influence of one observation but potentially including cases from the other side of a genuine boundary.

For regression, averaging more neighbours similarly trades local responsiveness against smoothing. Distance weighting changes the trade-off by giving nearby observations more influence within the selected set.

### Assumptions

The metric and feature representation should make nearby cases informative. Scale, irrelevant dimensions, training density and tie handling affect results. The same neighbour count can represent very different physical neighbourhood sizes in sparse and dense regions.

### Common mistake

Calling nearest neighbours training-free hides computation and storage. Index construction, retaining examples and prediction-time search can be costly. Select neighbour count and preprocessing within validation rather than using training accuracy, which is particularly misleading at one neighbour.
keyTakeaways: Explain local sensitivity versus smoothing.
Account for metric, scale and density.
Separate simple fitting from storage and search costs.

questions.title: Why can correlated features hide permutation importance?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain what held-out permutation importance measures and why two substitute predictors may each look unimportant.
questions.tldrAnswer: It measures a fitted model's score change after disrupting one feature; another correlated feature may preserve the information that was removed.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Permutation importance shuffles one feature across evaluation observations and measures the change in a chosen score. The model is held fixed, so the result describes its reliance on that feature under this perturbation, not the best achievable performance after retraining without it.

If another feature contains similar information, the fitted model may continue predicting well, yielding a small score drop. Conversely, shuffling can create combinations that never occur naturally and exaggerate a feature's apparent importance.

### Assumptions

The evaluation set and score should match the intended task. Repeated shuffles measure perturbation variability, and a poorly performing model may have importances that are not substantively useful.

### Common mistake

A small value does not establish that the underlying concept is irrelevant or causally ineffective. Grouped permutations or conditional approaches can answer different questions, but require their own justified grouping or conditional-distribution assumptions.
keyTakeaways: Define the fixed-model score perturbation.
Explain substitution by correlated predictors.
Distinguish reliance, retraining value and causal effect.

questions.title: What coverage does split conformal prediction guarantee?
questions.questionMarkdown: Describe residual-based split conformal regression and distinguish marginal coverage from person-specific coverage.
questions.tldrAnswer: Under exchangeability, a properly chosen calibration quantile gives finite-sample marginal coverage over new cases, not a guarantee for every feature value.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Fit a regression model on a training subset, then compute absolute residuals on a separate calibration subset of size $n$. For error level $\alpha$, use the residual order statistic at rank $\lceil(n+1)(1-\alpha)\rceil$ as radius $q$, with an infinite radius if that rank exceeds $n$. Predict the interval $[\hat f(x)-q,\hat f(x)+q]$.

Exchangeability makes the new residual's rank comparable to calibration ranks, giving coverage at least $1-\alpha$ under the usual construction. The fitted regression model need not be correctly specified.

### Assumptions

Training must remain separate from calibration, and calibration cases and the new case must be exchangeable. Distribution shift can break this argument.

### Common mistake

Marginal coverage averages over the new-case distribution. It does not promise the same coverage for each person, subgroup or feature value. A procedure can meet its overall guarantee while giving wide intervals or weak coverage in particular regions.
keyTakeaways: Describe training/calibration separation and the corrected quantile rank.
State exchangeability and finite-sample marginal coverage.
Distinguish marginal from conditional or subgroup guarantees.

questions.title: When can unlabelled observations help classification?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the structural assumption behind using unlabelled data and a situation where it could hurt.
questions.tldrAnswer: Unlabelled data help only when their geometry or distribution is related to the class boundary; extra features alone do not reveal labels.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Unlabelled observations reveal where inputs are common, sparse or connected. A semi-supervised method can use this structure if nearby points or points in the same high-density region are likely to share a label. This favours boundaries through low-density regions rather than through dense groups.

Graph-based label propagation spreads information along neighbourhood connections. Self-training instead assigns provisional labels using the current classifier and retrains, relying on its confident predictions being sufficiently reliable.

### Assumptions

The unlabelled population should be relevant to the labelled task, and the structural assumption must align with the outcome. A dense group can contain several classes, or unlabelled observations may come from a different distribution.

### Common mistake

More unlabelled data are not guaranteed to improve performance. Incorrect provisional labels can reinforce errors, and a misleading graph can spread them. Keep a representative labelled evaluation set and compare against a supervised baseline before claiming a benefit.
keyTakeaways: Explain how feature geometry can relate to labels.
Distinguish label propagation from self-training.
Identify distribution mismatch and error reinforcement risks.

questions.title: Why can reversing a conditional probability be wrong?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the difference between the probability of an alarm given a fault and the probability of a fault given an alarm.
questions.tldrAnswer: The conditioning event defines the reference population, so reversing it changes the denominator and generally the result.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Conditional probability is $\Pr(A\mid B)=\Pr(A\cap B)/\Pr(B)$ when $\Pr(B)>0$. Reversing the condition keeps the intersection but replaces the denominator with $\Pr(A)$. The two quantities are equal only in particular cases, not by symmetry of the intersection.

For an alarm system, sensitivity asks what fraction of faulty units trigger an alarm. The reverse question asks what fraction of alarmed units are faulty. The latter also depends on how common faults are and how often healthy units trigger alarms.

### Assumptions

Both conditions must have positive probability, and all probabilities must refer to the same population and measurement process.

### Common mistake

A phrase such as “the alarm is 99% accurate” does not specify which probability is meant. Write the event and conditioning event explicitly before calculating or interpreting a percentage.
keyTakeaways: Define the conditional denominator.
Distinguish the two reference populations.
Require explicit event definitions instead of vague accuracy claims.

questions.title: How can a sensitive alarm mostly detect healthy units?
questions.questionMarkdown: A fault affects one in 1,000 units. An alarm has 99% sensitivity and 99% specificity. Estimate the probability of a fault after an alarm.
questions.tldrAnswer: The posterior fault probability is about 9%; the large healthy population creates roughly ten false alarms for every true alarm.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Among 100,000 units, expect 100 faults and 99,900 healthy units. Sensitivity 0.99 gives 99 true alarms. A false-positive rate of 0.01 gives 999 false alarms. Thus the fault probability among alarmed units is $99/(99+999)\approx0.0902$.

The same calculation in odds form multiplies prior odds $1/999$ by the positive likelihood ratio $0.99/0.01=99$. Posterior odds are $99/999$, which convert to the same probability. Strong evidence can increase a very small prior probability substantially while leaving it below one half.

### Assumptions

The stated sensitivity and specificity apply to this population, and fault prevalence is known or estimated adequately.

### Common mistake

The result does not mean the alarm is useless. Its value depends on follow-up costs and missed faults. Repeated alarms also cannot be multiplied as independent evidence unless their conditional dependence is addressed.
keyTakeaways: Compute expected true and false alarm counts.
Connect likelihood ratio, prior odds and posterior odds.
Distinguish posterior probability from the decision value of testing.

questions.title: How do independent and mutually exclusive events differ?
questions.questionMarkdown: Can two events with positive probability be both independent and disjoint? Explain using the probability rules.
questions.tldrAnswer: No. Disjoint events have zero intersection probability, whereas independence would require the product of their positive probabilities.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Disjoint events cannot occur together, so $\Pr(A\cap B)=0$. Independent events satisfy $\Pr(A\cap B)=\Pr(A)\Pr(B)$: learning that one occurred does not change the probability of the other.

If both probabilities are positive, their product is positive, contradicting the zero intersection required by disjointness. For example, rolling a one and rolling a two on the same die are disjoint, but observing a one makes a two impossible and therefore changes its probability.

### Assumptions

The events belong to the same probability experiment. A probability-zero event is a special case that can satisfy both definitions, while elementary conditional probabilities given that event are undefined.

### Common mistake

“Unrelated possibilities” is not a mathematical definition of independence. Outcomes from separate trials may be independent under a model, but outcomes competing within one trial are often mutually exclusive instead.
keyTakeaways: State the intersection rules for both concepts.
Show the positive-probability contradiction.
Handle zero-probability conditioning carefully.

questions.title: How do you combine rates across population groups?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the law of total probability and why averaging subgroup rates equally can be wrong.
questions.tldrAnswer: Weight each conditional rate by the population probability of its group, using an exhaustive and disjoint partition.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If $B_1,\ldots,B_k$ partition the population, then $\Pr(A)=\sum_j\Pr(A\mid B_j)\Pr(B_j)$. Every outcome belongs to exactly one group, so the weighted contributions cover the event without omissions or double counting.

Suppose 20% of deliveries use one route with a 10% delay rate, while 80% use another with a 2% delay rate. Overall delay probability is $0.2(0.10)+0.8(0.02)=0.036$, not the unweighted 6% average.

### Assumptions

The groups are mutually exclusive and exhaustive, their weights sum to one, and conditional rates refer to the same period and population. Zero-weight groups contribute nothing.

### Common mistake

Weights from a convenience sample may not describe the target population. Changing the group mix changes the aggregate rate even if every within-group rate stays fixed, so compare composition as well as subgroup performance.
keyTakeaways: State the partition and weighted-sum formula.
Calculate the population-weighted rate.
Check whether sample weights represent the target population.

questions.title: Why can expected values add without independence?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the expected value of a sum of dependent random variables and contrast a product.
questions.tldrAnswer: Expectation distributes over finite sums when the relevant expectations exist; multiplying expectations generally requires additional conditions.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For integrable random variables, $\mathbb{E}[X+Y]=\mathbb{E}[X]+\mathbb{E}[Y]$ whether or not they are independent. Integration is linear, so dependence does not alter this identity.

If a project total is the sum of costs from several activities, its expected total equals the sum of expected activity costs even when overruns occur together. Dependence matters for the uncertainty of that total, not this mean calculation.

### Assumptions

Finite absolute expectations avoid undefined combinations such as infinity minus infinity. Infinite sums require additional conditions before expectation and summation can be interchanged.

### Common mistake

The same rule does not extend to products: $\mathbb{E}[XY]$ need not equal $\mathbb{E}[X]\mathbb{E}[Y]$. Independence with suitable integrability is sufficient for that factorisation. Similarly, expected ratios and nonlinear transformations are not generally obtained by substituting expected values.
keyTakeaways: State linearity without an independence requirement.
Distinguish total expectation from total variance.
Avoid extending the rule to products or nonlinear functions.

questions.title: How does covariance affect the uncertainty of a total?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the variance of two dependent quantities and explain why common shocks matter.
questions.tldrAnswer: The variance includes twice their covariance, so shared fluctuations can make a total more variable than separate variances suggest.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Expanding the squared centred sum gives $\operatorname{Var}(X+Y)=\operatorname{Var}(X)+\operatorname{Var}(Y)+2\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)$. For many terms, add twice every distinct pairwise covariance.

Positive covariance means the quantities tend to move above or below their means together. Common weather or demand shocks can therefore increase the uncertainty of a total. Negative covariance can reduce it, as one component partly offsets another.

### Assumptions

The variables have finite second moments and covariance describes the same joint experiment. Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence.

### Common mistake

Adding standard deviations is not the general rule either. For independent equal-variance terms, variances add and the standard deviation grows with the square root of count. For perfectly positively correlated scaled terms, very different behaviour follows. Estimate dependence at the level relevant to the decision.
keyTakeaways: Expand the variance including covariance.
Explain positive and negative dependence effects.
Distinguish adding variances from adding standard deviations.

questions.title: How do conditional averages recover an overall average?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the law of iterated expectation and why group means require population weights.
questions.tldrAnswer: Averaging conditional means over the distribution of the conditioning variable gives the marginal mean.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The tower property states $\mathbb{E}[\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]]=\mathbb{E}[Y]$ for an integrable outcome. Within each value or group of $X$, first average $Y$. Then average those conditional means using how frequently each value of $X$ occurs.

If small stores represent 80% of stores with mean sales 10, while large stores represent 20% with mean sales 50, average sales per store are $0.8(10)+0.2(50)=18$. The unweighted average of group means, 30, answers a different weighting question.

### Assumptions

The target unit and its distribution must be explicit. Average sales per store differ from average sales experienced by a randomly selected customer, who is more likely to visit larger stores.

### Common mistake

Averaging estimated subgroup means does not remove selection bias in those estimates. The identity concerns the true joint distribution; sampling and missingness still determine whether the empirical calculation estimates it.
keyTakeaways: State the tower property.
Use the conditioning-variable distribution as weights.
Distinguish different target units and sampling bias.

questions.title: How does total variance split into within-group and between-group parts?
questions.questionMarkdown: State and interpret the law of total variance for an outcome grouped by X.
questions.tldrAnswer: Overall variance equals average conditional variance plus the variance of conditional means.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For finite second moments,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(Y)=
\mathbb{E}[\operatorname{Var}(Y\mid X)]
+\operatorname{Var}(\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]).
$$

Write $Y-\mathbb{E}Y$ as the sum of $Y-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]$ and $\mathbb{E}[Y\mid X]-\mathbb{E}Y$. Their cross-product has expectation zero because the first component has conditional mean zero.

The first term describes remaining variation within groups. The second describes differences between group means. Both are non-negative, and the within-group term uses population group weights.

### Assumptions

This is a descriptive probability identity, requiring no causal interpretation of $X$. Conditional distributions must refer to the same population.

### Common mistake

A large between-group term does not prove that intervening on the grouping variable would change outcomes. It can reflect selection or confounding. Nor should subgroup standard deviations be averaged and squared as a substitute for the expected conditional variance.
keyTakeaways: State and derive the zero cross-term decomposition.
Interpret both non-negative components.
Use appropriate weights without inferring causality.

questions.title: Can two variables be dependent with zero correlation?
questions.questionMarkdown: Construct an example and identify a special distributional case where zero correlation does imply independence.
questions.tldrAnswer: Yes. A symmetric variable and its square can be dependent but uncorrelated; jointly Gaussian variables are a special exception.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let $X$ be uniform on $[-1,1]$ and set $Y=X^2$. Then $\mathbb{E}X=0$ and $\mathbb{E}[XY]=\mathbb{E}[X^3]=0$ by symmetry, so $\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=0$. Both variances are positive, giving zero Pearson correlation.

Nevertheless $Y$ is determined exactly by $X$, so the variables are strongly dependent. A scatterplot shows a curved relationship that a linear association measure misses.

### Assumptions

Covariance and correlation require suitable finite moments, with non-zero variances for correlation. For a jointly Gaussian pair, zero covariance does imply independence, but normal marginal distributions alone are not enough to establish joint Gaussianity.

### Common mistake

A non-significant correlation test does not prove either zero population correlation or independence. Inspect possible nonlinear relationships and use a dependence assessment appropriate to the question rather than treating one linear summary as complete.
keyTakeaways: Calculate the symmetric-variable counterexample.
Distinguish linear association from dependence.
State the jointly Gaussian qualification accurately.

questions.title: How do you obtain a marginal distribution from a joint distribution?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain marginalisation and what information is lost when only marginals are retained.
questions.tldrAnswer: Sum or integrate over the other variable; the remaining marginal does not preserve the dependence structure.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For discrete variables, $\Pr(X=x)=\sum_y\Pr(X=x,Y=y)$. For a joint density, $f_X(x)=\int f_{X,Y}(x,y)\,dy$ over the other variable's support. This totals every way the second variable can accompany the chosen first-variable value.

Marginals describe each variable separately. Many different joint distributions can share the same marginals while having very different dependence. For example, two fair binary variables can be independent or always equal, yet each remains marginally fair.

### Assumptions

The sum or integral must cover the correct support, which may depend on the retained variable. A joint distribution must be non-negative and normalised.

### Common mistake

Multiplying marginals reconstructs the joint distribution only under independence. Conditioning is also different from marginalising: conditioning restricts to a given value or event and renormalises, while marginalisation aggregates over possibilities.
keyTakeaways: Write discrete and continuous marginalisation.
Explain why marginals do not determine dependence.
Distinguish marginalisation, conditioning and independence factorisation.

questions.title: How can a probability density exceed one?
questions.questionMarkdown: Use a continuous uniform distribution to distinguish density height from event probability.
questions.tldrAnswer: Density has probability per unit of the outcome scale; only its integral over a region is a probability.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A uniform variable on $[0,0.2]$ has density 5 on that interval. Its total probability is the area $5(0.2)=1$. A density height greater than one is therefore valid; the interval width supplies the remaining units.

For a continuous distribution, the probability of one exact point is zero, while a non-zero-width interval can have positive probability. Under a change of measurement units, density heights change so that the corresponding integrated probabilities remain consistent.

### Assumptions

These statements concern an absolutely continuous distribution. A mixed distribution may include both point masses and a continuous density, which must be represented separately.

Reading $f(x)$ as $\Pr(X=x)$ confuses density with mass. Similarly, comparing density heights across different unit systems without accounting for their widths can create meaningless probability claims. Integrate over the event of interest and check normalisation.

questions.title: How do you define a quantile when the distribution has jumps?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain a generalised-inverse quantile and why discrete distributions require care.
questions.tldrAnswer: A conventional quantile is the smallest value whose cumulative probability reaches the requested level; probability jumps prevent ordinary inversion.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The cumulative distribution function is $F(x)=\Pr(X\leq x)$. One quantile convention is $Q(p)=\inf\{x:F(x)\geq p\}$ for $0<p<1$. This works when the CDF has jumps or flat stretches, where a unique ordinary inverse does not exist.

For a binary variable with probability 0.8 at zero and 0.2 at one, this convention gives zero for probabilities through 0.8 and one above that. There is no observed intermediate outcome even though software may interpolate sample quantiles differently.

### Assumptions

State the population or sample convention being used. A median more generally satisfies the required half-probability inequalities and need not be unique; the generalised inverse selects one conventional value.

### Common mistake

Different sample quantile algorithms can disagree on small datasets without either being an arithmetic error. Report the convention when exact thresholds affect decisions, especially with discrete outcomes or ties.

questions.title: Why is binary variance largest at probability one half?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive Bernoulli variance and distinguish it from the variance of a sample proportion.
questions.tldrAnswer: A Bernoulli variable has variance p times one minus p; an average of n independent such variables has that variance divided by n.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For $X\in\{0,1\}$ with success probability $p$, $\mathbb{E}X=p$ and $X^2=X$. Thus $\operatorname{Var}(X)=p-p^2=p(1-p)$. Rewriting it as $1/4-(p-1/2)^2$ shows the maximum is $1/4$ at $p=1/2$.

When outcomes are nearly always zero or nearly always one, individual variation is small. At one half, both outcomes remain equally plausible and variation is largest.

### Assumptions

For a sample proportion, variance becomes $p(1-p)/n$ only under independent common-probability trials. Dependence or differing probabilities changes the calculation.

### Common mistake

A small variance for a rare binary outcome does not mean its relative rate is estimated precisely. With very few expected successes, relative uncertainty can be large and normal approximations poor. Distinguish individual outcome spread, absolute rate uncertainty and relative precision.
keyTakeaways: Use the identity X squared equals X.
Locate the variance maximum.
Distinguish a binary outcome from its sample proportion.

questions.title: When is a success count binomial?
questions.questionMarkdown: State the assumptions for a binomial model and explain what changes if trial probabilities differ.
questions.tldrAnswer: A binomial count requires a fixed number of independent trials with the same success probability.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If $X$ counts successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials with common probability $p$, then $\Pr(X=k)=\binom nkp^k(1-p)^{n-k}$. The combinatorial factor counts arrangements of the same number of successes.

If independent trials have different success probabilities, the count generally follows a Poisson-binomial distribution instead. Shared shocks or repeated observations from one person can create dependence, invalidating the ordinary binomial variance even if the marginal success rates look similar.

### Assumptions

The number of trials is fixed by the design or conditioned upon appropriately, and the success event is defined consistently. A procedure that stops after a target number of successes has a different sampling distribution.

### Common mistake

Calling every count of binary outcomes binomial skips the design. Check independence, common probability and stopping rules before using a binomial confidence interval or test, rather than relying only on the count's integer appearance.
keyTakeaways: State fixed count, independence and common probability.
Distinguish heterogeneous probabilities and dependence.

questions.title: When is a Poisson model suitable for event counts?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the count properties implied by a homogeneous Poisson process and a reason for overdispersion.
questions.tldrAnswer: A homogeneous Poisson process gives independent interval counts with mean proportional to exposure and equal count mean and variance.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a homogeneous Poisson process with rate $\lambda$, the count in an interval of length $t$ has mean and variance $\lambda t$. Counts in disjoint intervals are independent, and the event rate does not depend on the interval's position.

Real data may mix units with different rates or contain clustering after an event. Mixing rates adds variation beyond the conditional Poisson variation: total variance includes both average conditional variance and variance of the conditional mean.

### Assumptions

Exposure is measured consistently, and a constant rate over the relevant interval is reasonable. A Poisson count model can be used without asserting every process property, but its equal mean-variance implication still needs attention.

### Common mistake

A count being non-negative does not establish a Poisson distribution. Excess variation can arise from heterogeneity, dependence or a wrong mean model. Diagnose the mechanism before choosing a more flexible count family or a robust variance estimate.
keyTakeaways: Relate count mean and variance to rate times exposure.
Explain overdispersion through heterogeneous rates.
Separate count support from distributional assumptions.

questions.title: What does exponential memorylessness mean?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the residual-waiting-time identity and explain why it is unsuitable for ageing equipment without further assumptions. If the chance of at least one event in one interval is p, what is it over k independent equal intervals?
questions.tldrAnswer: After surviving to any age, an exponential waiting time has the same remaining-time distribution because its hazard is constant.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For waiting time $T$ with survival function $\Pr(T>t)=e^{-\lambda t}$, conditional survival gives $\Pr(T>s+t\mid T>s)=e^{-\lambda(s+t)}/e^{-\lambda s}=e^{-\lambda t}$. Time already waited does not change the remaining distribution.

The associated hazard is the constant rate $\lambda$. This can describe time to the next event in a homogeneous Poisson process, where no accumulating age effect changes event risk.

### Assumptions

The rate remains constant and conditioning is on survival, not additional information about hidden subgroups. A mixture of different exponential rates generally does not retain memorylessness.

### Common mistake

Real lifetimes can have wear-out, early failures or changing operating conditions. Assuming exponential waiting times then imposes a substantive restriction, not a neutral default. Check whether the event rate depends on age or history before interpreting the remaining lifetime as unchanged.

### Combining equal intervals

If equal intervals independently have no event with probability $1-p$, the probability of no event over k intervals is $(1-p)^k$. Hence the probability of at least one event is $1-(1-p)^k$, not generally $kp$. For a homogeneous Poisson process with interval duration $\Delta$, $p=1-e^{-\lambda\Delta}$ and the result is $1-e^{-\lambda k\Delta}$. This interval argument needs independence and the same interval probability; a marginal event probability alone does not justify it.
keyTakeaways: Derive the conditional survival identity.
Connect memorylessness to constant hazard.
Recognise ageing and rate mixtures as violations.
Derive 1−(1−p)^k under independent equal-interval assumptions.

questions.title: Why are there two common means for a geometric variable?
questions.questionMarkdown: Distinguish counting trials until success from counting failures before success.
questions.tldrAnswer: The two variables differ by one: trial count has mean 1/p, while failure count has mean (1-p)/p.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Under independent trials with common success probability $p$, let $T$ count trials through the first success. Its support is $1,2,\ldots$ and $\Pr(T=k)=(1-p)^{k-1}p$. Its mean is $1/p$.

If $F$ counts failures before that success, then $F=T-1$, its support begins at zero and its mean is $(1-p)/p$. Both are commonly called geometric, so software and textbook conventions must be checked.

### Assumptions

Success probability is constant across independent trials. Learning, fatigue or sampling without replacement generally changes the waiting distribution. For $p=0$, a finite first success does not occur under this model.

### Common mistake

Using the probability formula from one convention with the mean from the other produces a one-unit error that can matter for small expected counts. Name the counted quantity explicitly and distinguish discrete trial waiting from continuous exponential waiting.
keyTakeaways: State both supports and probability conventions.
Derive the one-unit relationship between means.
Check independence and constant success probability.

questions.title: Does standardising data make them normal?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the distribution of a standardised normal variable and what happens for non-normal data.
questions.tldrAnswer: Standardisation changes location and scale; it preserves distributional shape rather than turning arbitrary data into a normal distribution.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If $X\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$ with $\sigma>0$, then $Z=(X-\mu)/\sigma$ follows a standard normal distribution. A value $Z=2$ lies two population standard deviations above the mean.

For an arbitrary distribution with finite non-zero variance, the same transformation gives mean zero and variance one, but skewness, tail structure or discrete support remain. A standardised binary variable still has only two possible values.

### Assumptions

Population parameters differ from sample estimates. Under iid normal sampling, the centred statistic $(\bar X-\mu)/(s/\sqrt n)$ follows $t_{n-1}$, not exactly a standard normal.

### Common mistake

Reading standardised observations through a normal probability table without checking the distribution can give wrong tail probabilities. Standard scores describe relative location, while probability statements require a distributional model or an empirical reference.
keyTakeaways: Apply the normal location-scale transformation.
Explain why arbitrary shapes remain non-normal.
Distinguish standardised observations from studentised sample means.

questions.title: Why is exponentiating a log mean not the arithmetic mean?
questions.questionMarkdown: For normally distributed log outcomes, derive the median and mean on the original scale.
questions.tldrAnswer: The median is exp(mu), while the mean is exp(mu plus half sigma squared); the difference reflects the nonlinear transformation.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If $Z=\log Y\sim N(\mu,\sigma^2)$, monotonicity of exponentiation gives median$(Y)=e^\mu$. The arithmetic mean uses the normal moment-generating function: $\mathbb{E}[Y]=\mathbb{E}[e^Z]=e^{\mu+\sigma^2/2}$.

The mean exceeds the median when log variance is positive because large positive values contribute disproportionately to the average. Exponentiating an estimated log-scale mean therefore targets a geometric or median-type quantity under this model, not the arithmetic mean.

### Assumptions

The log outcome is normally distributed and the relevant log variance is correctly specified. In regression, conditional variance can depend on predictors, so one global correction may be inappropriate.

### Common mistake

Adding half a sample variance is not a universally unbiased retransformation method. Outside the lognormal model, the correction depends on the residual distribution. Specify whether the desired prediction is a median, mean or another quantity before transforming.
keyTakeaways: Derive the median by monotonicity.
Derive the mean including log variance.
Qualify retransformation by the conditional distribution.

questions.title: Why does a t distribution have heavier tails than a normal?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the random-denominator representation and how degrees of freedom affect moments.
questions.tldrAnswer: A t variable divides a normal variable by an uncertain scale estimate; small denominators create heavier tails.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If $Z$ is standard normal and $U$ is an independent chi-squared variable with $\nu$ degrees of freedom, then $T=Z/\sqrt{U/\nu}$ has a t distribution. Random variation in the denominator allows more extreme values than a fixed scale would.

As $\nu$ grows, $U/\nu$ concentrates near one and the distribution approaches standard normal. Its mean exists and is zero for $\nu>1$; its variance is $\nu/(\nu-2)$ for $\nu>2$ and is not finite at smaller degrees of freedom.

### Assumptions

The ratio representation requires independence and the stated distributions. The familiar t statistic for a sample mean follows this construction under independent normal observations.

### Common mistake

“Heavy-tailed” does not mean every moment exists but is merely larger. At low degrees of freedom some moments are undefined. Conversely, using a t reference does not automatically make inference robust to arbitrary dependence or extreme contamination.
keyTakeaways: Explain the normal divided by random-scale construction.
State mean and variance existence thresholds.
Distinguish heavy tails from universal robustness.

questions.title: What does the law of large numbers guarantee?
questions.questionMarkdown: Distinguish convergence of a sample average from a normal approximation to its fluctuations.
questions.tldrAnswer: Under suitable sampling assumptions, the average approaches the population mean; the theorem does not by itself specify a normal shape or finite-sample error rate.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For independent identically distributed observations with $\mathbb{E}|X|<\infty$, the strong law gives $\bar X_n\to\mathbb{E}X$ almost surely. Averaging increasingly many observations stabilises around the target mean under this model.

This differs from the central limit theorem, which concerns the scaled fluctuations around the mean and needs additional conditions in its familiar form. A sample average can converge even when finite variance, required by the classical normal approximation, is absent.

### Assumptions

The sampling process matters. Dependent sequences can satisfy other laws of large numbers, but their conditions must be checked rather than assumed from a large observation count.

### Common mistake

More data do not remove systematic sampling bias. An average from the wrong population can converge very precisely to the wrong target. Nor does convergence imply that the next observation becomes predictable or that temporary deviations cannot occur.
keyTakeaways: State convergence of averages under iid integrability.
Distinguish stabilisation from a central-limit approximation.
Explain why large samples do not repair a wrong sampling population.

questions.title: What can variance alone tell you about tail probability?
questions.questionMarkdown: State Chebyshev's inequality and compare its three-standard-deviation bound with a normal-model calculation.
questions.tldrAnswer: Finite variance bounds the probability of a large deviation without a normality assumption, but the bound can be loose.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For mean $\mu$ and finite variance $\sigma^2$, Chebyshev's inequality gives $\Pr(|X-\mu|\geq t)\leq\sigma^2/t^2$ for $t>0$. Writing $t=k\sigma$ gives a bound of $1/k^2$ when $\sigma>0$.

At three standard deviations, the bound is $1/9$, about 11.1%. For a normal distribution, the corresponding probability is $2[1-\Phi(3)]\approx0.0027$, about 0.27%, where $\Phi$ is the standard normal CDF. That stronger claim uses distributional shape information absent from Chebyshev's assumptions.

### Assumptions

The mean and variance must exist, and the stated values are population quantities. Replacing them with uncertain sample estimates does not automatically preserve the same probability guarantee.

### Common mistake

A bound above one should be capped at one and is uninformative. The inequality is an upper limit, not an estimate of the actual tail probability. Its looseness is the cost of making only a moment assumption.
keyTakeaways: State the finite-variance inequality.
Compare the 11.1% Chebyshev bound with the 0.27% normal tail probability.
Distinguish a distribution-free bound from an estimated tail rate.

questions.title: When is the median a better description of a typical value?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare the response of a mean and median to one extreme observation, and explain why the mean may still be the desired target.
questions.tldrAnswer: The median resists extreme magnitudes, while the mean reflects their contribution to the total; the right choice depends on the question.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The mean uses every value's magnitude. Replacing one observation with an arbitrarily large number can move it arbitrarily far. The median depends mainly on ordering, so changing an already extreme value often leaves it unchanged.

For a skewed income distribution, the median can describe the middle person's income more directly. For planning total expenditure, the mean times the population count is the relevant quantity, and large legitimate expenses should contribute.

### Assumptions

The observations represent the target population, and extreme values are distinguished from recording errors. Small samples and ties affect how precisely either centre is estimated.

### Common mistake

Robustness does not make the median a substitute for every mean-based decision. Reporting only one centre can also conceal multimodality or a long tail. Show spread or relevant quantiles, and define whether typical means middle-ranked, average contribution or another operational concept.
keyTakeaways: Compare magnitude sensitivity with order sensitivity.
Choose the centre from the target question.
Distinguish legitimate extremes from data errors.

questions.title: Why does sample variance divide by n minus one?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the loss from estimating the mean and derive the expected centred sum of squares.
questions.tldrAnswer: Estimating the mean from the same sample removes one degree of freedom and reduces expected squared deviations by one population variance.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For iid observations with mean $\mu$ and variance $\sigma^2$, the identity

$$
\sum_i(X_i-\bar X)^2
=\sum_i(X_i-\mu)^2-n(\bar X-\mu)^2
$$

has expectation $n\sigma^2-n(\sigma^2/n)=(n-1)\sigma^2$. Dividing the centred sum by $n-1$ therefore gives an unbiased estimator of population variance.

The residuals sum to zero, so knowing $n-1$ of them determines the last. This supplies the familiar degrees-of-freedom interpretation.

### Assumptions

Observations are independent with a common finite variance. The sample mean, rather than a known population mean, is used for centring. Weighted or dependent data require different calculations.

### Common mistake

The correction makes sample variance unbiased, not its square root. Sample standard deviation remains biased in general. Dividing by $n-1$ also does not repair a non-representative sample or create an appropriate covariance estimate for clustered observations.
keyTakeaways: Use the centred-sum identity.
State iid finite-variance and estimated-mean assumptions.
Distinguish unbiased variance from standard deviation.

questions.title: How does standard error differ from standard deviation?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain what each quantity describes and why collecting more observations affects them differently.
questions.tldrAnswer: Standard deviation describes variation among outcomes; standard error describes sampling variation of a chosen estimator.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If individual outcomes have standard deviation $\sigma$, their spread does not shrink merely because more are observed. Under independent common-distribution sampling, the sample mean has variance $\sigma^2/n$, so its standard error is $\sigma/\sqrt n$, usually estimated by $s/\sqrt n$.

The first quantity concerns differences between people or measurements. The second concerns how much the estimated average would change across repeated samples. Other estimators have different standard-error formulas.

### Assumptions

The square-root-n expression requires the appropriate independence and common-variance structure. Clustering, serial dependence and unequal weighting can change it substantially.

### Common mistake

Plotting standard-error bars and describing them as the spread of individual outcomes understates that spread. Conversely, reporting only an outcome standard deviation does not communicate precision of the estimated mean. Label error bars with their actual meaning, including whether they are standard errors or confidence intervals.
keyTakeaways: Separate outcome variability from estimator uncertainty.
Derive the independent-sample mean standard error.
Label error bars and account for dependence.

questions.title: What does positive skewness mean?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain moment-based skewness and one reason it may not give a complete description of distribution shape.
questions.tldrAnswer: Positive third standardised moment indicates stronger positive cubic deviations overall, but does not establish a universal mean-median ordering or simple one-tail shape.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Population skewness is $\mathbb{E}[(X-\mu)^3]/\sigma^3$ when the required moments exist and $\sigma>0$. Cubing gives large deviations strong weight and preserves their sign. Positive skewness therefore reflects a positive balance of these weighted deviations.

A long right tail often produces positive skewness, but multimodal or irregular distributions can defeat simple visual rules. Zero skewness also does not prove symmetry: positive and negative third-moment contributions can cancel without mirror symmetry.

### Assumptions

The third absolute moment should be finite for a well-defined stable population interpretation. Sample skewness can be highly sensitive to rare extreme observations and to small sample size.

### Common mistake

Rules such as “mean exceeds median whenever skewness is positive” are not universal mathematical laws. Inspect quantiles, histograms and the substantive distribution rather than inferring every aspect of shape from one moment.
keyTakeaways: Define the third standardised moment.
Explain sensitivity to extremes and moment existence.
Avoid treating skewness as proof of symmetry or mean-median order.

questions.title: What does the median absolute deviation measure?
questions.questionMarkdown: Define MAD and explain the purpose and limits of its normal-consistency scaling.
questions.tldrAnswer: MAD is the median distance from the sample median; a scaling constant can align it with standard deviation under a normal model, not under every distribution.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The raw median absolute deviation is $\operatorname{median}_i|x_i-\operatorname{median}_j x_j|$. Because both stages use medians, a few extreme magnitudes have limited influence compared with squared-deviation spread.

For a normal population, dividing raw MAD by approximately 0.67449 makes the population quantity equal to the normal standard deviation. The corresponding multiplier is about 1.4826. This is a model-based scale convention, not a distribution-free identity.

### Assumptions

The target distribution and use of raw or scaled MAD must be stated. With many repeated values, raw MAD can be zero even when some observations differ greatly, so it may not support a useful normalisation denominator.

### Common mistake

A robust scale estimate does not establish that tail events are harmless or erroneous. If the task concerns extreme losses, summarising only central spread can omit the very variation that matters.
keyTakeaways: Define the two median operations.
Explain the normal-specific scaling constant.
Address ties, zero MAD and tail-sensitive decisions.

questions.title: What information does an empirical CDF retain?
questions.questionMarkdown: Define the empirical distribution function and explain how ties appear in it.
questions.tldrAnswer: It assigns equal mass to observations and reports the fraction at or below each threshold, without assuming a smooth density.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, the empirical CDF is $F_n(x)=n^{-1}\sum_i\mathbf{1}\{X_i\leq x\}$. It is a right-continuous step function. A distinct observed value increases it by $1/n$; tied values produce a larger jump.

The empirical CDF directly estimates threshold probabilities and supports quantile calculations. Unlike a histogram, it does not require selecting bin widths, although its usefulness still depends on the sample representing the population.

### Assumptions

Equal weighting corresponds to an ordinary sample. Survey weights or unequal sampling probabilities require a justified weighted construction and different uncertainty calculations.

### Common mistake

The steps do not imply the underlying population is discrete. They reflect finite observed data. Conversely, smoothing those steps into a density adds assumptions and tuning choices rather than uncovering an exact population curve.
keyTakeaways: Write the indicator-average definition.
Explain ties and right-continuous steps.
Distinguish finite empirical mass from population discreteness.

questions.title: Why is bandwidth central to density estimation?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how a kernel density estimate changes with its bandwidth and identify a boundary problem.
questions.tldrAnswer: Small bandwidths reveal local detail with high variability; large bandwidths smooth more strongly and can erase meaningful structure.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A one-dimensional kernel estimate has form $\hat f_h(x)=(nh)^{-1}\sum_iK((x-X_i)/h)$. Each observation contributes a scaled bump. The bandwidth $h$ controls how widely each bump spreads.

A small bandwidth can produce many peaks driven by individual observations. A large bandwidth can merge genuine modes and distort shape. In many practical settings, bandwidth choice affects results more than choosing among reasonable smooth kernel shapes.

### Assumptions

The observations should support density estimation under the chosen sampling model. For non-negative outcomes, an ordinary symmetric kernel can place mass below zero near the boundary; transformations or boundary corrections may be appropriate.

### Common mistake

Every visible peak is not necessarily a separate population. Assess sensitivity to bandwidth and uncertainty before interpreting modes. Cross-validation or other selection rules provide a procedure, not proof that one displayed curve is the true density.
keyTakeaways: State how bandwidth scales kernel contributions.
Explain variation-versus-smoothing effects.
Check boundaries and stability of apparent modes.

questions.title: Why can a large random sample still be biased?
questions.questionMarkdown: Distinguish random sampling from a sampling frame and explain a coverage error.
questions.tldrAnswer: Random sampling represents the frame from which it draws, which may exclude important parts of the target population.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A sampling frame lists or otherwise makes reachable the units that can be selected. Drawing randomly from that frame controls selection within it, but cannot include people who are absent from it. A large online survey drawn randomly from one platform may therefore describe that platform's users rather than all residents.

Increasing sample size reduces some random error while leaving systematic coverage differences intact. The resulting estimate can become more precise around the wrong population quantity.

### Assumptions

Define the target population, eligibility period and unit before judging coverage. Duplicate entries, non-response and inaccurate contact information introduce additional design problems.

### Common mistake

Weighting observed respondents cannot automatically recover a completely absent group whose outcomes differ in unknown ways. Weighting requires auxiliary information and transport assumptions. Document who could be sampled and who actually responded, rather than equating a large response count with representativeness.
keyTakeaways: Separate target population from accessible frame.
Explain why sample size does not remove coverage bias.
State the information and assumptions needed for weighting.

questions.title: How do unequal sampling rates affect an overall estimate?

questions.tldrAnswer: Estimate each stratum's mean and combine them using population shares, not the proportions created by the oversampling design.

If a region contains 10% of residents but 40% of respondents, its mean should receive 10% weight in an overall resident mean, assuming suitable sampling and response within regions. Equivalently, inverse-inclusion-probability weights can adjust individual contributions.

### Assumptions

Population stratum sizes and selection probabilities must be known or credibly estimated. Variance estimation must reflect stratification, unequal weights and any clustering. Non-response may require further assumptions beyond the initial design.

Using the unweighted sample mean answers a different mixture question. This is also distinct from stratified treatment randomisation, whose purpose is balancing assignments rather than correcting who enters a population sample.

questions.title: How can selecting observations by outcome distort an association?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why a dataset restricted to unusually successful applicants can show misleading relationships among predictors.
questions.tldrAnswer: Conditioning on selection can change the joint distribution and create or reverse associations, even without changing the underlying population mechanism.

Suppose admissions depend on both examination performance and interview performance. Among admitted applicants, a lower score on one may need a higher score on the other to meet the threshold. The selected dataset can then show a negative association even if the two scores were independent in the applicant population.

Selection acts on a common consequence of the predictors. More data from the selected group estimate that selected relationship more precisely, without recovering the original population relationship.

### Assumptions

The selection mechanism and intended target population determine the problem. Outcome-based sampling has specialised valid analyses in some designs, but those require explicit likelihood or weighting arguments.

### Common mistake

A regression fitted only among survivors, winners or accepted cases does not automatically describe all candidates. Adjusting for more variables is not a universal cure and can introduce further conditioning bias. Draw the assumed selection structure and identify what additional information is needed.

questions.title: How do MCAR, MAR and MNAR differ?
questions.questionMarkdown: Define the three missingness mechanisms and explain why observed data usually cannot establish MAR.
questions.tldrAnswer: MCAR does not depend on observed or missing values; MAR may depend on observed information; MNAR still depends on missing values after that information is considered.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let the missingness indicator describe which values are absent. Missing completely at random means its distribution does not depend on the data values. Missing at random means that, conditional on the observed information, it does not additionally depend on values that are missing. Missing not at random allows such remaining dependence.

For example, response probability depending on recorded age may be compatible with MAR after conditioning on age. Response probability depending on an unreported income, beyond recorded variables, is generally MNAR for that analysis.

### Assumptions

MAR is relative to the variables actually observed and included in the model. Imputation and likelihood procedures still need appropriate models and regularity assumptions.

### Common mistake

MAR does not mean missingness is haphazard or unrelated to every variable. Observed data alone usually cannot distinguish MAR from plausible MNAR alternatives. Use knowledge of collection and sensitivity analyses rather than claiming a successful imputation diagnostic proves the mechanism.
keyTakeaways: Define all three mechanisms conditionally.
Make MAR relative to observed information.

questions.title: Why is likelihood not a probability distribution over parameters?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how the same model expression is interpreted as probability or likelihood.
questions.tldrAnswer: Probability varies possible data for a fixed parameter; likelihood varies the parameter while holding the observed data fixed.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A statistical model specifies a probability mass or density for data given a parameter. Once the data are observed, the same expression can be viewed as a function of the parameter, called the likelihood. Relative likelihood values compare how strongly parameter choices support the observed result under the model.

The likelihood need not integrate or sum to one over parameters. Multiplying it by a positive constant that does not depend on the parameter does not change its maximiser or likelihood ratios.

### Assumptions

The sampling model and data-generating design must be specified. For continuous data the expression is a density, not the probability of observing that exact real-valued point.

### Common mistake

A high likelihood does not directly give the probability that a parameter is true. A Bayesian posterior requires a prior and normalisation. A maximum-likelihood estimate is an optimisation result, not a probability mass assigned to one parameter value.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish what is fixed and what varies.

Separate likelihood from a normalised posterior.

questions.title: How do you derive the Bernoulli maximum-likelihood estimate?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the success-probability estimate and describe the all-success or all-failure cases.
questions.tldrAnswer: For independent common-probability trials, maximising likelihood gives the sample proportion, including boundary estimates zero or one.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
With $s$ successes in $n$ independent Bernoulli trials, the likelihood is proportional to $p^s(1-p)^{n-s}$. For $0<s<n$, the log-likelihood derivative is $s/p-(n-s)/(1-p)$. Setting it to zero gives $\hat p=s/n$, and the concavity of the log likelihood establishes the maximum.

If $s=0$, the likelihood is maximised at $p=0$; if $s=n$, it is maximised at $p=1$. The interior derivative argument must not be applied blindly at those boundaries.

### Assumptions

Trials are independent with the same success probability and the observation count is appropriate for the sampling design.

### Common mistake

A boundary estimate does not prove future outcomes are certain. A small sample can contain no observed failures while substantial uncertainty remains. Wald intervals based on the estimated variance can collapse at boundaries, so choose an interval method appropriate to binomial uncertainty.
keyTakeaways: Differentiate the Bernoulli log likelihood.
Handle boundary outcomes separately.

questions.title: How does a MAP estimate differ from maximum likelihood?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the optimisation objectives and why a posterior mode is not generally a posterior mean.
questions.tldrAnswer: MAP maximises likelihood times prior density, adding a prior term to the log objective; it summarises the posterior by its mode.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Maximum likelihood chooses the parameter with largest data likelihood. Maximum a posteriori estimation chooses the largest posterior density, equivalently maximising log likelihood plus log prior when the posterior normalising constant is parameter-independent.

A normal prior on coefficients can produce a squared-coefficient penalty; a Laplace prior can produce an absolute-value penalty under matching conventions. These are interpretations of particular objectives, not universal identities between every regularised implementation and Bayesian inference.

### Assumptions

The prior, likelihood and parameterisation are specified. Posterior density changes under transformations through a Jacobian, so a MAP estimate need not transform like a maximum-likelihood estimate under a one-to-one reparameterisation.

### Common mistake

The highest-density point is not generally the posterior average or the best estimate under every loss. Reporting only MAP also discards uncertainty and can be misleading for skewed or multimodal posteriors.
