questions.title: What does a sufficient statistic preserve?
questions.questionMarkdown: Use independent Bernoulli data to explain sufficiency and its dependence on the chosen model.
questions.tldrAnswer: A sufficient statistic retains all sample information about the parameter within the specified model; for common-probability Bernoulli trials, the success count is sufficient.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A statistic $T(X)$ is sufficient for parameter $\theta$ when the conditional distribution of the complete data given $T$ does not depend on $\theta$. Under suitable conditions, the likelihood factorisation criterion expresses the same idea as $f_\theta(x)=g_\theta(T(x))h(x)$.

For iid Bernoulli observations, the likelihood depends on the sequence only through its number of successes. Given that count, the ordering of successes supplies no additional information about the common probability.

### Assumptions

Sufficiency is relative to the family of distributions and parameter being considered. If probabilities vary over time, the order can become informative and the same count need not be sufficient.

### Common mistake

A sufficient statistic is not necessarily an accurate estimate on its own or a minimal-size summary. It preserves the model's parameter information, not every feature useful for checking whether the model itself is wrong.
keyTakeaways: State conditional-distribution or factorisation sufficiency.
Apply it to the Bernoulli success count.
Make the claim relative to a specified model.

questions.title: Can an estimator be unbiased but inconsistent?
questions.questionMarkdown: Distinguish finite-sample expectation from large-sample convergence and give an example.
questions.tldrAnswer: Yes. An estimator using only the first observation can remain unbiased for a mean while never becoming more concentrated as the sample grows.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Unbiasedness means $\mathbb{E}[\hat\theta_n]=\theta$ at a specified sample size. Consistency means $\hat\theta_n$ converges in probability to $\theta$ as sample size increases under the sampling model.

For iid observations with mean $\mu$ and non-zero variance, taking $\hat\mu_n=X_1$ is unbiased for every $n$ but ignores all additional observations. Its distribution does not concentrate around $\mu$, so it is inconsistent. Conversely, $n\bar X_n/(n+1)$ is generally biased at finite $n$ but is consistent when the sample mean is consistent.

### Assumptions

The examples use a fixed underlying distribution with suitable moments. Consistency refers to a sequence of procedures, not one realised estimate.

### Common mistake

Neither property alone establishes small error at the available sample size. A slightly biased estimator can have lower mean squared error, and a consistent estimator may converge too slowly to be useful in practice.
keyTakeaways: Define expectation-based bias and convergence-based consistency.
Give examples showing neither property implies the other.
Evaluate finite-sample error as well as asymptotic labels.

questions.title: Why can a biased estimator have lower mean squared error?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the estimator MSE decomposition and explain the possible benefit of shrinkage.
questions.tldrAnswer: Mean squared error equals variance plus squared bias, so a variance reduction can outweigh introduced bias.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For an estimator $\hat\theta$ with finite second moment,

$$
\mathbb{E}[(\hat\theta-\theta)^2]
=\operatorname{Var}(\hat\theta)+(\mathbb{E}\hat\theta-\theta)^2.
$$

Add and subtract $\mathbb{E}\hat\theta$ inside the square. The cross-term vanishes because the centred estimator has mean zero. This is estimation error relative to a fixed parameter, distinct from a prediction decomposition that also includes new-outcome noise.

Shrinking a noisy estimate towards a chosen reference may lower variance while introducing bias. Whether total error falls depends on the true parameter, shrinkage strength and sampling distribution.

### Assumptions

Squared error is the loss of interest. Other losses need different comparisons, and the shrinkage target should have a justified role.

### Common mistake

Unbiasedness is not a complete ranking of estimators. Conversely, shrinkage is not automatically beneficial for every parameter value. Compare the risk under relevant scenarios and disclose the target towards which estimates are pulled.
keyTakeaways: Derive variance plus squared bias.
Separate parameter-estimation from prediction error.
Explain why shrinkage risk depends on the true parameter.

questions.title: What does the Cramer-Rao bound actually restrict?
questions.questionMarkdown: State a scalar information bound and explain why it is not a universal limit on estimator mean squared error.
questions.tldrAnswer: Under regularity conditions it bounds the variance of unbiased estimators; biased procedures and non-regular models require different arguments.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a regular scalar model, Fisher information is the expected square of the score, $I(\theta)=\mathbb{E}_\theta[(\partial_\theta\log f_\theta(X))^2]$. With $n$ iid observations from this same model, information adds to $nI(\theta)$; independent non-identical observations instead contribute a sum of their individual information.

An unbiased estimator of $\theta$ satisfying the required regularity conditions has variance at least $1/(nI(\theta))$. The bound describes the information available for that restricted class of estimators, and equality need not be achievable at a given sample size.

### Assumptions

Differentiation and integration must be interchangeable, score identities must hold, and parameter-dependent support can break the familiar derivation. A uniform distribution with an unknown endpoint is a standard reason to inspect these conditions.

### Common mistake

A biased estimator can have smaller MSE than the unbiased variance bound without violating it. Also, an asymptotic maximum-likelihood information approximation does not guarantee an exact finite-sample variance or normal sampling distribution.
keyTakeaways: Define score-based Fisher information.
State the unbiased-estimator variance restriction.
Check regularity and distinguish finite-sample from asymptotic claims.

questions.title: How does the delta method approximate transformed uncertainty?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive a first-order variance approximation for a smooth function of an estimator and identify a failure case.
questions.tldrAnswer: Linearise the transformation around the true parameter, then propagate the estimator's covariance through its derivative.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If $\sqrt n(\hat\theta-\theta)$ approaches a normal distribution with variance $V$, a differentiable transformation gives $\sqrt n(g(\hat\theta)-g(\theta))$ approximately normal with variance $[g'(\theta)]^2V$, provided the derivative is suitable.

The argument uses the first-order Taylor term $g(\hat\theta)-g(\theta)\approx g'(\theta)(\hat\theta-\theta)$. For a vector estimator, the corresponding variance is $\nabla g^\top\Sigma\nabla g$ using its covariance matrix.

### Assumptions

The estimator has the required asymptotic distribution and the transformation is sufficiently smooth near the parameter. A zero derivative can eliminate the first-order term and require a higher-order analysis.

### Common mistake

For a ratio, a denominator near zero makes linearisation unreliable and can produce strongly asymmetric uncertainty. Plugging estimates into the formula does not make the approximation exact. Check scale, sample size and whether a more suitable interval construction is needed.
keyTakeaways: Derive the Taylor-based variance propagation.
Include covariance for a multivariate transformation.
Identify zero-derivative and unstable-denominator failures.

questions.title: How does a beta prior update after binary outcomes?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the posterior parameters and interpret the posterior mean after successes and failures.
questions.tldrAnswer: A Beta(a,b) prior becomes Beta(a+s,b+f), with posterior mean (a+s)/(a+b+s+f).
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The beta prior density is proportional to $p^{a-1}(1-p)^{b-1}$ for $a,b>0$. Independent Bernoulli data with $s$ successes and $f$ failures contribute likelihood $p^s(1-p)^f$. Multiplying adds the exponents, giving a Beta$(a+s,b+f)$ posterior.

Its mean is $(a+s)/(a+b+s+f)$, which combines the prior mean with the observed proportion. The prior's concentration controls how strongly it influences the result relative to the data.

### Assumptions

Trials share one probability and are conditionally independent under the model. The prior must represent information appropriate to this population rather than a convenient unexplained default.

### Common mistake

The posterior mean, mode and maximum-likelihood estimate differ. The mode formula needs additional shape conditions, and prior parameters should not always be described as literal historical observations. Predictive probabilities follow by integrating over this posterior rather than assuming parameter certainty.
keyTakeaways: Multiply prior and likelihood to obtain updated shapes.
Calculate the posterior mean.
Distinguish mean, mode and the interpretation of prior concentration.

questions.title: What probability statement does a credible interval make?
questions.questionMarkdown: Interpret a 95% Bayesian credible interval and distinguish it from a confidence interval.
questions.tldrAnswer: It contains 95% of posterior probability conditional on the observed data, likelihood and prior; repeated-sampling coverage is a separate property.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A posterior distribution combines the specified prior with the data likelihood. A 95% credible interval is a region containing 0.95 posterior probability, so it supports a probability statement about the parameter within that model.

Equal-tailed intervals place 2.5% in each tail. Highest-density regions instead favour parameter values with larger posterior density and can be disconnected for multimodal distributions. Different constructions need not produce the same endpoints.

### Assumptions

The interpretation is conditional on the model, prior and data-processing choices. Model misspecification or an inappropriate prior can produce misleading certainty.

### Common mistake

A 95% posterior interval is not automatically a procedure with 95% frequentist coverage under every true parameter. Likewise, a frequentist confidence interval does not itself assign posterior mass. Choose the interpretation that matches the method and report important prior or model sensitivity.
keyTakeaways: State the conditional posterior probability meaning.
Distinguish interval constructions.
Separate posterior mass from repeated-sampling coverage.

questions.title: Why does prediction require more than a posterior point estimate?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how a posterior predictive distribution combines parameter uncertainty with new-observation variation.
questions.tldrAnswer: Average the likelihood of future data over the full posterior, rather than substituting one estimated parameter.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The posterior predictive distribution is $p(\tilde y\mid y)=\int p(\tilde y\mid\theta,y)p(\theta\mid y)\,d\theta$. In a conditionally independent sampling model, the first term simplifies to $p(\tilde y\mid\theta)$.

Simulation draws a parameter from its posterior, then draws a future observation conditional on that parameter. This includes both uncertainty about the parameter and randomness remaining even if it were known. Predicting an average of many future observations is different from predicting one observation because the latter retains more outcome noise.

### Assumptions

The future-data mechanism and relevant covariates are specified. Distribution changes not represented by the model are not automatically covered by posterior uncertainty.

### Common mistake

An interval for a population mean is not an interval for an individual future outcome. A plug-in predictive distribution can understate uncertainty by freezing parameters, especially with limited data or nonlinear models.
keyTakeaways: Write the posterior predictive integral.
Describe parameter then observation simulation.
Distinguish parameter intervals, individual predictions and future averages.

questions.title: Why can many MCMC draws contain little independent information?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain effective sample size and why diagnostics are quantity-specific.
questions.tldrAnswer: Serial correlation changes Monte Carlo precision, so the relevant information can be much smaller than the stored draw count and differs by summary.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a stationary scalar chain with suitable summable autocorrelations, a rough effective sample size is $N/(1+2\sum_{k\geq1}\rho_k)$. Positive persistence makes successive draws partly redundant for estimating an expectation. Negative dependence can sometimes increase effective information relative to the draw count.

Different functions of the parameters have different autocorrelation patterns, so effective sample size for a mean, tail probability or quantile need not agree. Modern diagnostics often report separate central and tail measures.

### Assumptions

The chain must be sampling the intended posterior with suitable stationarity and ergodicity. The formula is not a substitute for checking convergence, divergent transitions or exploration of multiple modes.

### Common mistake

A large stored count or acceptable convergence statistic alone does not prove correctness. Use multiple chains, relevant diagnostic summaries and Monte Carlo error for the actual reported quantity. Thinning usually discards information rather than curing poor exploration.
keyTakeaways: Connect autocorrelation to Monte Carlo precision.
Explain quantity-specific and tail effective sample sizes.
Use several diagnostics rather than treating draw count as evidence of convergence.

questions.title: What does a prior predictive check test?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how to inspect a prior's implications before fitting to the observed outcomes.
questions.tldrAnswer: Simulate parameters from the prior and data from the likelihood, then examine whether the resulting observable scenarios are plausible.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A prior can look mild on the parameter scale yet imply extreme outcomes after a nonlinear transformation. Prior predictive simulation draws parameters from the prior and then generates hypothetical datasets using the observation model. Inspect ranges, event rates, group differences and other quantities meaningful in the application.

For example, broad normal coefficients on a logistic scale may imply many populations with probabilities almost zero or one. That consequence can be easier to judge than the coefficient standard deviation alone.

### Assumptions

Use the actual planned covariate scale and sampling design. Plausibility should reflect substantive knowledge available before the outcome data, while allowing reasonable uncertainty.

### Common mistake

A prior predictive check does not establish that the posterior fits the observed data. Posterior predictive checks answer a later question. Repeatedly adjusting priors to obtain a preferred observed result also needs transparent reporting rather than being presented as entirely prior judgement.
keyTakeaways: Simulate parameters and then observable data.
Inspect implications on meaningful outcome scales.
Distinguish prior and posterior predictive checks.

questions.title: Why should paired measurements be analysed through differences?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the paired t statistic and the independence assumption it actually needs.
questions.tldrAnswer: Treat each pair's difference as one observation, using variation between differences rather than pretending both measurements are independent.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For paired outcomes, define $D_i=X_i-Y_i$. A test of mean difference $\delta_0$ uses $T=(\bar D-\delta_0)/(s_D/\sqrt n)$. Positive within-pair correlation can make differences less variable than a comparison that ignores matching.

The pair may represent the same person before and after, or deliberately matched units. Pairing identifies which measurements should be compared, but a before-after difference alone does not remove time trends or establish a causal treatment effect.

### Assumptions

Pairs are independent of one another. Exact small-sample t inference requires normally distributed differences, not necessarily normality of each original measurement separately. Missing one member can create selection problems if complete pairs are analysed uncritically.

### Common mistake

Using an independent-samples standard error discards the covariance supplied by the pairing. Conversely, inventing pairs between unrelated observations does not create a justified matched design. Preserve the actual pairing and state what the mean difference represents.
keyTakeaways: Construct one difference per genuine pair.
State independence across pairs and normality of differences for exact inference.
Distinguish matched comparison from causal identification.

questions.title: What does rejecting a one-way ANOVA null tell you?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the global null and why it does not identify which groups differ.
questions.tldrAnswer: The null sets all group means equal; rejection provides evidence that at least one mean differs, without specifying the responsible pairs.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Classical one-way ANOVA compares between-group variation in sample means with pooled within-group variation. Under its null, the population group means are all equal, so a sufficiently large ratio is inconsistent with the reference model.

Rejection does not imply that every pair differs or identify a particular pair. Planned contrasts or follow-up comparisons address more specific questions, with error control appropriate to the family of claims.

### Assumptions

The classical finite-sample F reference assumes independent normal errors with a common variance. Unequal variances, clustering and repeated measurements require suitable alternatives or extensions. Group sizes influence sensitivity to violations.

### Common mistake

Running many unadjusted pairwise tests after a significant global test does not automatically control every desired error rate. Also, statistical rejection does not establish that differences are large enough to matter. Report estimated group effects and uncertainty alongside the global result.
keyTakeaways: State equality of all population means.
Separate a global finding from pairwise conclusions.
Check variance, independence and follow-up multiplicity.

questions.title: How are expected contingency-table counts calculated?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive expected cell counts under independence and explain when the chi-square approximation needs care.
questions.tldrAnswer: Expected counts equal row total times column total divided by the grand total, with the approximation relying on the sampling design and adequate counts.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Under independence, the probability of cell $(i,j)$ is the product of its row and column probabilities. Estimating these by marginal proportions gives $E_{ij}=R_iC_j/N$. Pearson's statistic sums $(O_{ij}-E_{ij})^2/E_{ij}$ across cells.

For a usual $r$ by $c$ table with independently sampled observations and no structural constraints, the large-sample reference has $(r-1)(c-1)$ degrees of freedom. Sparse expected cells can make the approximation inaccurate.

### Assumptions

Use counts from a defined sampling process, not percentages with an unknown denominator. Repeated observations, structural zeros or survey weighting can change the appropriate reference distribution.

### Common mistake

Large total sample size alone does not guarantee every expected cell is adequate. Consider an exact or simulation-based method suited to the design when sparse cells matter. A significant result indicates association, not its causal direction or practical size.
keyTakeaways: Derive expected counts from marginal proportions.
State the usual degrees of freedom and sampling assumptions.
Check sparse cells, structural zeros and association interpretation.

questions.title: Why does Fisher's exact test condition on table margins?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the reference distribution for a two-by-two table and what the word exact means.
questions.tldrAnswer: Conditioning on the margins gives a hypergeometric distribution under the null odds ratio, allowing finite-sample tail probabilities without a large-sample chi-square approximation.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a two-by-two table with fixed margins, choosing one cell determines the other three. Under the null of no association, that cell has a hypergeometric distribution. Fisher's test sums probabilities of tables considered at least as extreme according to the chosen alternative and two-sided convention.

Conditioning removes nuisance marginal probabilities from this reference calculation. The method is therefore useful for small counts, but its interpretation remains tied to the design and null being tested.

### Assumptions

Observations and the table-generating process must justify the conditional comparison. Different two-sided definitions can produce different p-values because discreteness does not supply one universal notion of extremeness.

### Common mistake

Exact does not mean assumption-free, maximally powerful or numerically equal to the nominal error level. Discrete rejection probabilities can be conservative. Report the alternative, odds-ratio estimate and interval method rather than presenting one p-value as a complete description.
keyTakeaways: Explain fixed margins and the hypergeometric reference.
Identify two-sided discreteness conventions.
Distinguish exact calculation from assumption-free or uniformly powerful inference.

questions.title: Does the Mann-Whitney test compare medians?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the rank-sum comparison and when a location-shift interpretation is justified.
questions.tldrAnswer: It assesses rank ordering and distributional differences; interpreting it solely as a median comparison requires additional shape assumptions.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The Mann-Whitney statistic counts pairwise ordering between two independent samples, with a convention for ties. It relates to the probability that a draw from one group exceeds a draw from the other, plus half the tie probability.

Under the usual exchangeable equal-distribution null, its sampling reference tests whether the groups have the same distribution. If the alternatives are restricted to a common-shaped location shift, a rejection can be interpreted as evidence of a shifted centre, including a median shift.

### Assumptions

Observations are independent within and across groups. Different spreads or shapes complicate a pure location interpretation, and ties affect exact and asymptotic calculations.

### Common mistake

Two populations can have equal medians while differing in ways that affect rank comparisons. Conversely, a p-value does not directly estimate the median difference. State the estimand and use an effect estimate that matches the scientific question.
keyTakeaways: Connect the statistic to pairwise ordering.
State the equal-distribution null and location-shift qualification.
Handle ties and avoid an automatic median-only interpretation.

questions.title: Why does the Wilcoxon signed-rank test need symmetry?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain its use of paired differences and distinguish it from a sign test.
questions.tldrAnswer: Signed ranks combine the signs and ordered magnitudes of differences; the usual location interpretation relies on a symmetric difference distribution.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Compute a difference within each genuine pair, remove or handle exact zeros according to the selected convention, rank absolute non-zero differences and compare the ranks carrying positive and negative signs. Large signed rank imbalance is evidence against the reference symmetry around the hypothesised centre.

Unlike a sign test, signed ranks use information about magnitude ordering. The sign test uses only whether each difference is above or below the hypothesised median and therefore makes a different trade-off in assumptions and information.

### Assumptions

Differences are independent across pairs. The standard signed-rank location test assumes a continuous distribution symmetric around the centre; ties and zeros require appropriate handling.

### Common mistake

Calling every nonparametric test assumption-free is incorrect. Asymmetric differences can invalidate the simple median interpretation of signed ranks. Inspect the paired-difference distribution and choose a procedure aligned with the target and plausible assumptions.
keyTakeaways: Describe signed absolute-difference ranks.
State symmetry and independence across pairs.
Distinguish signed-rank and sign-test information.

questions.title: When is shuffling labels a valid test?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the exchangeability requirement and why paired or clustered designs restrict permutations.
questions.tldrAnswer: Permutations must reproduce transformations that are equally plausible under the null and the actual assignment or sampling structure.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A permutation test calculates the observed statistic, generates allowed rearrangements under the null, and compares the observed value with that reference distribution. Validity comes from the rearrangements being justified by random assignment or exchangeability, not merely from having many shuffles.

For independently assigned treatment labels, the design may permit reassignment across units. A matched design may permit swaps only within pairs, while cluster randomisation requires moving whole clusters. Arbitrarily shuffling individual rows would represent a different experiment.

### Assumptions

The null and statistic must support the exchangeability argument. Equal means alone do not generally make observations exchangeable when group distributions or variances differ.

### Common mistake

Simulation precision cannot repair an invalid permutation scheme. For Monte Carlo permutations, use a p-value construction that accounts for the observed arrangement and finite resampling, rather than reporting zero simply because no simulated statistic was more extreme.
keyTakeaways: Explain validity through allowed null rearrangements.
Respect pairs, clusters and the assignment mechanism.
Distinguish equal means from exchangeability and avoid zero Monte Carlo p-values.

questions.title: When should a one-sided alternative be chosen?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why selecting the tail after seeing the estimate changes the test's error control.
questions.tldrAnswer: The directional question and rejection tail must be specified before the result is used to select them.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A one-sided test allocates its rejection probability to one direction, such as improvement above a specified baseline. It can have more power in that direction than a corresponding two-sided test, but does not supply the same evidence rule for an effect in the opposite direction.

Choosing whichever direction looks favourable after observing the data gives both tails an opportunity to trigger a claim. The original one-sided significance threshold no longer describes that combined procedure.

### Assumptions

The scientific or decision question genuinely supports the chosen direction. Potential harm in the other direction still needs appropriate measurement and safety decisions, even if it is not the efficacy alternative.

### Common mistake

Halving a two-sided p-value after seeing a result is not automatically valid. It depends on the pre-specified alternative, statistic and reference distribution. Declare the hypothesis and stopping plan before examining treatment differences.
keyTakeaways: Tie direction to a pre-specified question.
Explain the two-opportunity problem from post-result tail selection.
Separate efficacy direction from monitoring possible harm.

questions.title: How do you establish that an effect is small enough to be equivalent?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain two one-sided tests and why non-significance in an ordinary difference test is insufficient.
questions.tldrAnswer: Test whether the effect lies inside pre-defined acceptable margins, rather than asking only whether it differs from zero.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Suppose effects between lower margin $L$ and upper margin $U$ are practically equivalent. The equivalence null says the true effect is at or below $L$, or at or above $U$. Two one-sided tests reject both unacceptable regions before declaring equivalence.

For a compatible continuous test, two tests at level $\alpha$ correspond to checking whether a $100(1-2\alpha)$% two-sided confidence interval lies entirely within the margins. This is an intersection-union decision, not an invitation to choose margins after seeing the interval.

### Assumptions

Margins are scientifically or operationally justified beforehand, and the effect scale and analysis model are appropriate. Unequal margins may be justified by asymmetric consequences.

### Common mistake

Failing to reject zero difference can occur because an estimate is imprecise. Such an interval may include both substantial benefit and harm. Evidence of equivalence requires sufficiently narrow uncertainty within the accepted region.
keyTakeaways: State the outside-margins equivalence null.
Explain the two-test or interval criterion.
Distinguish practical equivalence from non-significance.

questions.title: What does false discovery rate control?
questions.questionMarkdown: Define FDR and contrast Benjamini-Hochberg with an arbitrary-dependence adjustment.
questions.tldrAnswer: FDR is the expected fraction of false rejections among all rejections, taking that fraction as zero when there are none; its control depends on the procedure's assumptions.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let $V$ be false rejections and $R$ total rejections. False discovery rate is $\mathbb{E}[V/\max(R,1)]$, unlike family-wise error, which is $\Pr(V\geq1)$.

Benjamini-Hochberg orders $m$ p-values and rejects through the largest rank $k$ satisfying $p_{(k)}\leq kq/m$. It controls FDR under independence and certain positive-dependence conditions with valid null p-values. Benjamini-Yekutieli uses an additional harmonic-sum adjustment to support arbitrary dependence, generally sacrificing power.

### Assumptions

The hypothesis family and p-values must represent the actual analysis, including selection and stopping. Dependence conditions are substantive rather than merely software settings.

### Common mistake

An FDR target of 5% does not assign a 5% probability of being false to each reported finding or guarantee that every realised discovery list contains at most 5% false findings. It controls an expectation over repeated applications.
keyTakeaways: Define the expected false-discovery fraction.
Describe the ordered BH threshold and its dependence assumptions.
Separate ensemble error control from individual posterior probabilities.

questions.title: Why does fitting a distribution change a KS test?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why estimating normal mean and variance from the tested sample invalidates the usual one-sample KS reference.
questions.tldrAnswer: The reference assumes a fully specified continuous CDF; fitting it to the same observations changes the discrepancy's null distribution.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
The one-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic is the largest vertical distance between the empirical CDF and a specified continuous CDF. Its standard null distribution relies on that reference CDF being fixed independently of the tested sample.

If normal mean and variance are estimated from those observations, the fitted CDF adapts to them. The distribution of the resulting maximum discrepancy is therefore different from the fully specified case. A suitable adjusted test or parametric bootstrap can reproduce the fitting step under the null.

### Assumptions

The reference distribution's continuity and the sampling independence matter. Discrete data, ties or parameter estimation can require different calibration.

### Common mistake

Passing fitted parameters into software does not automatically tell the test to account for their estimation. Read the method's assumptions. Also, a non-significant goodness-of-fit result does not establish that the model is true or adequate in the tail relevant to the application.
keyTakeaways: Define the maximum CDF discrepancy.
Explain same-sample fitting's effect on the null distribution.
Calibrate estimation, discreteness and application-relevant discrepancies.

questions.title: Why can normality tests be unhelpful at both small and large sample sizes?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how power affects the interpretation of rejection and non-rejection.
questions.tldrAnswer: Small samples may miss important departures, while large samples may detect tiny deviations that do not materially affect the intended analysis.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A normality test asks whether the observed departure from a normal model is surprising under its reference distribution. With little data, it can have low power against substantial skewness or heavy tails. Failure to reject then gives weak evidence for normality.

With very large samples, small departures can become statistically detectable even when a planned mean-based approximation remains adequate. The significance result does not directly quantify the effect of non-normality on the downstream estimate or decision.

### Assumptions

Apply the diagnostic to the relevant quantity, such as model residuals or paired differences, rather than automatically to raw outcomes. Dependence and fitted-parameter handling also matter.

### Common mistake

Using a normality p-value as an automatic switch between tests can obscure the actual robustness question. Inspect quantile plots, tails and influential observations, then assess the sensitivity of the intended inference under plausible alternatives.
keyTakeaways: Explain low power and high sensitivity at different sample sizes.
Diagnose the distribution relevant to the analysis.
Assess consequences rather than automatically switching methods.

questions.title: When would you use an exact binomial test?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how it tests a success probability without a normal approximation and why it can be conservative.
questions.tldrAnswer: It calculates tail probabilities from the binomial distribution under the null; discrete outcomes mean achievable rejection probabilities may lie below the nominal level.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a fixed number of independent common-probability trials, the null specifies a binomial distribution for the success count. An exact test sums probabilities of counts considered at least as extreme as the observed count under the chosen alternative. No large expected-success approximation is needed.

Because only integer counts are possible, rejection probabilities change in steps. A non-randomised rule may therefore have a null rejection probability below the requested significance level rather than exactly equal to it.

### Assumptions

The trials, common probability and stopping design must justify the binomial model. Two-sided definitions should be stated, since discreteness permits different tail-ordering conventions.

### Common mistake

Exact calculation does not correct dependence, selective stopping or outcome misclassification. Also, non-rejection with a small sample can leave a wide range of plausible rates. Report the estimated rate and an appropriate interval alongside the test.
keyTakeaways: Use the null binomial distribution directly.
Explain discreteness and conservative rejection probabilities.
Retain binomial design assumptions and report uncertainty.

questions.title: What does Pearson correlation measure?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the sign and scale of Pearson correlation and why a value near zero can be misleading.
questions.tldrAnswer: It standardises covariance to summarise linear association, not every form of dependence or a causal relationship.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Pearson correlation is $\rho=\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)/(\sigma_X\sigma_Y)$ when the variances are finite and non-zero. Its sign describes the direction of linear co-movement, and its magnitude measures how closely the variables align in that standardised linear sense.

Multiplying one variable by a positive constant or adding a constant does not change correlation. A negative rescaling reverses its sign. Nonlinear relationships, restricted ranges and influential outliers can produce summaries that poorly reflect the substantive pattern.

### Assumptions

A descriptive sample correlation can be computed broadly, but a confidence interval or test requires an appropriate sampling model. Dependence among observations reduces the validity of ordinary independent-sample inference.

### Common mistake

Correlation does not show that changing one variable changes the other. A scatterplot and study design remain essential. Zero correlation can coexist with a deterministic nonlinear relationship, and a high correlation can arise from a shared cause or trend.
keyTakeaways: Define standardised covariance and scale behaviour.
Recognise nonlinear and outlier limitations.
Separate descriptive association from causal and inferential claims.

questions.title: What does rank correlation capture that Pearson correlation may miss?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain Spearman correlation and its limits for nonlinear relationships.
questions.tldrAnswer: Spearman measures association between ranks and can detect monotone relationships without requiring their original-scale shape to be linear.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Spearman correlation is Pearson correlation applied to rank-transformed values, with a convention such as average ranks for ties. If one variable rises consistently as the other rises, their ranks can align strongly even when the numerical relationship is curved.

For example, an increasing exponential transformation changes spacing substantially but preserves ordering. Rank correlation therefore focuses on monotonicity rather than the sizes of original-scale changes.

### Assumptions

The measurements support meaningful ordering. Ties reduce distinct rank information and affect inference, while small-sample p-values may require an exact or permutation approach appropriate to the design.

### Common mistake

Rank correlation is not a universal detector of nonlinear dependence. A U-shaped relationship can have low rank correlation because increases on one side are offset by decreases on the other. It also does not supply an effect in original units or remove confounding merely by replacing values with ranks.
keyTakeaways: Explain correlation of ranks and tie handling.
Distinguish monotone from arbitrary nonlinear association.
Recognise loss of magnitude interpretation and causal limitations.

questions.title: What does partial correlation remove?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain partial correlation after adjustment for Z and why controlling for Z is not automatically causal adjustment.
questions.tldrAnswer: It correlates residuals after the chosen linear adjustments, removing those linear associations but not proving that the adjusted relationship is causal.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Regress X on the adjustment variables, including an intercept, and retain its residuals. Do the same for Y using the same adjustment variables. Their correlation is the corresponding partial correlation, under the usual non-degenerate linear definition.

This asks whether deviations of X from its linear prediction co-vary with deviations of Y from its linear prediction. Nonlinear relationships with the adjustment variables can remain if the fitted adjustments do not represent them.

### Assumptions

The adjustment set and functional form must match the question. Correlation requires non-zero residual variances. Zero partial correlation implies conditional independence only under additional assumptions, such as a jointly Gaussian model.

### Common mistake

Conditioning on a mediator can remove part of a causal effect, while conditioning on a common consequence can introduce an association. Choose controls from the assumed data-generating structure rather than assuming that adding every available variable always reduces bias.
keyTakeaways: Describe residualising both variables consistently.
Explain the linear-adjustment limitation.
Avoid causal claims without a justified adjustment set.

questions.title: How can an aggregate comparison reverse every subgroup comparison?
questions.questionMarkdown: Give a numerical example and explain why the appropriate comparison depends on the causal question.
questions.tldrAnswer: Groups can have different outcome baselines and different mixture weights, so aggregation can reverse within-group ordering.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Suppose option A succeeds in 80 of 100 easy cases and 1 of 10 hard cases. Option B succeeds in 9 of 10 easy cases and 20 of 100 hard cases. B is better within easy cases, 90% versus 80%, and hard cases, 20% versus 10%.

Aggregated success is nevertheless 81/110, about 73.6%, for A and 29/110, about 26.4%, for B. A receives far more easy cases. The different case mix drives the reversal.

### Assumptions

The subgroup variable's role matters. It may be a pre-treatment confounder, a consequence of treatment or a selection variable, and these imply different valid comparisons.

### Common mistake

The subgroup comparison is not automatically the causal truth, nor is the aggregate. Define the target population and causal structure, then standardise or adjust using justified weights. The arithmetic reversal alone does not determine the right intervention conclusion.
keyTakeaways: Verify subgroup and aggregate rates.
Explain different mixture weights.
Choose adjustment from the causal role of the grouping variable.

questions.title: Which assumptions are needed for OLS unbiasedness and inference?
questions.questionMarkdown: Separate computing least squares, unbiased coefficient estimation, minimum variance and exact t inference.
questions.tldrAnswer: Least squares can be computed algebraically; stronger conclusions require exogeneity and additional assumptions about error covariance and distribution.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a full-column-rank design, least squares is $\hat\beta=(X^\top X)^{-1}X^\top y$. Under $y=X\beta+\varepsilon$ and $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon\mid X]=0$, its conditional expectation equals $\beta$. Normal errors are not needed for this unbiasedness result.

With uncorrelated errors of common finite variance, the Gauss-Markov result gives minimum variance among linear unbiased estimators conditional on the design. Conditional normal errors additionally support the familiar exact finite-sample t and F reference distributions.

### Assumptions

The conditional-mean specification and full-rank requirement are central. Heteroskedasticity changes the standard covariance formula, while correlated errors require treatment of their dependence.

### Common mistake

A normal-looking residual histogram does not establish exogeneity, correct causal interpretation or independence. Conversely, non-normal errors do not automatically invalidate coefficient estimation. Identify which conclusion needs which assumptions rather than applying one undifferentiated checklist.
keyTakeaways: Separate algebraic fitting from unbiased estimation.
State exogeneity and the additional Gauss-Markov conditions.
Reserve exact t and F claims for the appropriate normal model.

questions.title: What do heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors change?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain what remains the same after changing an OLS covariance estimator and what problems remain unsolved.
questions.tldrAnswer: They change estimated coefficient uncertainty, not the fitted coefficients or biases from an incorrect conditional mean.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Ordinary OLS coefficients minimise the same squared-error objective regardless of whether their covariance is estimated with a constant-variance formula or a heteroskedasticity-consistent sandwich formula. The robust version uses residual information to allow error variance to differ across observations.

Under suitable large-sample conditions, this can support inference without assuming constant variance. Different finite-sample corrections account for leverage in different ways, but they do not turn every small-sample result into exact inference.

### Assumptions

The mean model and exogeneity conditions still matter. Ordinary heteroskedasticity-robust formulas do not account for serial or within-cluster dependence; suitable cluster or time-series covariance methods are needed instead.

### Common mistake

Robust standard errors do not repair omitted-variable bias, endogeneity or measurement error. Large row counts can also conceal very few independent clusters. Report the covariance method and the unit supporting independent information rather than simply calling the analysis robust.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish coefficient fitting from covariance estimation.
State asymptotic and exogeneity requirements.
Separate heteroskedasticity from dependence and bias problems.

questions.title: When does omitting a variable bias a regression coefficient?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the simple omitted-variable expression and explain why both outcome relevance and association with the included predictor matter.
questions.tldrAnswer: The omitted variable contributes bias when it affects the outcome and co-varies with the included predictor under the relevant conditioning.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Suppose $Y=\beta X+\gamma Z+\varepsilon$ with an intercept and $\operatorname{Cov}(X,\varepsilon)=0$. Regressing Y only on X gives population slope

$$
\tilde\beta=\beta+\gamma\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
$$

The extra term is zero if Z has no outcome contribution or is uncorrelated with X. Its sign depends on both relationships. With additional controls, the analogous statement uses residualised relationships after those controls.

### Assumptions

This derivation uses a correctly specified linear population model and non-zero predictor variance. Calling the omitted term causal requires further identification assumptions.

### Common mistake

Adding every measured variable is not a general remedy. A mediator, collider or badly measured control can change the estimand or introduce other bias. Use substantive structure to decide what belongs in the model, then assess sensitivity to plausible unmeasured factors.
keyTakeaways: Derive the omitted contribution to the slope.
Identify both required relationships and their signs.
Distinguish justified adjustment from indiscriminate control inclusion.

questions.title: Why is an individual prediction interval wider?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare uncertainty about the mean response at an input with uncertainty about a new individual outcome. Write the two intervals for simple linear regression at x₀.
questions.tldrAnswer: An individual prediction includes both uncertainty in the fitted mean and the irreducible variation of the new outcome.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A confidence interval for a regression mean concerns the expected outcome at a specified input. Its uncertainty comes from estimating model parameters. A prediction interval for a new observation adds the new observation's error variation, even if the fitted mean were known perfectly.

In a homoskedastic normal linear model, the prediction variance combines the fitted-mean variance with an additional error-variance term. As training data increase, the parameter component can shrink, while the individual outcome component remains.

### Assumptions

The new observation follows the model's error distribution and is independent of the estimation errors in the appropriate conditional sense. Heteroskedasticity requires input-dependent outcome variation, and extrapolation can make both intervals unreliable.

### Common mistake

Displaying a narrow mean-response interval as if it covered most individual outcomes materially understates uncertainty. Label the target clearly and check empirical prediction coverage on representative held-out observations rather than relying solely on a formula.

### Simple-regression formulas

Assume $Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1x_i+\epsilon_i$ with independent normal errors of common variance, fixed inputs, $n>2$ and $S_{xx}=\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2>0$. Let $s^2=\sum_i(y_i-\hat y_i)^2/(n-2)$ and $h_0=1/n+(x_0-\bar x)^2/S_{xx}$. A pointwise two-sided $1-\alpha$ confidence interval for the mean is

$$\hat y_0\pm t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2}s\sqrt{h_0}.$$

For one independent new outcome at the same input, the prediction interval is

$$\hat y_0\pm t_{n-2,1-\alpha/2}s\sqrt{1+h_0}.$$

The extra one represents new-outcome noise. These are pointwise intervals, not simultaneous bands across all inputs, and normal-error assumptions underpin their exact finite-sample coverage.
keyTakeaways: Separate parameter uncertainty from new-outcome noise.
Explain why more training data cannot remove all individual variation.
Label the interval target and check model assumptions.
Write the matched t intervals and identify the extra new-outcome variance.

questions.title: How do leverage and influence differ?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why an unusual predictor position is not necessarily an influential observation.
questions.tldrAnswer: Leverage measures predictor geometry; influence measures how much fitting changes when an observation is perturbed or removed.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
In linear regression, leverage is the corresponding diagonal of the hat matrix and reflects how unusual an observation's predictor combination is relative to the design. A high-leverage point has potential to pull the fitted relationship because few other observations constrain that region.

Influence also depends on disagreement with the fitted relationship. A high-leverage point lying close to the existing trend can have modest influence, while one with a substantial residual can change coefficients noticeably. Measures such as Cook's distance combine these aspects.

### Assumptions

Diagnostics depend on the fitted model and predictor representation. A point can be ordinary in each separate feature yet unusual in their joint combination.

### Common mistake

An influential observation is not automatically wrong and should not be deleted merely to improve significance. Check data quality, explain sensitivity with and without it, and consider whether the model is inadequate for a legitimate part of the population.
keyTakeaways: Define leverage from predictor geometry.
Explain the additional role of residual size.
Investigate influence without automatic deletion.

questions.title: How does serial dependence affect the uncertainty of an average?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why a long time series may contain less independent information than its row count suggests.
questions.tldrAnswer: Covariances between time points enter the mean's variance, so persistent positive dependence can substantially increase standard error.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a weakly stationary series with autocovariance $\gamma_k$, the variance of its mean is

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\bar X)=
\frac{1}{n}\left[\gamma_0+
2\sum_{k=1}^{n-1}(1-k/n)\gamma_k\right].
$$

Positive autocovariances add uncertainty compared with the independent formula $\gamma_0/n$. Negative terms can offset it, so dependence does not always reduce information in the same way.

### Assumptions

The expression uses finite second moments and stationarity of the covariance structure. Long-run variance approximations additionally require suitable decay or summability conditions.

### Common mistake

Using the ordinary standard deviation divided by square-root-n ignores serial covariance. Block resampling or a justified long-run covariance estimator can address some settings, but require tuning and assumptions. A highly persistent or non-stationary process may need a different model rather than merely an adjusted effective sample count.
keyTakeaways: Include lag covariances in mean uncertainty.
Distinguish positive from negative dependence effects.
State stationarity and long-run approximation conditions.

questions.title: What does weak stationarity require?
questions.questionMarkdown: Define weak stationarity and distinguish it from independence and strict stationarity.
questions.tldrAnswer: It requires a constant finite mean and covariance depending only on lag; it does not require independent observations.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A weakly stationary process has a time-invariant mean and finite second moments, and the covariance between two observations depends on their time separation rather than their absolute dates. The variance is therefore constant as the zero-lag covariance.

Strict stationarity is stronger in a different sense: every finite joint distribution is unchanged by a common time shift. Strict stationarity with finite second moments implies weak stationarity, but weak stationarity need not determine higher-order distributional behaviour.

### Assumptions

The concepts refer to a stochastic process, not merely a flat-looking observed plot. A stationary process can have substantial autocorrelation, and a deterministic seasonal mean violates constant-mean weak stationarity unless represented separately.

### Common mistake

Removing an apparent trend does not prove stationarity. Structural changes, changing variance and long dependence can remain. Choose diagnostics and models aligned with the forecasting or inferential use, and recognise that finite data cannot establish every population property.
keyTakeaways: State mean and lag-covariance conditions.
Distinguish weak, strict and independent behaviour.
Avoid treating detrending or a plot as proof.

questions.title: Why can ADF and KPSS tests appear to disagree?
questions.questionMarkdown: State their different null hypotheses and explain the role of deterministic trends and lag choices.
questions.tldrAnswer: ADF tests a unit-root null, while KPSS tests stationarity around a specified level or trend; they ask different questions and can both be inconclusive.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
An augmented Dickey-Fuller test has a unit-root null against a stationary alternative under the chosen deterministic terms. A KPSS test instead takes level or trend stationarity as its null. Their rejection directions therefore have different meanings.

Rejecting ADF's null while not rejecting KPSS can support the chosen stationarity model. Failing to reject both can reflect limited power; rejecting both can indicate features such as structural breaks or misspecification not captured cleanly by either simple model.

### Assumptions

Intercept, trend and lag or bandwidth settings affect the reference and power. A trend-stationary series differs from a difference-stationary one, so deterministic terms should reflect the question.

### Common mistake

Non-rejection is not proof of either a unit root or stationarity. Do not choose whichever test supports a preferred answer. Inspect the series, plausible breaks and modelling assumptions, and report sensitivity to defensible specifications.
keyTakeaways: State the opposing null hypotheses.
Explain level versus trend specifications.
Interpret disagreement through power and model mismatch.

questions.title: What does a right-censored event time tell you?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how a person without an observed event still contributes information to a survival estimate.
questions.tldrAnswer: The event time exceeds the censoring time; the person contributes observed survival up to that point without being treated as event-free forever.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If follow-up ends before an event is observed, right censoring records that the event time is later than the last observed time. It does not reveal how much later. A survival estimator such as Kaplan-Meier uses the person in the risk set while observed, then removes them from later risk sets at censoring.

This allows partial follow-up to contribute without pretending all participants have complete event times. Event probabilities are built from the observed event counts and numbers at risk over time.

### Assumptions

Censoring must be independent of the event process in the sense required by the model, possibly conditional on measured covariates. Dropping out because of unobserved worsening health can violate that assumption.

### Common mistake

Coding censored times as exact event times or permanent non-events biases the analysis. Record censoring separately, inspect reasons for loss to follow-up and recognise when competing events require a different estimand.
keyTakeaways: Interpret censoring as an event-time lower bound.
Explain contribution to the risk set.
State censoring assumptions and distinguish competing events.

questions.title: Why is a hazard not an event probability?
questions.questionMarkdown: Define a continuous-time hazard and relate it to survival probability.
questions.tldrAnswer: Hazard is an instantaneous event rate conditional on survival, measured per unit time; survival probability is obtained by accumulating that rate.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For a continuous event time with density $f(t)$ and survival $S(t)>0$, the hazard is $h(t)=f(t)/S(t)$. It is the limit of an event probability over a short interval divided by the interval length, conditional on having survived to its start.

The cumulative hazard is $H(t)=\int_0^t h(u)\,du$, and $S(t)=e^{-H(t)}$. A hazard of two per year is valid; it is not a 200% event probability. Under a constant hazard, the one-year event probability is $1-e^{-2}$.

### Assumptions

These formulas describe a continuous-time setting. A proportional-hazards model adds the assumption that group hazards have a constant ratio over time; that is not part of the hazard definition.

### Common mistake

A hazard ratio is not generally a risk ratio or a difference in expected survival time. Its interpretation conditions on changing survivor populations and requires the model assumptions.
keyTakeaways: Define the conditional instantaneous rate and its units.
Relate cumulative hazard to survival.
Distinguish hazard ratios from risks and proportional-hazards assumptions.

questions.title: What can an A/A test reveal about an experiment system?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why two randomly assigned groups receiving the same experience can still produce a small p-value.
questions.tldrAnswer: It checks assignment and measurement under no intended treatment difference, but chance alone produces some apparently significant comparisons.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
An A/A test routes observations through the experiment machinery while both groups receive the same product. This can expose inconsistent assignment, missing exposure logs, metric calculation differences and unexpected group-size patterns before a substantive treatment is introduced.

A valid test can still reject by chance. Across repeated independent continuous-null tests, p-values should have the appropriate null behaviour rather than all being large; discrete tests require a different expectation. Investigate systematic patterns, not one isolated threshold crossing.

### Assumptions

The experiences truly match, apart from the experiment labels, and the test exercises the production paths that matter. Instrumentation changes after the A/A test can invalidate that reassurance.

### Common mistake

One non-significant A/A result does not prove the system is correct. Low power can hide a problem, and repeated testing until a favourable result appears is selection. Combine statistical checks with direct assignment, logging and metric audits.
keyTakeaways: State what identical-experience testing exercises.
Expect some chance false alarms under a valid system.
Combine repeated diagnostics with direct implementation checks.

questions.title: Why analyse participants by their assigned group?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the intention-to-treat effect when some people never use the feature they were offered.
questions.tldrAnswer: Assignment-based analysis preserves the randomised comparison and estimates the effect of offering or assigning treatment, including imperfect uptake.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
An intention-to-treat analysis compares outcomes according to random assignment, regardless of whether participants complied, used the feature or crossed over. Randomisation balances potential outcomes in expectation at this assignment boundary.

If only half the treatment group uses an offered feature, the resulting effect may be smaller than an effect of actual use. That is not automatically dilution to be corrected: the assignment effect can be exactly the policy question, because real rollout also includes non-use.

### Assumptions

Outcome observation and analysis must preserve the assigned population, and the usual consistency and interference assumptions must be addressed. Missing outcomes can still undermine a simple comparison.

### Common mistake

Comparing actual users with non-users discards randomisation because usage is a post-assignment choice related to outcomes. Estimating an effect of receipt requires additional design or identification assumptions, not merely relabelling the groups.
keyTakeaways: Define the effect of assignment rather than receipt.
Explain why post-assignment usage selection breaks the simple comparison.
Address missing outcomes and the policy target.

questions.title: When does assignment identify an effect among compliers?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the Wald ratio for a binary randomised encouragement with incomplete treatment uptake.
questions.tldrAnswer: Under instrumental-variable assumptions, the assignment effect on outcome divided by its effect on uptake identifies a complier average effect.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let $Z$ be random assignment, $D$ treatment receipt and $Y$ outcome. The Wald ratio is

$$
\frac{\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z=1]-\mathbb{E}[Y\mid Z=0]}
{\mathbb{E}[D\mid Z=1]-\mathbb{E}[D\mid Z=0]}.
$$

The denominator measures how much assignment changes receipt. Under the required assumptions, the numerator's assignment effect is attributable to participants whose receipt changes with assignment, allowing the ratio to identify their average treatment effect.

### Assumptions

Assignment is independent of potential outcomes, changes receipt, and affects outcome only through receipt. Monotonicity excludes people who would take treatment only when assigned control, and consistency and interference conditions must hold.

### Common mistake

This is not automatically the effect for every participant or every future user. Exclusion can fail if the encouragement itself affects motivation, and a small uptake difference produces an unstable ratio. Report the first-stage effect and justify each assumption.
keyTakeaways: Write outcome and uptake assignment contrasts.
State relevance, exclusion, random assignment and monotonicity.
Interpret the result for compliers and recognise weak uptake differences.

questions.title: What is the average treatment effect in potential-outcome notation?
questions.questionMarkdown: Define the ATE and explain how randomisation helps despite observing only one outcome per participant.
questions.tldrAnswer: ATE averages the difference between each unit's treatment and control potential outcomes; randomisation identifies this average under the design assumptions.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For participant $i$, let $Y_i(1)$ be the outcome under treatment and $Y_i(0)$ under control. The population ATE is $\mathbb{E}[Y(1)-Y(0)]$. Only the outcome corresponding to the received assignment is observed, so an individual's contrast is unavailable.

Random assignment makes group membership independent of potential outcomes. Under consistency and suitable assignment probabilities, the difference in observed group means estimates the difference in their potential-outcome means and hence the average effect.

### Assumptions

Treatment versions must be well defined, observed outcomes must correspond to the specified assignment, and interference between units must be absent or incorporated into the estimand. The target population must also be explicit.

### Common mistake

Randomisation does not reveal every person's effect or ensure effects are equal. A zero average can combine positive and negative individual effects. Distinguish population identification from sampling uncertainty and from transport to a different deployment population.
keyTakeaways: Define both potential outcomes and their average contrast.
Explain randomisation's independence role.
Distinguish an average effect from individual effects and transport.

questions.title: How do percentage-point change and relative lift differ?
questions.questionMarkdown: A conversion rate rises from 4% to 5%. Report both changes and explain a limitation of relative lift.
questions.tldrAnswer: The increase is one percentage point and 25% relative to the 4% control rate.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Absolute change subtracts the two rates: 5% minus 4% equals one percentage point. Relative lift divides that difference by the control rate: 0.01/0.04 equals 0.25, or 25%. Saying only that conversion improved by 1% leaves the intended quantity unclear.

The two measures answer different questions. Absolute change can translate directly into additional events per eligible person, while relative lift expresses proportional improvement compared with the baseline.

### Assumptions

Both rates use compatible populations, time windows and denominators. The relative comparison needs a non-zero baseline, and uncertainty in both estimates contributes to uncertainty in the ratio.

### Common mistake

A large relative percentage can accompany a small absolute change when the baseline is rare. Near-zero control rates can also make relative estimates unstable. Report baseline, treatment rate, absolute change and uncertainty alongside any relative claim.
keyTakeaways: Calculate both scales correctly.
State the control denominator.
Explain near-zero instability and practical absolute impact.

questions.title: What should determine the minimum detectable effect?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how an MDE enters experiment planning and why it should not be chosen only to make the experiment short.
questions.tldrAnswer: It is a sensitivity target at specified power and error rates, chosen in relation to a meaningful decision and feasible resources.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
An MDE is an effect size at which the planned design achieves a chosen probability of detection under stated assumptions. It links baseline variability, sample size, allocation, significance and power. It is not a boundary below which effects cannot exist or can never yield significance.

Choose a target related to the smallest improvement that would change the decision, while considering implementation costs and plausible harms. If detecting that effect requires more data than available, the limitation should be explicit rather than hidden by selecting a convenient larger effect.

### Assumptions

Planning inputs such as baseline rate, variance, independent units and analysis method should match deployment. Estimates from historical data have uncertainty.

### Common mistake

An observed effect below the MDE is not automatically unimportant, and a significant estimate above it may still be exaggerated by noise. Interpret the effect interval and decision threshold after the experiment, not the planning number alone.
keyTakeaways: Define MDE through power at a specified effect.
Connect it to a meaningful decision and design inputs.
Distinguish planning sensitivity from post-experiment interpretation.

questions.title: When is equal traffic allocation statistically efficient?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain why a balanced split often minimises variance and when a different allocation can be justified.
questions.tldrAnswer: With fixed total sample size and equal outcome variances, equal allocation minimises difference-in-means variance; unequal variances, costs or risks can change the choice.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For independent groups, the variance of a mean difference is $\sigma_T^2/n_T+\sigma_C^2/n_C$. With fixed total count and equal variances, this sum is minimised by $n_T=n_C$. If variances differ and costs are equal, the variance-minimising allocation has $n_T/n_C=\sigma_T/\sigma_C$.

Operational constraints may favour less exposure to a risky treatment even when that sacrifices precision. Different per-observation costs also change the optimisation problem.

### Assumptions

Planning variances are relevant and the observations are independent at the analysis unit. Allocation probabilities and any later changes must be recorded so the analysis can represent the actual design.

### Common mistake

A small treatment allocation is not free protection against all risk: it can lengthen the experiment and delay detection. Conversely, 50:50 is not universally optimal. State whether the design optimises precision, cost, risk or another criterion.
keyTakeaways: Derive the independent-group variance.
State equal-variance and unequal-variance allocation results.
Separate statistical efficiency from operational constraints.

questions.title: Why does reaching the sample target not always mean the experiment is ready to stop?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the roles of calendar cycles, delayed outcomes and a pre-specified stopping plan.
questions.tldrAnswer: The count target addresses one source of precision, while duration determines which behaviour and outcome windows are represented.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
An experiment may collect enough users in a few hours while missing weekday-weekend differences, billing cycles or delayed conversions. If treatment effects vary across those conditions, the short period estimates a different mixture from the intended rollout.

Specify an exposure duration and follow-up window that represent the decision. Distinguish when enrolment stops from when all enrolled participants have completed outcome measurement. Account for planned calendar variation in analysis or design where appropriate.

### Assumptions

The relevant cycles and delays are known well enough to plan. Extending duration can introduce other changes, such as seasonality or product updates, so longer is not automatically more representative.

### Common mistake

Stopping when significance appears changes a fixed-horizon design even if a minimum calendar period has elapsed. Likewise, running for a full week does not remove every time-related threat. Follow the declared stopping and measurement rules and state the period to which the result applies.
keyTakeaways: Separate precision count from represented calendar conditions.
Distinguish enrolment and outcome follow-up.
Retain a valid stopping rule and qualify time transport.

questions.title: How can an early treatment effect differ from a durable effect?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain novelty and learning responses and how you would investigate them without selecting a favourable window.
questions.tldrAnswer: Initial reactions and adaptation can change effects over exposure time, so pre-planned cohort and time comparisons help distinguish temporary from sustained behaviour.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A new interface may initially attract attention, causing a temporary increase in engagement. It may instead slow users until they learn the layout, producing an initially negative effect that later improves. Neither pattern is guaranteed, and effects can vary by previous experience.

Track time since first exposure separately from calendar time. New cohorts arriving later can help distinguish adaptation from a simultaneous external event, provided the design and sample sizes support those comparisons.

### Assumptions

The exposure history is measured reliably and the analysis accounts for repeated observations. The intended target may be first-use experience, established use or their rollout mixture, which are different questions.

### Common mistake

Discarding the first days only after seeing an unfavourable result changes the estimand and creates selection. Pre-specify the relevant windows or label later analyses exploratory, and use a longer confirmatory design when persistence determines the decision.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish novelty from learning and calendar changes.
Define the exposure-age target.
Avoid post-result window selection.

questions.title: Why can earlier treatment contaminate a later control period?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain carryover in a repeated-period experiment and how a washout interval should be justified.
questions.tldrAnswer: Treatment can change persistent state, habits or resources, so later outcomes may depend on assignment history rather than only current assignment.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A treatment may fill a cache, alter user expectations or change a marketplace's supply. Switching the nominal assignment to control does not instantly undo those effects. A later control period can therefore inherit consequences of earlier treatment, weakening a simple current-period comparison.

A washout period excludes or separately models time during which persistence is expected to dissipate. Its length should be supported by knowledge of the mechanism or data from a suitable design, not chosen solely to obtain a cleaner result.

### Assumptions

The relevant treatment history and time scale are identified. Randomising period sequences helps distinguish history effects only when the design and analysis actually account for them.

### Common mistake

Alternating treatment and control deterministically does not remove carryover and can align treatment with predictable time patterns. Define the effect of a treatment sequence if history is unavoidable, rather than claiming an instantaneous effect the data cannot isolate.
keyTakeaways: Identify persistent mechanisms linking periods.
Justify washout or history modelling.
Avoid equating alternating labels with independent periods.

questions.title: What changes when one participant's treatment affects another?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how peer effects or marketplace interactions alter the ordinary treatment-effect question.
questions.tldrAnswer: A participant's outcome can depend on other assignments, so own-treatment labels alone no longer define all relevant potential outcomes.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
In a social feature, treating one user may change messages received by untreated friends. In a marketplace, treating buyers can alter prices or availability for control buyers. The outcome then depends on both own assignment and an exposure pattern involving others.

A design may randomise connected groups, vary treatment saturation or model a defined exposure mapping to estimate direct and spillover effects. The target must state which surrounding assignments are held fixed or averaged over.

### Assumptions

The interference structure is sufficiently understood for the chosen design. Cluster boundaries do not automatically stop interactions across clusters, and a small experiment may alter the environment differently from full rollout.

### Common mistake

An ordinary user-level difference can be a valid contrast for that particular mixed-assignment environment while failing to estimate the full-rollout effect. Do not assume randomisation alone removes interference; define the policy comparison and check whether the design supports it.
keyTakeaways: Explain outcomes depending on other participants' assignments.
Distinguish direct, spillover and policy effects.
Recognise that full rollout can differ from mixed exposure.

questions.title: How does within-cluster correlation reduce effective sample size?
questions.questionMarkdown: Derive the simple equal-cluster-size design effect and state its limitations.
questions.tldrAnswer: With common cluster size m and intracluster correlation rho, the variance inflation relative to independent observations is one plus (m minus one) rho.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
For $m$ equal-variance observations in one cluster with common pairwise correlation $\rho$, their mean has variance $\sigma^2[1+(m-1)\rho]/m$. Compared with $\sigma^2/m$ under independence, the inflation factor is $1+(m-1)\rho$.

For example, clusters of 50 with correlation 0.05 give a factor of 3.45. Adding more observations within existing clusters then yields less information than adding comparable independent units, making the number of assigned clusters crucial.

### Assumptions

This simple formula uses independent clusters, equal cluster sizes, a common within-cluster variance and correlation, and an appropriate cluster-based design. Unequal sizes, informative cluster size and more complex correlation require different calculations.

### Common mistake

Dividing row count by this factor is only a planning approximation, not a substitute for cluster-aware inference. A large number of rows spread over very few clusters can still give unreliable standard errors and weak randomisation support.
keyTakeaways: Derive covariance-driven variance inflation.
Calculate and interpret a design effect.
State equal-size assumptions and the importance of cluster count.
