questions.title: How does QLoRA combine low-bit weights with trainable adapters?
questions.questionMarkdown: Distinguish weight storage, computation precision and trainable state.
questions.tldrAnswer: It stores a frozen base model in a low-bit representation while training small adapter parameters, with computation and optimiser state using their own precisions.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A quantised frozen base reduces memory needed to store pretrained weights. Low-rank adapters add trainable updates without requiring full optimiser state for every base parameter. During computation, quantised values are interpreted through their scales and a supported calculation format; this does not mean every arithmetic operation uses four bits.

The original QLoRA approach combines a particular low-bit weight format with additional memory-saving techniques. Total training memory still includes activations, adapter gradients, optimiser state and implementation buffers.

### Assumptions

Quantisation and adapter placement are supported by the model and kernels. Approximation error depends on the weights, format and task, so quality should be compared with suitable higher-precision baselines.

### Common mistake

A low-bit base is not updated like full-precision fine-tuning, and its storage ratio is not the ratio of total training memory. Distinguish frozen parameter storage, dequantised computation and trainable adapter state when estimating hardware requirements.
keyTakeaways: Separate frozen low-bit base weights from trainable adapters.
Distinguish storage and computation precision.
Account for activations, optimiser state and quality changes.

questions.title: How should model size and training data be balanced under fixed compute?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the trade-off between adding parameters and training on more tokens.
questions.tldrAnswer: Both consume training compute, so the best allocation depends on empirical loss scaling, data quality and the operating regime rather than one universal ratio.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A larger dense model generally costs more per training token. With a fixed compute budget, increasing parameter count leaves fewer tokens or updates available. A smaller model trained on more suitable data can therefore outperform a larger undertrained model under the same budget.

Compute-optimal studies fit empirical relationships between loss, parameter count and token count, then optimise those relationships subject to a compute constraint. The resulting recommendations apply to the measured architecture, data and scale range.

### Assumptions

Additional tokens have useful quality and diversity, and the compute estimate reflects the actual training setup. Inference cost, data availability and latency can change the practical optimum even when training loss is the original objective.

### Common mistake

A published parameter-to-token rule is not a timeless constant for every language, domain or architecture. Repeated low-quality data need not provide the same benefit as fresh informative data. Validate scaling estimates within the intended regime and include deployment costs.
keyTakeaways: Explain the fixed-compute trade-off.
Describe empirical scaling as regime-dependent.
Include data quality and inference constraints.

questions.title: Why do total and active parameter counts differ in a mixture of experts?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain sparse expert routing and the costs that remain despite activating only a subset.
questions.tldrAnswer: A router selects a few expert modules per token, reducing some per-token arithmetic while all experts still require storage and coordination.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A sparse mixture-of-experts layer contains several expert networks and a routing mechanism that chooses a subset for each token. Different tokens can use different experts, so total model capacity exceeds the parameters actively applied to one token. Shared layers, such as attention, may still run for every token.

This separates parameter-storage cost from some arithmetic cost. On multiple devices, routing can also require communication to move tokens to the selected experts and combine their outputs.

### Assumptions

The top-k routing rule, expert dimensions and shared architecture determine active count. Load balancing, expert capacity and batching affect realised throughput and whether tokens receive the intended processing.

### Common mistake

Sparse activation does not make unused parameters free. Memory, communication and imbalanced routing can dominate performance. Total count alone overstates per-token compute, while active count alone understates system requirements. Report both and measure the intended serving workload.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish total, active and shared parameters.
Explain routing and communication costs.
Account for load balancing and actual workload performance.

questions.title: What can a smaller model learn from a teacher?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare distillation using soft token targets with training on teacher-generated responses.
questions.tldrAnswer: A student can imitate probability patterns or generated behaviour, but capacity and data choices limit transfer and can also transmit teacher errors.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Soft-target distillation trains a student to match a teacher's probability distribution, sometimes after temperature scaling. Relative probabilities can communicate similarities that one hard target omits. Sequence-level approaches instead use teacher-generated responses as supervised examples, transferring observed behaviour through text.

The student need not copy the teacher's architecture, but its smaller capacity and training coverage can limit which abilities it reproduces. Different tasks may transfer unevenly.

### Assumptions

Teacher outputs and the training data are suitable for the intended use. The objective, generation settings and evaluation distribution determine what behaviour is emphasised.

### Common mistake

Distillation is not the same as quantising an existing model's weights. It trains a different model and can inherit hallucinations, biases or systematic omissions from its teacher. Evaluate independent task outcomes and retained capabilities rather than assuming a smaller student preserves every teacher skill.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish soft-distribution and generated-sequence supervision.
Explain capacity and coverage limits.
Separate distillation from quantisation and check inherited errors.

questions.title: How can speculative decoding preserve the target distribution?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain drafting, target verification and the correction required when a draft token is rejected.
questions.tldrAnswer: A fast model proposes tokens, and a specific acceptance-and-resampling rule corrects its proposals to match the target model's sampling law.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Let q be the draft distribution and p the target distribution for a prefix. A proposed token x is accepted with probability $\min(1,p(x)/q(x))$. If rejected, sample from the normalised positive part of $p-q$ and discard incompatible later draft tokens.

Several draft positions can be checked in a target-model pass, creating a speed opportunity when many proposals are accepted. With the specified algorithm and conditions, the resulting token distribution matches ordinary sampling from p rather than the uncorrected draft model.

### Assumptions

Probabilities correspond to the actual decoding transformations and prefixes. Acceptance calculations and residual sampling must be implemented correctly; target and draft vocabularies must be compatible.

### Common mistake

Accepting every plausible draft token changes the distribution. Preservation also does not mean identical random outputs on every run. Speedup depends on acceptance rate, draft overhead, batching and hardware, so a larger or more accurate draft is not always faster overall.
keyTakeaways: State the acceptance ratio and residual correction.
Explain parallel verification without accepting every proposal.
Separate distribution preservation from identical samples and guaranteed speedup.

questions.title: Why can a model miss evidence that fits inside its context window?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the difference between supported context length and reliable use of information at every position.
questions.tldrAnswer: Capacity to accept tokens does not guarantee equal retrieval or reasoning quality across their positions and surrounding distractors.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A model may accept a long sequence yet fail to use the decisive passage. Research has found position-dependent performance in some models and tasks, including cases where evidence in the middle is used less reliably than evidence near the beginning or end. This is an empirical pattern, not a universal law for every model.

Relevant evidence must compete with distractors, repeated passages and conflicting information. Training lengths, position representations and task demands all affect the outcome.

### Assumptions

Evaluate the actual model version and workload, moving equivalent evidence across positions while controlling other changes. Token-limit compliance alone tests only whether the request fits.

### Common mistake

Increasing the context budget is not a substitute for evidence selection. More text can add irrelevant material or contradictions. Test answer quality, citation support and abstention with realistic long documents rather than relying solely on a maximum-window specification.
keyTakeaways: Separate input capacity from effective evidence use.
Describe position sensitivity as an empirical finding.
Test controlled positions and realistic distractors.

questions.title: How do passage boundaries affect retrieval?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain the trade-off between small focused chunks and larger context-preserving passages.
questions.tldrAnswer: Small passages can match a query precisely but omit necessary context; large passages preserve context while diluting relevance and consuming more tokens.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Splitting documents determines the units retrieved and supplied to the generator. A short chunk may contain a definition but omit the exception in the next paragraph. A long chunk may preserve that relationship while embedding several unrelated topics that weaken retrieval precision.

Overlap can reduce boundary losses, but it duplicates text and can cause several retrieved results to repeat the same evidence. Structural boundaries such as headings, tables and complete procedures can be more useful than blindly cutting at one token count.

### Assumptions

The corpus, query types and downstream context budget determine an appropriate policy. Preserve source identifiers, section locations and document versions through splitting.

### Common mistake

There is no universally optimal chunk size. Evaluate retrieval coverage and answer support together, including questions whose evidence crosses boundaries. More overlap or more retrieved chunks can increase cost without adding independent information.

questions.title: Why might dense and lexical retrieval find different passages?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare semantic embedding retrieval with exact-term matching and explain a hybrid approach.
questions.tldrAnswer: Dense retrieval can connect paraphrases, while lexical methods often preserve rare identifiers and exact terms; their strengths can complement one another.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Dense retrieval maps queries and passages to learned vectors and ranks by a similarity function. It can retrieve a passage phrased differently from the question when training has captured the relevant semantic relationship.

Lexical retrieval scores term matches and their corpus statistics. It can be strong for error codes, product identifiers and unusual names whose exact characters matter. A dense representation may blur those distinctions, while lexical matching may miss an otherwise clear paraphrase.

### Assumptions

The embedding model, distance measure, text processing and corpus language suit the task. Hybrid ranking requires a justified way to combine or rerank candidates because raw score scales are not automatically comparable.

### Common mistake

Calling a method semantic does not guarantee relevance or factual support. Evaluate both recall of required evidence and ranking quality on representative queries, including exact identifiers, paraphrases and out-of-domain vocabulary.

questions.title: Why rerank a small retrieved candidate set?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain how a cross-encoder differs from independently embedded query and document vectors.
questions.tldrAnswer: Joint query-passage scoring can model detailed interactions, but its greater per-pair cost makes it useful after broad retrieval.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A bi-encoder computes query and passage representations separately, allowing passage vectors to be stored and searched efficiently. A cross-encoder processes a query and candidate passage together, so token interactions can influence a relevance score directly.

A common pipeline retrieves a larger candidate set cheaply, then applies the more expensive joint scorer to that smaller set. This can improve ordering when initial similarity scores miss fine distinctions, such as whether a passage answers the specific condition in the query.

### Assumptions

The reranker is trained or evaluated for the domain and query style. Its score must represent the intended relevance criterion, and candidate count trades latency against possible evidence coverage.

### Common mistake

Reranking cannot recover a decisive document that never entered the candidate set. Nor does a high relevance score certify that a passage is current, authorised or true. Check initial recall and preserve access controls throughout both stages.

questions.title: How can an answer be faithful to evidence but factually wrong?
questions.questionMarkdown: Distinguish source faithfulness, factual correctness and citation support.
questions.tldrAnswer: An answer can accurately repeat a false or outdated source, so agreement with retrieved text is not the same as external truth.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Faithfulness asks whether the answer's claims follow from the supplied evidence. Factual correctness asks whether those claims are true in the relevant world and time. Citation support asks whether the linked passage actually substantiates the claim it accompanies. These dimensions overlap but are not identical.

A model can faithfully summarise an outdated policy and still give the wrong current advice. It can also state a true fact while attaching a citation that does not support it, or add unsupported details to otherwise relevant evidence.

### Assumptions

The evaluation has a defined truth reference, document version and claim granularity. Some questions require acknowledging conflicting or insufficient evidence rather than selecting one fluent answer.

### Common mistake

An automated judge's high score is not a substitute for validating that judge on human-reviewed examples. Evaluate separate dimensions and inspect disagreements, especially where source quality or time sensitivity matters.
keyTakeaways: Define faithfulness, truth and citation support separately.
Give cases where the dimensions disagree.
Validate automated judging and handle insufficient evidence.

questions.title: How can training overlap inflate an evaluation score?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain direct and near-duplicate benchmark exposure and why detecting it is difficult.
questions.tldrAnswer: Prior exposure can reward memorisation or familiarity rather than the intended transfer, while overlap checks remain incomplete evidence.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
If evaluation questions, answers or close variants occur in training, a model may perform well without solving the task in the intended unseen setting. Leakage can also enter through instruction tuning, generated training data or repeated development against a public benchmark.

Exact string matching detects only some cases. Reformatting, paraphrases, translated versions and shared source material complicate detection, while generic phrases can produce false suspicions. Fresh or carefully held-out evaluations help but still require a documented data boundary.

### Assumptions

The benchmark's purpose determines what exposure is disallowed. Knowing general domain facts is different from seeing the actual test items and answers.

### Common mistake

A high score alone does not prove contamination, and failure to find duplicates does not prove absence. Report known overlap checks, uncertainty about training data and performance on additional tasks designed to test transfer rather than relying on one headline number.
keyTakeaways: Identify several routes of evaluation exposure.
Explain limitations of exact and semantic overlap checks.
Separate general knowledge from disallowed item exposure.

questions.title: Why can retrieved documents contain unsafe instructions?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain indirect prompt injection and how a system should separate evidence from action authority.
questions.tldrAnswer: External text can ask the model to change behaviour, but it should be treated as untrusted data while tool permissions and action checks are enforced separately.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A retrieved page, email or repository file may contain text that tells the model to ignore its task, reveal information or invoke a tool. The attack arrives inside material the system was meant to read as evidence, rather than as a direct authorised user request.

The application should preserve the distinction between trusted instructions and external content. Tool access, allowed destinations, data disclosure and consequential actions need controls outside the text-generation step, with the least authority required for the task.

### Assumptions

Legitimate documents can contain quoted commands or examples, so handling must preserve useful reading without granting those words authority. The threat depends on which data and tools the application exposes.

### Common mistake

Adding one warning prompt or removing a few suspicious phrases is incomplete protection. A syntactically valid tool request can still be unauthorised. Validate actions against the actual user's scope and use defence measures that do not rely solely on the model recognising every attack.
keyTakeaways: Identify external-content instructions as a different authority source.
Enforce tool and disclosure controls independently.
Avoid equating prompt filtering or valid syntax with authorisation.

questions.title: What can grammar-constrained generation guarantee?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain token constraints for structured output and distinguish syntax from semantic correctness.
questions.tldrAnswer: It restricts continuations to a permitted formal language, but valid structure does not establish truthful values or a successful action.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
A constrained decoder tracks which token continuations remain compatible with a grammar or supported schema. It masks disallowed choices so a completed sequence follows the permitted structure. This can reduce malformed JSON, invalid field names or impossible syntactic combinations when those constraints are represented correctly.

The constraint concerns the output language. It does not determine whether a supplied date exists in the source, a price is correct or an action is authorised. Some schema features may also exceed the decoder's supported constraint system.

### Assumptions

The grammar, tokenizer integration and completion procedure are correct, and generation reaches a valid accepting state. A token budget can still interrupt an unfinished structure.

### Common mistake

Parsing successfully is not the same as meeting the task. Apply semantic validation, source checks and business rules after generation. Report truncation or validation failure rather than treating every well-shaped response as trustworthy.
keyTakeaways: Explain restricting allowed continuations.
Qualify guarantees by grammar support and completed generation.
Separate syntax from semantic, factual and action validation.

questions.title: Why can task specialisation reduce earlier capabilities?
questions.questionMarkdown: Explain forgetting during fine-tuning and how to evaluate a mitigation.
questions.tldrAnswer: Updates that improve the new training objective can alter representations or output behaviour needed for earlier tasks, so both new and retained abilities must be measured.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
Fine-tuning optimises performance on a new data distribution. If that distribution is narrow, the updates can weaken behaviour learned earlier or make the model overuse the new task's style. Improvement on the fine-tuning set therefore does not establish improvement across the original range of uses.

Possible mitigations include mixing relevant earlier data, constraining updates, distillation objectives or adapter-based approaches. Their effectiveness depends on data, capacity and optimisation, and each introduces trade-offs in cost or specialisation.

### Assumptions

Retained capabilities are defined through representative evaluation tasks rather than a vague claim of general ability. Keep evaluation data separate from choosing mitigation settings.

### Common mistake

Freezing base weights does not guarantee unchanged behaviour when an active adapter modifies the model's outputs. A smaller learning rate also offers no universal protection. Compare the specialised model, the original model and any mitigation across both target and retained tasks, including uncertainty and failure cases.
keyTakeaways: Explain conflict between the new objective and retained behaviour.
Evaluate both task families on separate data.
Avoid guarantees from frozen bases, adapters or smaller learning rates.

questions.title: Does quadrupling a mini-batch remove four times as much gradient noise?
questions.questionMarkdown: At fixed model parameters, each independently sampled training example gives a gradient component with variance 36. Compare the mean-gradient estimates from batches of 9 and 36 examples. What changes if the batch is sampled without replacement? Relate these estimates to full-batch, single-example stochastic and mini-batch gradient descent.
questions.tldrAnswer: Independent averaging gives variances 4 and 1, so the standard deviation halves rather than quarters. Uniform sampling without replacement adds a finite-population correction.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Fix the parameters and a dataset of $N$ examples. The objective is the average of differentiable per-example losses. Sample uniformly; exclude operations whose per-example loss changes with batch composition, such as training-mode batch normalisation.

### Reasoning

Let $g_i$ be one gradient component, $\bar g$ its dataset mean and $\sigma^2=N^{-1}\sum_i(g_i-\bar g)^2$. Independent sampling with replacement gives

$$
E[\hat g_B]=\bar g,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(\hat g_B)=\frac{\sigma^2}{B}.
$$

Thus the stated batches have variances $36/9=4$ and $36/36=1$, and standard deviations 2 and 1. For a uniformly chosen subset without replacement, with $N>1$ and $B\le N$,

$$
\operatorname{Var}(\hat g_B)=\frac{\sigma^2}{B}\frac{N-B}{N-1}.
$$

A full-data batch has no sampling noise at these fixed parameters. Larger batches cost more work and memory per update; their benefit depends on hardware, learning rate and the training budget.

### Common mistake

Lower estimator variance does not guarantee faster training or better test performance. The calculation concerns a single update, not the whole optimisation trajectory.

### Update regimes

Full-batch gradient descent evaluates the whole training objective for each update, giving an exact data gradient but potentially costly updates. Single-example stochastic gradient descent updates from one sampled example, using little per-update memory but a noisy estimate. Mini-batch gradient descent averages an intermediate number, allowing useful vectorised computation while retaining sampling noise. The term SGD is also commonly used for mini-batch training. Compare elapsed time and validation performance at a specified budget, not just the number of updates.
keyTakeaways: State fixed parameters, uniform sampling and an additive per-example objective.
Calculate variances 4 and 1, and distinguish variance from standard deviation.
Explain the finite-population correction and zero sampling noise for a full batch.
Separate gradient-estimation precision from training speed and generalisation. Distinguish full-batch, single-example and mini-batch updates.

questions.title: Why can uncertain examples consume labels without improving a model?
questions.questionMarkdown: A document classifier can request 80 new labels. Its highest-uncertainty queue contains repeated scans and badly corrupted pages. Why might labelling this queue disappoint, and how would you assess a better selection rule?
questions.tldrAnswer: Uncertainty can reflect irreducible ambiguity, unusual inputs or repeated information. Combine uncertainty with diversity and relevance, then compare against random selection on a separate representative evaluation set.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

This is pool-based active learning: unlabelled examples are available and a person can label selected examples before retraining. The aim is performance on the intended document population under a fixed annotation budget.

### Reasoning

A prediction close to a decision boundary does not establish that its label will help many future predictions. Corrupted pages may remain ambiguous even to annotators. Repeated scans spend several labels on nearly the same evidence. Unusual pages can dominate uncertainty while being rare in the target population. Conversely, confident model errors can be missed entirely.

Remove duplicates, record unanswerable cases, and select a diverse batch that also covers relevant parts of the input distribution. Density weighting or a mixture of uncertain and random examples are options to test, not guaranteed improvements; rare but important classes must not be discarded merely for being rare.

Compare learning curves at equal labelling cost against random sampling, using an untouched representative evaluation set and repeated runs.

### Common mistake

Accuracy on the actively selected labels is not an unbiased estimate of target-population accuracy because the selection rule changes which examples receive labels.
keyTakeaways: Explain why uncertainty need not imply useful new information.
Identify duplicate, ambiguous and unrepresentative selections.
Propose diversity or mixed selection while retaining important rare cases.
Compare against random selection using a separate representative evaluation set.

questions.title: Can accurate reconstruction hide a poor representation for classification?
questions.questionMarkdown: An image autoencoder reconstructs held-out product photographs accurately, but a classifier trained on its frozen codes struggles to identify defects. Why is this possible, and what evidence would justify changing the representation? Name other uses of autoencoders and explain what must be checked for each.
questions.tldrAnswer: Reconstruction rewards preserving the input, which may favour background and lighting over subtle defects. Test the codes on the intended task; bottlenecks and regularisation can help but do not guarantee useful features.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The autoencoder receives no defect labels. It learns an encoder $f$ and decoder $g$ by reducing a reconstruction loss such as $\lVert x-g(f(x))\rVert^2$. The downstream classifier has limited labelled data and capacity.

### Reasoning

Most pixels might describe packaging and background. Reconstructing them well can dominate the loss even if a small defect is poorly represented. A sufficiently flexible network can preserve input details without organising its codes in a form the chosen classifier can use. Even low held-out reconstruction error therefore does not establish downstream usefulness.

Compare classifiers trained on the frozen codes with sensible alternatives, using separate training, validation and test data. Inspect performance across defect types. Vary the code dimension or regularisation using validation results. A denoising objective or a smaller bottleneck may encourage useful structure, but could also remove subtle defect information.

### Common mistake

A smaller code does not automatically capture semantic meaning. Select representation changes by the intended task and evaluate the final choice on held-out examples; reconstruction loss alone cannot settle the decision.

### Uses beyond a frozen classifier

The encoder maps an input into a code and the decoder reconstructs an input from that code; a bottleneck or regulariser constrains what is retained. A compact code can support dimensionality reduction, but storage or downstream utility needs measurement. A denoising autoencoder learns to reconstruct a clean target from a corrupted input, so its training corruption must match the intended use. Reconstruction error can also be an anomaly score when trained on representative normal data, but unusual inputs can still reconstruct well and normal variation can reconstruct poorly. Validate anomaly thresholds with relevant examples rather than treating reconstruction error as a universal detector.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish reconstruction loss from downstream classification performance.
Explain how background detail or model capacity can undermine useful codes.
Describe a held-out downstream comparison with alternative representations.
State why bottlenecks and denoising are hypotheses to test, not guarantees. Identify dimensionality reduction, denoising and anomaly-scoring uses with their limitations.

questions.title: How much computation does separating spatial and channel filtering save?
questions.questionMarkdown: A convolution uses a 5 by 5 kernel to map 12 input channels to 40 output channels. Replace it with one depthwise filter per input channel followed by a 1 by 1 convolution. Count weights and multiply-accumulates per output position. Is the replacement equivalent?
questions.tldrAnswer: The standard layer uses 12,000 weights; the separated layers use 300 + 480 = 780. Their multiply-accumulate count is 6.5% of the original per output position, but they constrain the filters and need not preserve accuracy.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Ignore biases, normalisation and nonlinearities. Use one depthwise filter per input channel, stride one and padding that preserves spatial size, followed by a pointwise layer producing the same output channels.

### Reasoning

A standard convolution has $k^2C_{\mathrm{in}}C_{\mathrm{out}}$ weights. A depthwise layer has $k^2C_{\mathrm{in}}$; the pointwise layer has $C_{\mathrm{in}}C_{\mathrm{out}}$.

Here the counts are $25\times12\times40=12000$ versus $25\times12+12\times40=780$. Each weight contributes one multiply-accumulate per output position. At equal spatial size, the ratio is

$$
\frac{1}{C_{\mathrm{out}}}+\frac{1}{k^2}=\frac{1}{40}+\frac{1}{25}=0.065.
$$

Without intervening nonlinearities, the effective kernel satisfies $W_{u,v,i,o}=D_{u,v,i}P_{i,o}$. For each input channel, all output channels share a spatial filter up to scaling. An arbitrary standard kernel need not satisfy that constraint.

### Common mistake

A 93.5% arithmetic reduction does not imply identical accuracy or a 93.5% latency reduction. Memory traffic, kernel implementation and hardware utilisation also matter; measure the trained model on the target device.
keyTakeaways: Count 12,000 standard weights and 780 separated weights under explicit assumptions.
Derive the cost ratio and relate it to equal output spatial size.
Explain the restriction imposed by sharing one spatial filter per input channel.
Distinguish arithmetic savings from measured latency and predictive accuracy.

questions.title: Why is the largest uniform observation a biased endpoint estimate?
questions.questionMarkdown: A simulator draws independent values uniformly from $[0,\theta]$, with known lower endpoint zero and unknown $\theta>0$. From 9 draws, the maximum is 18. Derive the maximum-likelihood estimate and an unbiased endpoint estimate. Must the unbiased estimate have the smallest mean squared error?
questions.tldrAnswer: The likelihood is maximised at the observed maximum, 18. Since the expected maximum is 9θ/10, multiplying it by 10/9 gives the unbiased estimate 20. Unbiasedness alone does not establish minimum mean squared error.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The $n\ge1$ observations are independent draws from the same continuous uniform distribution with known lower bound zero, without censoring or rounding.

### Reasoning

Let $M=\max_i X_i$. Using the density convention that includes the endpoints,

$$
L(\theta)=\theta^{-n}\mathbf{1}\{\theta\ge M\}.
$$

For $M>0$, which holds almost surely, this decreases over the feasible range, so the maximum-likelihood estimate is $M$. Independence gives $P(M\le m)=(m/\theta)^n$ for $0\le m\le\theta$. Integrating the survival function yields

$$
E[M]=\int_0^\theta\left[1-(m/\theta)^n\right]dm=\frac{n\theta}{n+1}.
$$

Hence $(n+1)M/n$ is unbiased. The observed estimates are 18 and 20. Its unbiasedness concerns repeated samples; it does not mean 20 equals the unknown endpoint for this sample.

### Common mistake

Zero bias does not minimise every error criterion. Mean squared error equals variance plus squared bias, so eliminating bias can cost enough variance to worsen that criterion. An unbiased correction is not automatically an optimal estimator under squared-error loss.
keyTakeaways: Use the parameter-dependent support to derive the likelihood and MLE.
Derive the maximum distribution and its expectation.
Calculate the correction and the observed values 18 and 20.
Distinguish unbiasedness from minimum mean squared error.

questions.title: Which overlapping coin pattern finishes first?
questions.questionMarkdown: A monitor reads independent fair coin flips. It stops when either HHT or HTH appears as three consecutive flips. Starting with no flips, what is the probability that HHT appears first? Show how partial matches change the calculation.
questions.tldrAnswer: HHT wins with probability 2/3. Track the longest observed suffix that is a prefix of either target; the two patterns are not equally likely to win merely because each has length three.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Flips are independent with P(H)=P(T)=1/2. Matching uses overlapping consecutive triples, and the process stops at the first completed target.

### Reasoning

Let $p_0,p_H,p_{HH},p_{HT}$ be the probabilities of eventually seeing HHT first from the empty state and the three relevant partial matches. A T from the empty state leaves it empty, so $p_0=(p_H+p_0)/2$, giving $p_0=p_H$.

From HH, another H leaves the suffix HH; T completes HHT. Thus $p_{HH}=(p_{HH}+1)/2=1$. From HT, H loses immediately and T resets the state, so $p_{HT}=p_0/2$. Finally,

$$p_H=\tfrac12p_{HH}+\tfrac12p_{HT}=\tfrac12+\tfrac14p_0.$$

Solving gives $p_0=2/3$. Absorption occurs almost surely: disjoint blocks each have a positive chance of containing a target, so indefinite avoidance has probability zero.

### Common mistake

Counting the eight possible triples once ignores the history retained after a failed match. Equal probabilities for one fixed triple do not imply equal winning probabilities in an overlapping race.
keyTakeaways: Define states using useful suffixes rather than complete histories.
Write correct transitions for HH and HT.
Solve the recurrence to obtain 2/3.
Explain why equal pattern length does not imply an equal race.

questions.title: How do overlapping alert runs affect a trigger probability?
questions.questionMarkdown: A sensor produces an alert independently on each of three checks with probability 0.2. A trigger fires if any two adjacent checks both alert. Find the trigger probability and explain why adding the two pair probabilities is wrong.
questions.tldrAnswer: The probability is 0.072: add 0.04 for each adjacent pair and subtract 0.008 for the all-alert sequence counted twice.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The three alert indicators are independent and share probability p=0.2. The trigger requires at least one adjacent pair, including the case of three alerts.

### Reasoning

Let $A$ be alerts on checks 1 and 2 and $B$ alerts on checks 2 and 3. Then $P(A)=P(B)=p^2$. Their intersection requires all three checks to alert, so $P(A\cap B)=p^3$.

Inclusion-exclusion gives $P(A\cup B)=2p^2-p^3=0.08-0.008=0.072$. Although the underlying checks are independent, the pair events share the middle check and are not independent. In fact $P(A\cap B)=0.008$ differs from $P(A)P(B)=0.0016$.

### Common mistake

Do not subtract the all-alert sequence if the question instead asks for the expected number of alert pairs. That expectation is 2p² by linearity; a probability of any trigger and a count expectation are different quantities.
keyTakeaways: Define the two overlapping pair events.
Compute the intersection as three alerts.
Obtain 0.072 with inclusion-exclusion.
Distinguish an event probability from an expected pair count.

questions.title: When is discarding incomplete rows a poor baseline?
questions.questionMarkdown: A delivery-time dataset has missing parcel weights, especially for manually processed parcels. Compare dropping incomplete rows, median imputation and multivariate imputation. How would you evaluate them without making the validation set easier than deployment?
questions.tldrAnswer: Deletion may remove a systematically different group. Compare imputation methods fitted within training folds, evaluate the same deployment-relevant cases, and investigate why weights are missing.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The target is observed, parcel weight is sometimes missing at prediction time, and the missingness pattern can be associated with other recorded features or delivery time.

### Reasoning

Deleting rows sacrifices information and can select a different population. A complete-case score alone says little about performance on parcels with missing weights. Median imputation offers a simple training-fitted baseline but discards conditional relationships and understates uncertainty if treated as an observed measurement. Multivariate imputation predicts weights from available variables, adding modelling assumptions and possible error.

Choose folds that reflect deployment, fit each imputer on the training portion only, and transform held-out records without refitting. Compare all deployable alternatives on a common population, report results for missing-weight cases separately, and include missingness indicators where justified. If deletion means abstaining at deployment, report that coverage explicitly alongside error.

### Common mistake

More elaborate imputation does not by itself remove bias when missingness depends on unobserved values. Treat the missingness mechanism and sensitivity of conclusions as separate questions from predictive validation.
keyTakeaways: Explain the population change caused by complete-case deletion.
Compare median and conditional imputation assumptions.
Fit imputation within each training fold.
Evaluate missing cases and report abstention coverage consistently.

questions.title: Does a model with parameters have to be parametric?
questions.questionMarkdown: Compare a cubic regression curve with a fixed four coefficients and a nearest-neighbour predictor that stores the training set. Which is parametric in the usual statistical sense, and why does nonlinear shape not settle the distinction?
questions.tldrAnswer: The fixed cubic family is parametric; nearest-neighbour prediction is commonly nonparametric because its representation can grow with the data. Nonparametric does not mean parameter-free.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The polynomial degree and input dimension are fixed as sample size grows. The nearest-neighbour method retains training examples rather than compressing them into a fixed finite-dimensional family.

### Reasoning

A parametric family describes its members using a fixed finite-dimensional parameter, such as $f(x)=a+bx+cx^2+dx^3$. A nonlinear curve can therefore be parametric. Fixed-architecture neural networks are another finite-parameter example even when they contain many weights.

A nearest-neighbour predictor can retain more support points as observations accumulate. Its flexibility is not restricted to the same four-coefficient family. It still has hyperparameters, such as the number of neighbours and distance metric, and it still makes assumptions about local similarity. Kernel density estimation is another common nonparametric example.

The choice concerns approximation assumptions, data requirements, memory and validation performance. It does not establish that one class is universally more accurate.

### Common mistake

Counting whether any tunable number exists confuses a statistical family with its hyperparameters. Likewise, calling every nonlinear model nonparametric misclassifies the fixed polynomial.
keyTakeaways: Define fixed-dimensional parametric modelling.
Classify the fixed cubic and stored-neighbour examples.
Separate nonlinearity from the parametric distinction.
State that nonparametric methods still have assumptions and tuning choices.

questions.title: Why can balanced training data give misleading probabilities?
questions.questionMarkdown: Only 2% of deployment records are positive. A team oversamples positive training records until the classes are balanced, then interprets a model score of 0.8 as an 80% deployment risk. What must be checked, and where should resampling occur during validation?
questions.tldrAnswer: Resampling changes class prevalence and often the effective training objective. Keep it inside training folds, evaluate at deployment prevalence, and calibrate or apply a justified prior correction before interpreting scores as risks.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

For the explicit prior correction, sampling changes only class proportions, preserves P(X|Y), and the score is a calibrated posterior for the resampled distribution. Real models may violate these assumptions.

### Reasoning

Oversampling before splitting can put copies or related synthetic points in both training and validation. Split first, resample only training folds and keep validation prevalence representative. Class weighting is another way to change the objective, but does not guarantee calibrated deployment probabilities.

Let $q$ be the resampled posterior, $\pi_s=0.5$ the sampling prevalence and $\pi=0.02$ the deployment prevalence. Under the stated assumptions,

$$\frac{p}{1-p}=\frac{q}{1-q}\frac{\pi/(1-\pi)}{\pi_s/(1-\pi_s)}.$$

For $q=0.8$, the corrected odds are $4/49$, giving $p=4/53\approx0.0755$. This numerical result is illustrative, not a universal correction for an arbitrary classifier. Check calibration on untouched representative data and select decision thresholds using deployment costs.

### Common mistake

Balanced class counts do not imply balanced deployment risks. Also, evaluating on a balanced validation set can conceal how precision changes with prevalence.
keyTakeaways: Keep resampling within training folds.
Identify the change in class prior or weighted objective.
Derive the odds correction and its restrictive assumptions.
Validate calibration and decisions on representative data.

questions.title: Which PCA variant fits a memory-limited problem?
questions.questionMarkdown: A matrix of ten million rows cannot fit in memory, only 30 components are needed, and a separate task appears to require a nonlinear representation. Compare incremental PCA, randomised PCA and kernel PCA for these requirements.
questions.tldrAnswer: Incremental PCA processes batches; randomised PCA approximates a low-rank linear decomposition; kernel PCA changes the representation through a kernel and usually needs costly pairwise computations. They solve different problems.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The feature dimension and a practical batch fit in memory. The request for 30 components concerns a low-rank approximation, and any kernel must be suitable for the task.

### Reasoning

Incremental PCA updates a linear component estimate using successive batches, reducing the need to store every row at once. Batch size and ordering can affect approximation quality. Randomised SVD can make a truncated linear PCA decomposition cheaper when the desired rank is small, but its speed advantage does not automatically make every implementation an out-of-core algorithm.

Kernel PCA performs PCA in an implicit feature space, allowing nonlinear structure in the original coordinates. A straightforward implementation uses an n-by-n kernel matrix, which is impractical at ten million rows. It is not simply a faster PCA solver. Compare validation quality, memory and runtime; consider approximations or smaller representative data if nonlinear structure is necessary.

When a matrix does fit in memory, ordinary PCA using a full linear decomposition is a useful reference calculation. Incremental and randomised methods trade computational resources against approximation within the linear PCA setting.

### Common mistake

Do not choose kernel PCA merely because the original matrix is large. Distinguish an approximate numerical method for linear PCA from a different nonlinear modelling objective.
keyTakeaways: Match incremental PCA to batch-wise memory constraints.
Explain the low-rank approximation in randomised PCA.
Explain kernel PCA and its pairwise scaling problem.
Separate computational constraints from representation choice.

questions.title: How can clustering work when all rows cannot be retained?
questions.questionMarkdown: You must group a stream of low-dimensional sensor summaries into a small number of clusters. Compare MiniBatchKMeans with BIRCH when memory is limited. What would you measure before accepting either result?
questions.tldrAnswer: MiniBatchKMeans updates centroids from small batches. BIRCH compresses observations into a tree of summary statistics before optional global clustering. Both require quality and resource checks; neither guarantees the same answer as full-data clustering.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Features have meaningful, consistently scaled Euclidean distances. The stream may be processed in batches and the expected cluster structure is compatible with distance-based grouping.

### Reasoning

MiniBatchKMeans uses subsets to update a fixed collection of centroids. It can reduce computation but produces an approximate solution and can depend on initialisation and stream order. BIRCH builds clustering-feature summaries organised in a tree, governed by a distance threshold and branching settings; the compressed subclusters can then be grouped globally.

Measure cluster stability across seeds or arrival orders, representative held-out assignment distances, and domain usefulness. Track peak memory, processing time and the number of BIRCH subclusters. The threshold may produce many subclusters, so memory is not automatically independent of the data. High-dimensional distance problems and non-spherical structure can undermine both methods.

### Common mistake

A smaller memory footprint does not establish that clusters represent real operating states. Do not use one attractive projection as the only quality check.
keyTakeaways: Describe centroid updates from minibatches.
Describe BIRCH summary-tree compression.
Identify order, threshold and geometry limitations.
Evaluate quality, stability, memory and runtime together.

questions.title: What changes when a loss is summed instead of averaged?
questions.questionMarkdown: One training script minimises the mean squared error plus λ times a weight penalty. Another sums the same errors and leaves λ unchanged. Do they optimise the same trade-off? Explain using n training examples.
questions.tldrAnswer: No. To preserve the minimiser when switching from mean to sum, multiply the penalty coefficient by n. Otherwise the penalty becomes weaker relative to the data term.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Both scripts use the same examples, per-example loss and penalty, and the comparison concerns objective minimisers rather than optimiser trajectories.

### Reasoning

Write the first objective as

$$J(\theta)=\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n\ell_i(\theta)+\lambda R(\theta).$$

Multiplying the entire objective by positive $n$ preserves its minimisers and gives $\sum_i\ell_i(\theta)+n\lambda R(\theta)$. Summing the loss but retaining only $\lambda R$ therefore divides the effective regularisation strength by $n$ relative to the original mean objective.

The per-example loss scores one prediction; empirical risk aggregates those scores; a penalised training objective adds other terms. Even when objectives differ only by an overall factor, gradients scale, so a fixed learning rate need not follow the same optimisation path. Library reduction conventions and optimiser weight decay should be checked explicitly.

### Common mistake

Do not assume that a coefficient named λ has the same meaning across implementations. Also distinguish an explicit penalty in the loss from decoupled weight decay.
keyTakeaways: Separate per-example loss, empirical risk and penalty.
Derive the factor n for the penalty coefficient.
Explain the weaker penalty if λ is unchanged.
Distinguish equal minimisers from equal optimisation trajectories.

questions.title: How would you recommend an item with no interaction history?
questions.questionMarkdown: A catalogue adds a new documentary with a description and topic tags but no views or ratings. A collaborative recommender cannot place it reliably. Propose an initial recommendation strategy and explain its limits.
questions.tldrAnswer: Use content features to connect the item to users or similar items, combine this with controlled exposure to gather feedback, and evaluate new-item performance separately. Pure interaction-based factors have little evidence for a new item.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Metadata is available before exposure, users have some usable history or stated interests, and feedback is affected by which items were shown.

### Reasoning

Collaborative filtering learns from patterns of user-item interactions, so an unseen item has no direct interaction evidence for its embedding. Content-based scores can compare its topics or text representation with previously liked items. A hybrid system can use those features initially and incorporate interactions as evidence accumulates.

Content similarity may recommend only familiar themes and miss appeal not expressed in metadata. Limited, controlled exploration provides feedback, but raw clicks also reflect exposure and position. Evaluate on genuinely new items using time-respecting splits, with relevance, coverage and exposure checks. A random split that leaves later interactions for the same item in training does not reproduce cold start.

### Common mistake

Cold start is an information problem, not simply a request for a larger collaborative model. Do not infer low quality from a new item receiving few clicks when it received few impressions.
keyTakeaways: Explain the missing interaction evidence for a new item.
Propose a content-based or hybrid initial score.
Describe metadata limitations and controlled exploration.
Use a time-respecting new-item evaluation.

questions.title: Can a classifier have low label error but low exact-match accuracy?
questions.questionMarkdown: Four documents each have five binary topic labels. A model makes exactly one label error on every document. Calculate exact-match accuracy and Hamming loss. Which metric answers whether a whole tag set is correct?
questions.tldrAnswer: Exact-match accuracy is zero; Hamming loss is 4/20=0.2. Exact match checks the complete label set, while Hamming loss averages individual label errors.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

All five labels are assessed for each document, positive and negative errors count equally, and predictions are binary decisions rather than ranked scores.

### Reasoning

Subset accuracy credits a document only if every predicted label matches its true label vector. Each of the four vectors contains an error, so none earns credit.

Hamming loss counts mismatched label entries and divides by the number assessed:

$$L_H=\frac{1}{NL}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{L}\mathbf1\{\hat y_{ij}\ne y_{ij}\}=\frac4{20}=0.2.$$

Neither metric alone describes which topics failed or the costs of false positives versus false negatives. With many mostly absent labels, an all-negative predictor can have a low Hamming loss while missing important positive labels. Inspect per-label precision and recall as well.

### Common mistake

Do not interpret 80% correct label entries as 80% completely correct documents. The aggregation unit changes the meaning of the score.
keyTakeaways: Calculate zero exact-match accuracy.
Calculate Hamming loss of 0.2.
Explain document-level versus label-entry evaluation.
Identify the risk of mostly negative labels hiding missed positives.

questions.title: Does a changed feature distribution prove the model is wrong?
questions.questionMarkdown: A repair-cost model sees a sudden increase in electric vehicles. Its input-distribution alert fires, but true repair costs arrive weeks later. What can you infer now, and what evidence would establish that the predictive relationship has changed?
questions.tldrAnswer: The alert shows a change in inputs, not necessarily in conditional repair costs. Check data quality and coverage now; use delayed representative labels to assess conditional errors, calibration and model quality.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The model predicts cost Y from features X. Use concept change here to mean a change in P(Y|X), distinguished from a change in P(X). Terminology varies across literature.

### Reasoning

A higher electric-vehicle share changes P(X). If expected costs given vehicle characteristics are unchanged and the model remains accurate in that region, the change alone need not invalidate it. Conversely, a new parts-pricing rule can change P(Y|X) even when the feature histogram looks the same.

Initially inspect logging changes, unseen categories and whether the affected region had training support. When labels mature, compare residuals and calibration by time and relevant groups using the same outcome horizon. Aggregate errors can change just because the mixture of easier and harder cases changes, so inspect conditional behaviour and business costs. Retraining needs trustworthy recent data and validation against the current model.

### Common mistake

A distribution test is not a performance test. Neither retraining on every alert nor ignoring a stable feature distribution is a sound substitute for labelled monitoring.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish P(X) changes from P(Y|X) changes.
Give a case where either can change without the other.
Use delayed labels and comparable outcome windows.
Separate mixture changes, data faults and conditional model failure.

questions.title: What does differencing change in an ARIMA forecast?
questions.questionMarkdown: Weekly demand trends upward. You fit ARIMA(1,1,1), obtain an apparently stationary differenced series, but residuals still show a repeating 52-week pattern. Explain the three orders and why differencing once has not completed model checking.
questions.tldrAnswer: The model uses one difference, one autoregressive lag and one moving-average error lag. Remaining seasonal residual dependence indicates structure still unmodelled; non-seasonal differencing is not a guarantee of adequate forecasts.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Observations are equally spaced, the candidate is a non-seasonal ARIMA model, and the innovation interpretation assumes a correctly specified model with uncorrelated errors.

### Reasoning

With $z_t=y_t-y_{t-1}$, an ARIMA(1,1,1) can be written, under one common sign convention,

$$z_t=c+\phi z_{t-1}+\epsilon_t+\theta\epsilon_{t-1}.$$

Thus $p=1$ controls past differenced observations, $d=1$ is the number of ordinary differences, and $q=1$ controls past innovations. The moving-average term is not a rolling average of observed demand.

Inspect residual autocorrelation and seasonal structure, forecast errors on rolling time splits, and whether transformations or seasonal terms are justified. An annual residual pattern suggests considering a seasonal specification or relevant explanatory variables. Additional differencing can introduce unnecessary dependence and increase uncertainty. Stationarity and invertibility constraints apply to the appropriate model components.

Gaussian innovations are an additional modelling assumption, often used for likelihood estimation and forecast intervals. The ARIMA linear dependence structure itself does not require every innovation to be Gaussian.

### Common mistake

Do not keep differencing until a single test stops rejecting. A stationary-looking series can still have predictable structure, and good in-sample fit does not establish forecast quality.
keyTakeaways: Interpret p, d and q correctly.
Write the model for the differenced series.
Explain why seasonal residual dependence matters.
Use residual diagnostics and time-ordered forecast evaluation.

questions.title: What does aggressive image downsampling lose?
questions.questionMarkdown: A defect classifier applies two 3×3 stride-one convolutions, each followed by 2×2 stride-two pooling. Tiny scratches disappear from the final feature map. Calculate the receptive-field size of one final interior feature and explain the design trade-off.
questions.tldrAnswer: The receptive field is 10×10 input pixels, with final feature centres four pixels apart. Wider context and lower computation come at the cost of spatial detail; small defects may be lost.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Layers are sequential, convolution dilation is one, and pooling has kernel two and stride two. Consider interior locations so boundary padding does not affect the receptive-field calculation.

### Reasoning

Track receptive-field size $r$ and the jump $j$ between neighbouring feature centres. Start with $r=1,j=1$. A layer of kernel $k$ and stride $s$ gives $r'=r+(k-1)j$ and $j'=sj$.

The first convolution gives $(r,j)=(3,1)$; pooling gives $(4,2)$; the second convolution gives $(8,2)$; the final pooling gives $(10,4)$. A feature can use a wider input region, but repeated reduction in resolution removes fine location information. Max pooling can preserve a strong local response while losing its precise position; it does not guarantee invariance to every translation.

For small defects, test less early downsampling, larger input resolution or a branch preserving detailed features. Compare small-defect recall and resource cost on held-out images.

A typical classifier combines convolutions and nonlinear activations to build local features, optional downsampling to reduce spatial resolution, and a classifier head acting on pooled or flattened features. The output head and loss must match the task; a segmentation system instead needs spatially resolved outputs.

### Common mistake

A larger theoretical receptive field is not proof that a trained feature uses all those pixels effectively. More pooling is not automatically better context handling.
keyTakeaways: Apply the receptive-field and jump recurrence.
Obtain a 10-pixel field and four-pixel spacing.
Explain the context versus spatial-detail trade-off.
Propose a measurable small-defect design comparison.

questions.title: How would you investigate a network that cannot learn?
questions.questionMarkdown: A network has almost constant training loss from the first epoch. Validation loss is similar. What short diagnostic sequence would distinguish an implementation error from an unsuitable learning rate or insufficient model capacity?
questions.tldrAnswer: Check targets and the loss contract, try to overfit a tiny fixed batch, inspect gradients and actual parameter updates, then vary optimisation settings. Flat training loss is different from a widening train-validation gap.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The task has a learnable relationship and a small batch can be held fixed. Diagnostics use training data and do not tune choices on the final test set.

### Reasoning

First inspect example-target alignment, target ranges, tensor shapes and whether the loss expects logits or probabilities. Compare the initial loss with a trivial predictor. Disable stochastic augmentation and heavy regularisation temporarily, then try fitting a few examples. Failure even there suggests a wiring, optimisation or capacity problem rather than generalisation alone.

Check finite gradients, whether intended weights require gradients, whether the optimiser contains those weights and whether they actually change after a step. For differentiable custom operations, compare automatic gradients with finite differences away from nondifferentiable points. Try a small learning-rate range and inspect scale. Once the tiny-batch test works, restore the full pipeline and investigate data, regularisation and capacity separately.

### Common mistake

Do not immediately add layers or train longer without checking that parameters update. A flat training loss does not diagnose overfitting, and one successful tiny-batch fit does not prove generalisation.
keyTakeaways: Check data-target alignment and loss inputs.
Use a controlled tiny-batch overfitting test.
Inspect finite gradients and actual parameter changes.
Separate optimisation debugging from generalisation evaluation.

questions.title: When should a pretrained image encoder be unfrozen?
questions.questionMarkdown: You have 600 labelled microscope images and an encoder pretrained on everyday photographs. Compare training a linear head on frozen features with fine-tuning the encoder. What evidence should determine the choice?
questions.tldrAnswer: Frozen features reduce trainable capacity and cost but may miss the target domain. Fine-tuning can adapt them, with greater overfitting risk. Compare carefully split validation results, including domain-specific failure cases.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Pretraining data differs from the target domain, labels are limited, and images from the same specimen must remain in the same split.

### Reasoning

Start with a frozen encoder and a simple head as a baseline. It tests whether the existing representation exposes useful target information without updating millions of weights. Fine-tuning later layers, or eventually the whole encoder with suitable learning rates, allows adaptation to microscope textures and structures. The added flexibility can memorise a small labelled set.

Select how many layers to unfreeze using specimen-grouped validation and compare repeated seeds where feasible. Check the input normalisation and resolution expected by the pretrained model. Keep an untouched test set; if labelled data is too limited for stable comparisons, report that uncertainty rather than declaring a small score difference decisive.

### Common mistake

Pretraining does not guarantee transfer, and a larger source dataset does not erase a domain mismatch. Training accuracy is especially weak evidence for whether unfreezing helped.
keyTakeaways: Explain the frozen-feature baseline.
Explain adaptation benefits and overfitting risk.
Use specimen-separated validation.
Check input contracts and uncertainty in small-data comparisons.

questions.title: How do LSTM gates keep or replace a memory value?
questions.questionMarkdown: In a one-dimensional LSTM cell, the previous cell state is 2, the forget gate is 0.8, the input gate is 0.25 and the candidate value is −0.4. The output gate is 0.5. Find the new cell state and describe how the hidden output differs from stored memory.
questions.tldrAnswer: The new cell state is 1.5; the hidden output is 0.5 tanh(1.5), about 0.453. The forget and input gates update memory, while the output gate controls its exposed transformed value.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Use the common LSTM formulation with sigmoid gates, a tanh candidate and tanh output transformation. Products are elementwise in a multidimensional cell.

### Reasoning

The cell update and hidden output are

$$c_t=f_tc_{t-1}+i_t\tilde c_t,\qquad h_t=o_t\tanh(c_t).$$

Here $c_t=0.8(2)+0.25(-0.4)=1.5$ and $h_t=0.5\tanh(1.5)\approx0.453$. The forget gate attenuates old memory; the input gate scales a proposed addition; the output gate selects how much transformed memory is exposed.

Holding gate values fixed, the direct derivative of the memory update with respect to the previous memory is $f_t$. A sequence of forget gates near one can preserve that direct gradient path better than repeated unconstrained nonlinear transformations. The total network derivative also includes dependencies through gates, and training can still suffer from unstable or vanishing gradients.

### Common mistake

The cell state and hidden state are not interchangeable. LSTM gates make long-term learning possible in some settings; they do not guarantee perfect memory or eliminate every gradient problem.
keyTakeaways: Calculate the cell state as 1.5.
Calculate the gated hidden output.
Explain the three gate roles.
Qualify the direct gradient-path benefit.

questions.title: Can a sequence convolution accidentally use future data?
questions.questionMarkdown: An online alarm uses two stacked one-dimensional convolution layers, each with kernel width 3, stride 1 and dilation 1. What input times should determine its output at time t, and why could symmetric padding leak information?
questions.tldrAnswer: A causal two-layer stack can use t−4 through t. Symmetric padding commonly allows future positions into the receptive field, which is invalid when the alarm must be produced immediately.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

There are no other layers that mix times, all input features are available at their stated timestamp, and the online target must be predicted without future observations.

### Reasoning

A causal width-three layer at $t$ reads $t,t-1,t-2$. Applying another such layer produces a receptive field of $1+2(3-1)=5$ positions, from $t-4$ to $t$. Left-only padding preserves sequence length without supplying future measurements; initial outputs have padded rather than observed history.

A centred width-three operation can read $t+1$, and stacking expands the future reach. That may be legitimate for an offline task with the entire sequence available, but it changes the online information contract. Check normalisation, preprocessing and labels too: a causal convolution does not repair a centred rolling statistic calculated earlier. Validate on chronological splits and test outputs against deliberately altered future inputs.

### Common mistake

A layer named Conv1d is not automatically causal. Convolution refers to a computation, not a guarantee about which timestamps the application may use.
keyTakeaways: Derive a five-position causal receptive field.
Specify left-only padding and startup effects.
Explain future leakage from centred convolutions.
Check all preprocessing and the online information contract.

questions.title: How would you turn a classifier into a numeric predictor?
questions.questionMarkdown: An image network predicts one of four age bands using softmax. You now need a continuous age estimate. Which output and loss changes are needed, and when would a plain linear output be insufficient?
questions.tldrAnswer: Replace the four-class head with a scalar regression output and a suitable numeric loss. Squared error targets a conditional mean; absolute error targets a conditional median. Enforce valid ranges only when justified by the target.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Training examples have numeric age labels. The image encoder can be reused, but its representation may require adaptation and evaluation for the new task.

### Reasoning

A four-way softmax produces a probability distribution over bins, not an unrestricted real number. A scalar linear head is a straightforward regression baseline. Under finite second moments, squared-error risk is minimised by the conditional mean; absolute-error risk is minimised by a conditional median. The preferred target and penalty for large errors guide the choice.

Scale targets using training-fitted statistics if helpful, undo the transformation for reporting, and evaluate errors in meaningful units. If the physical target is constrained, consider a compatible output transformation or distributional model. A linear head can predict negative values; clipping may be practical but changes errors and does not create a coherent uncertainty model.

### Common mistake

Changing the final activation alone is insufficient if class-index targets and classification loss remain. A numeric prediction also does not supply calibrated uncertainty by itself.
keyTakeaways: Replace the class-probability head with a regression output.
Match the loss to the intended conditional target.
Handle target scaling without validation leakage.
Discuss output constraints and uncertainty limitations.

questions.title: Why do batch-normalisation epsilon and momentum do different jobs?
questions.questionMarkdown: In PyTorch-style batch normalisation, the stored mean is 10, the current batch mean is 14 and momentum is 0.2. Compute the updated mean. Would increasing epsilon make those running statistics adapt faster?
questions.tldrAnswer: The updated mean is 10.8. Momentum controls the running-statistic update; epsilon stabilises the division by a small variance and does not change that update rate.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Running statistics are tracked, the layer is training, and the convention is new = (1−momentum)×old + momentum×batch. Other libraries may define momentum differently.

### Reasoning

The mean update is $0.8(10)+0.2(14)=10.8$. A larger momentum under this convention gives the latest batch more influence, adapting faster but making the estimate noisier.

Normalisation instead uses a denominator such as $\sqrt{v+\epsilon}$. Epsilon prevents division by zero and limits amplification when variance is tiny. Making it large changes the normalised activations and can reduce their scale, but does not make the running mean catch up faster. Learned scale and shift remain separate parameters.

Check the implementation's variance estimator: PyTorch distinguishes the batch variance used for normalisation from the estimator used in its running variance update. Do not infer that every statistic has precisely the same numerical update input.

### Common mistake

Batch-normalisation momentum is not optimiser momentum. The same name can mean a different convention or equation, so the numerical value alone is insufficient.
keyTakeaways: Calculate the updated mean as 10.8.
State the momentum convention.
Explain epsilon as a variance-denominator stabiliser.
Separate batch statistics, running estimates and optimiser momentum.

questions.title: Does zeroing half the activations halve training time?
questions.questionMarkdown: A dense neural network uses dropout with probability 0.5. A colleague expects half the matrix-multiplication work and a twofold training speed-up. Is that a valid expectation?
questions.tldrAnswer: No. Ordinary dropout masks values in fixed-size dense tensors; dense matrix kernels generally still process those shapes. Mask generation and application may add cost.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The implementation uses standard elementwise dropout and dense matrix operations, without a specialised sparse kernel or structural pruning.

### Reasoning

A zero activation is a numerical value in a tensor, not removal of a tensor dimension. Dense kernels commonly execute the same matrix multiplication regardless of which entries happen to be zero. Dropout also needs a random mask during training and an elementwise transformation. It changes regularisation behaviour rather than promising arithmetic savings.

Wall-clock effects depend on hardware, fused operations and whether computation or memory movement dominates. Benchmark representative training steps, including synchronisation where needed, instead of inferring speed from the dropout probability. Structured pruning or sparse computation can remove work, but needs an implementation that exploits the structure and may change the model.

### Common mistake

Do not confuse a randomly masked training network with a physically smaller deployed network. Ordinary evaluation disables dropout and uses the full dense architecture.
keyTakeaways: Separate zero values from removed tensor dimensions.
Explain why dense matrix work can remain unchanged.
Account for masking overhead and hardware effects.
Distinguish dropout from structural pruning or sparse execution.

questions.title: When might engineered features beat learning from raw inputs?
questions.questionMarkdown: A factory has 400 labelled machine runs and years of unlabelled vibration traces. Compare a small model on spectral summary features with an end-to-end neural model on raw traces. What would make the comparison informative?
questions.tldrAnswer: Engineered summaries impose useful structure with fewer labels; learned representations may capture patterns those summaries discard but need suitable data, training and validation. Compare whole procedures under the same deployment constraints.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Runs from the same machine can be dependent, labels are scarce, and the intended deployment includes machines or periods not represented in model fitting.

### Reasoning

Spectral peaks, energy bands and other justified summaries encode domain assumptions about meaningful signals. A small supervised model may use limited labels efficiently, but fixed summaries can discard transient or nonlinear patterns. An end-to-end model learns features and the predictor jointly; unlabelled traces may support pretraining if the objective transfers to the task.

Split by machine or time as deployment requires, and fit any learned preprocessing only on training data. Compare representative failure cases, data requirements, inference cost and validation uncertainty, not only parameter counts. Include the cost of feature construction and pretraining. A hybrid using learned features plus domain summaries is also testable.

### Common mistake

Do not equate deep learning with no human assumptions: architecture, augmentation and training objective all impose them. Neither handcrafted nor learned features are universally superior.
keyTakeaways: Explain the inductive assumptions in engineered summaries.
Explain what end-to-end feature learning can recover or overfit.
Use machine- or time-separated comparisons.
Compare data, compute and failure modes rather than labels such as deep.

questions.title: Why can transformer training be parallel while generation is sequential?
questions.questionMarkdown: A causal transformer trains on all positions in a sentence at once, yet generating a fresh sentence still emits tokens one after another. Explain why these statements are compatible and compare the within-layer dependency with an RNN.
questions.tldrAnswer: Training supplies the complete shifted target sequence, so masked attention can compute all token positions in parallel. During generation, future input tokens are unknown. An RNN additionally carries a hidden-state dependency from one position to the next.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Training uses teacher forcing and a causal mask; generation uses ordinary autoregressive sampling rather than a separate parallel decoding method. Compare fixed sequence length n and hidden width d.

### Reasoning

During training, each position receives its known prefix through masked attention. The mask blocks access to future tokens, but matrix operations can calculate every permitted pair simultaneously. Layers still depend on previous layers. An RNN within a layer computes its state at t from the state at t−1, giving a sequential path across positions.

At inference, the next generated token determines part of the following input, so ordinary autoregressive decoding cannot know all positions in advance. Caching past keys and values reduces repeated work without removing that dependency. Standard dense self-attention has pairwise work proportional to n²d, so shorter sequential depth is not the same as lower total work for every sequence length.

### Common mistake

Parallel training does not mean a causal transformer sees future target tokens or generates an entire sentence in one ordinary sampling step.
keyTakeaways: Explain known training tokens and causal masking.
Contrast attention with recurrent within-layer dependencies.
Explain the unknown-token dependency at generation time.
Distinguish parallel depth from quadratic attention work.
