questions.title: What can an average language-model score hide?
questions.questionMarkdown: A support assistant improves its overall answer score, but users writing in one dialect report more refusals and incorrect advice. How would you investigate this without treating the aggregate score as evidence that the system is acceptable?
questions.tldrAnswer: Measure errors and refusals for relevant groups and tasks, inspect examples with affected users, quantify uncertainty and test privacy and other harms separately. An average quality gain can coexist with concentrated harm.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Group definitions and data collection are appropriate for the setting, evaluation uses consented or otherwise permitted data, and an answer can be harmful even when it is fluent.

### Reasoning

Build a task-relevant evaluation that distinguishes incorrect answers, unjustified refusals, harmful stereotypes and disclosure of private information. Compare subgroup rates with enough examples to reveal uncertainty and inspect intersections where justified. A changed mix of easy and hard tasks can explain aggregate movement, so compare like tasks rather than relying only on raw group averages.

Consult affected users about meaningful failures and use qualified reviewers for consequential advice. Test mitigations on held-out data and monitor deployment complaints, with an escalation or abstention path where needed. Privacy leakage requires its own adversarial and data-governance checks; a fairness metric cannot establish that private training material will never be emitted.

### Common mistake

One parity statistic cannot certify safety or fairness. Do not collect sensitive attributes indiscriminately or conclude that an under-sampled group has no problem because a test lacks power.
keyTakeaways: Identify subgroup and intersectional failure patterns.
Separate task mix from conditional performance.
Measure distinct harms and evaluation uncertainty.
Include affected-user review and practical mitigation checks.

questions.title: How does image patch size change a vision transformer?
questions.questionMarkdown: A vision transformer splits a 256×256 image into non-overlapping 16×16 patches. How many image tokens result? If patch width is halved, how do token count and dense attention-score count change, and what information must distinguish patch locations?
questions.tldrAnswer: There are 256 image tokens. Halving patch width gives 1,024 tokens and sixteen times as many token-pair attention scores. Positional information is needed to distinguish the spatial arrangement.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Ignore any classification token, image dimensions divide evenly by patch size, and attention is dense over all patches with the same number of heads.

### Reasoning

For patch width $P$, the token count is $n=(256/P)^2$. Thus $P=16$ gives $16^2=256$, while $P=8$ gives $32^2=1024$. The attention-score matrix has $n^2$ entries per head, so four times as many tokens gives sixteen times as many pair scores.

Patch pixels are projected into embeddings, and position information is added or otherwise incorporated so that rearranging patches need not look equivalent. Smaller patches preserve finer spatial units but increase attention work. This ratio describes the pairwise attention component, not necessarily total runtime or memory for an optimised implementation. Compared with convolutions, a plain vision transformer has less built-in local and translation-related structure, making training data and regularisation important.

### Common mistake

Halving a two-dimensional patch side does not merely double the number of patches. Also, the pair-score ratio is not a universal sixteenfold end-to-end latency prediction.
keyTakeaways: Calculate 256 and 1,024 patch tokens.
Calculate the sixteenfold pair-score increase.
Explain patch projection and positional information.
Qualify the cost ratio and spatial inductive-bias trade-off.

questions.title: Which vision output does a repair workflow need?
questions.questionMarkdown: A road-inspection system must first flag images containing potholes, then mark each pothole with a box, and finally estimate the damaged area in pixels. Which tasks match these three outputs? What changes if touching potholes must be counted separately?
questions.tldrAnswer: Use image classification for presence, object detection for boxes and semantic segmentation for a pixel-level damage mask. Separating individual touching potholes requires instance-level output, such as instance segmentation.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The requested area is in image pixels. Physical area would additionally require camera geometry or another scale estimate.

### Reasoning

Classification assigns a label to the whole image and cannot by itself specify where each defect lies. Detection returns object locations, commonly bounding boxes, with classes and scores. A box includes background, so its area is not generally the true damaged area. Semantic segmentation assigns a class to each pixel and can estimate the total mask area.

A semantic mask labels both touching potholes as the same class without necessarily distinguishing their identities. Instance segmentation separates individual object masks, allowing counts and per-object measurements. Each output requires suitable annotations and evaluation: image labels, boxes or masks are different supervision contracts.

### Common mistake

Do not select a task by the architecture name alone. A highly accurate image classifier cannot supply reliable object boundaries simply because its hidden features contain spatial information.
keyTakeaways: Match classification, detection and segmentation to the outputs.
Explain why box area differs from mask area.
Distinguish semantic from instance segmentation.
State the extra requirement for physical area or suitable annotations.

questions.title: Why can pixel accuracy conceal a failed defect mask?
questions.questionMarkdown: Only 100 of 10,000 pixels in an inspection image are defective. One model predicts no defect. Another predicts 120 defect pixels, 80 of which are correct. Compare pixel accuracy and defect intersection-over-union.
questions.tldrAnswer: The empty mask has 99% pixel accuracy but zero defect IoU. The second mask has 99.4% accuracy and IoU 80/140≈0.571. Background prevalence makes accuracy look strong even for a useless defect mask.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Every pixel has one binary ground-truth label. Compute foreground IoU for this image and treat ground truth as fixed; the true defect mask is nonempty.

### Reasoning

For the empty prediction, all 9,900 background pixels are correct and all 100 defect pixels are missed. Foreground intersection is zero and union is 100, giving IoU zero.

For the second prediction, $TP=80$, $FP=40$ and $FN=20$. The union is $TP+FP+FN=140$, so

$$\mathrm{IoU}=\frac{80}{140}=\frac47\approx0.571.$$

There are 9,860 true-negative pixels, so accuracy is $(9860+80)/10000=0.994$. Report the aggregation convention across images and classes. Macro-averaged per-image IoU and one global pooled IoU can weight large objects differently; an empty ground-truth and empty prediction also needs an explicit convention.

### Common mistake

A high percentage of correct pixels is not evidence that small defects are found. Conversely, one IoU number does not explain whether errors are missed objects or inaccurate boundaries.
keyTakeaways: Calculate both pixel accuracies.
Compute the defect union as 140.
Calculate zero and 4/7 foreground IoUs.
Explain background imbalance and metric aggregation conventions.

questions.title: When does a correct object label still count as a false detection?
questions.questionMarkdown: A detector returns two high-confidence boxes for one labelled object. Both have the correct class, but only one exceeds the required IoU threshold. Explain how a standard one-to-one matching evaluation treats them and what would happen if both exceeded the threshold.
questions.tldrAnswer: At most one prediction matches that ground-truth object. A box below the IoU threshold is a false positive; even if both qualify, the unmatched duplicate normally remains a false positive.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Use class-aware one-to-one matching in descending confidence order with a fixed IoU threshold. Ignore crowd regions and other dataset-specific exceptions for this example.

### Reasoning

Intersection-over-union measures box overlap as intersection area divided by union area. A correct class alone is insufficient: the location must meet the threshold and the ground-truth object must still be unmatched. Greedy confidence-order evaluation marks a qualifying match as a true positive and consumes that object for later predictions.

If only one box qualifies, it can match regardless of the other box's class correctness; the poor localisation is a false positive. If both qualify, the earlier qualifying detection matches and the duplicate is a false positive. Precision-recall and average precision depend on the ordering across all predictions, so the exact AP cannot be inferred from this single object alone. Post-processing such as non-maximum suppression can reduce duplicates but can also suppress nearby true objects.

### Common mistake

Do not count each correct class prediction as a true positive. A detection metric evaluates classification, localisation, confidence ranking and duplicate handling together.
keyTakeaways: Define IoU and the localisation threshold.
Apply one-to-one matching to a ground-truth object.
Explain duplicate false positives even when boxes overlap well.
Distinguish a single match example from dataset-level average precision.

questions.title: Why can good detections still produce a poor tracker?
questions.questionMarkdown: Two visually similar carts cross behind a pillar. A camera detects both accurately before and after the occlusion, but their track IDs swap. Why is this a tracking error, and what information could reduce it?
questions.tldrAnswer: Detection locates objects per frame; tracking must associate the same physical object across time. Motion prediction and appearance cues can help, but occlusion and ambiguity can still cause identity switches.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The task requires persistent identities, frames have reliable timestamps, and objects may temporarily disappear rather than cease to exist.

### Reasoning

A tracker predicts where existing tracks might move and matches new detections to those predictions. Motion models, overlap costs and assignment methods can make short gaps manageable. Appearance features may help distinguish similar trajectories, although similar-looking carts can remain ambiguous. Track creation, deletion and re-identification policies determine what happens after longer gaps.

Evaluate identity continuity as well as detection recall and localisation. Inspect switches, fragmented tracks and recovery after occlusion, alongside processing latency. Using future frames can improve association for offline analysis but may violate a real-time requirement. The correct response to unresolved ambiguity may be reduced confidence rather than an unjustified identity claim.

### Common mistake

Per-frame accuracy does not measure identity preservation. Adding an appearance model is not a guarantee of correct identity under complete occlusion.
keyTakeaways: Separate per-frame detection from temporal association.
Explain motion and appearance evidence.
Identify switches, fragmentation and occlusion recovery as errors.
Respect real-time constraints and unresolved ambiguity.

questions.title: Why can good character recognition still fail document extraction?
questions.questionMarkdown: An invoice reader correctly recognises most cropped characters but often returns the wrong total. Describe failure points before and after recognition. For a 50-character reference string with two substitutions, one deletion and one insertion in its aligned output, calculate character error rate.
questions.tldrAnswer: Text localisation, reading order and field association can fail even when recognition is strong. Character error rate is (2+1+1)/50=0.08; field correctness must also be measured directly.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Use a minimum-edit alignment under the stated counts, with a 50-character reference. The pipeline includes locating text, recognising it and assigning it to document fields.

### Reasoning

Character error rate is $(S+D+I)/N$, where $N$ is the reference length. Here it is $4/50=8\%$. Insertions mean the rate can exceed 100% in other cases. Word error rate uses word-level edits and can react differently to spacing or tokenisation.

A missed crop may omit a digit entirely; incorrect reading order can pair a value with the wrong label; a correct string may represent a subtotal rather than the total. Test each stage and the final field output, using tolerances appropriate to the task. Compare performance on different layouts, image quality and languages. Character accuracy alone may underweight a one-character decimal or sign error with a large effect on the amount.

### Common mistake

Do not equate 92% character accuracy with a 92% chance that a monetary field is correct. Sequence and field errors are correlated, and their consequences differ.
keyTakeaways: Calculate an 8% character error rate.
Distinguish character and word edit measures.
Identify localisation, reading-order and field-association failures.
Evaluate final field correctness and consequential character errors.

questions.title: When does an image augmentation change the answer?
questions.questionMarkdown: A printed-digit classifier is trained with arbitrary rotations and random crops. Some 6s resemble 9s after rotation, and crops can remove the distinguishing stroke. Design a safer training and evaluation pipeline.
questions.tldrAnswer: Use transformations justified by the real capture process and preserve the label or update annotations correctly. Split original images first, augment training only, and keep validation representative and reproducible.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The labels distinguish digit identities, deployment has a known range of orientation and framing, and multiple captures from one source may be dependent.

### Reasoning

First split original sources into training, validation and test sets, keeping related captures together. Apply resizing or normalisation consistently, fitting any learned statistics on training data. Sample training augmentations within plausible capture variation and inspect transformed examples. Restrict rotations or remove transformations that turn one digit into another; avoid crops that erase essential evidence.

For localisation tasks, transform boxes and masks with the image rather than keeping stale annotations. Validate the full pipeline on representative unaugmented data, or on a predefined robustness suite reported separately. Prediction-time augmentation is a separate procedure whose latency and aggregation need evaluation. A larger synthetic dataset is useful only when its transformations encode suitable assumptions.

Begin by defining the prediction task and label rules, then collect representative labelled images and document ambiguous cases. After splitting and preprocessing, fit a baseline CNN and an appropriate output head before selecting augmentations or tuning architecture. This makes the effect of each change measurable.

### Common mistake

Do not split after creating augmented copies, which can leak near-identical images across sets. More transformations can introduce label noise rather than improve generalisation.
keyTakeaways: Identify rotations and crops that violate label preservation.
Split original groups before augmentation.
Keep preprocessing and spatial annotations consistent.
Use representative evaluation and inspect transformed examples.

questions.title: Can a large sample rescue a mean with no finite variance?
questions.questionMarkdown: A diagnostic reports the sample mean and its usual standard error for independent observations from a standard Cauchy distribution. The analyst argues that a million observations make the normal approximation safe. What is wrong, and what could be estimated instead?
questions.tldrAnswer: The Cauchy distribution has no finite mean or variance, so the usual mean and variance-based central limit theorem do not apply. A location quantity such as its median is a different, well-defined target.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Observations truly follow an untruncated standard Cauchy distribution. A physically bounded measurement would be a different model and needs separate analysis.

### Reasoning

The density is $f(x)=1/[\pi(1+x^2)]$. Its tails are too heavy for the absolute first moment or second moment to be finite. Symmetry around zero identifies its median and location, but does not make the undefined expectation equal zero.

The familiar standard error $s/\sqrt n$ and normal approximation for a sample mean require conditions that fail here. A sample variance is a finite number for almost every finite dataset, yet it does not consistently estimate a finite population variance in this model. Rare observations can dominate the sample mean even after many measurements.

If location is the scientific target, consider the median with an inference method justified for that quantile. Trimming changes the target unless additional modelling assumptions connect the trimmed statistic to the intended quantity.

### Common mistake

Do not infer existence of population moments from finite values returned by software. More data does not repair a theorem whose assumptions are false.

### A finite mean can still be insufficient

A Pareto distribution with positive lower scale and shape 1.5 has a finite mean but infinite variance. The usual finite-variance central limit theorem and standard-error formula still do not apply, even though a mean exists. By contrast, genuinely bounded observations have finite moments; they may still require large samples for a useful approximation, but that is different from a nonexistent variance.
keyTakeaways: Identify the missing first and second moments.
Distinguish symmetry and median from an expectation.
Explain why the usual standard error is unjustified.
Propose a well-defined alternative target and suitable inference.

questions.title: Why can two skewness measures disagree?
questions.questionMarkdown: A dataset has quartiles Q1=10, median=12 and Q3=18. Calculate its quartile-based skewness. Could a few extreme observations change third-moment skewness substantially while leaving these quartiles unchanged?
questions.tldrAnswer: Quartile-based skewness is (10+18−24)/(18−10)=0.5. Extreme observations can strongly change moment skewness without changing the central quartiles, so the two measures describe different aspects of shape.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The reported quartiles use a fixed convention and Q3 exceeds Q1. Moment skewness is meaningful only when the relevant moments exist; sample calculations still depend on the chosen estimator.

### Reasoning

Bowley or Galton skewness compares the two halves of the interquartile range:

$$B=\frac{(Q_3-Q_2)-(Q_2-Q_1)}{Q_3-Q_1}=\frac{6-2}{8}=0.5.$$

It describes asymmetry of the central half of the distribution. Third-moment skewness instead weights deviations from the mean cubically after standardisation. Changing a few tail values without moving their ranks across quartile boundaries can leave the quartiles fixed while changing the mean, variance and third moment substantially.

This robustness is also a limitation: quartile skewness can miss tail asymmetry entirely. Report which definition is used and inspect the distribution rather than interpreting disagreement as a software error.

### Common mistake

A zero quartile coefficient does not prove symmetry, just as zero third-moment skewness does not. When Q1=Q3, this quartile formula is undefined rather than automatically zero.
keyTakeaways: Compute the quartile coefficient as 0.5.
Contrast central-quantile and tail-sensitive summaries.
Explain how fixed quartiles can coexist with changing moments.
State denominator and moment-existence limitations.

questions.title: How do you combine variances from groups with different means?
questions.questionMarkdown: Two non-overlapping groups each contain three observations. Their means are 2 and 6, and each unbiased sample variance is 1. Calculate the mean and unbiased sample variance of all six observations without reconstructing the raw data.
questions.tldrAnswer: The combined mean is 4. Within-group sums of squares total 4 and between-group sums of squares total 24, so the combined sample variance is 28/5=5.6.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The summaries describe disjoint observations on the same scale. Each reported variance uses denominator n−1. The algebra does not require normality or equal population variances.

### Reasoning

For groups $g$ with sizes $n_g$, means $\bar x_g$ and sample variances $s_g^2$, let $N=\sum_gn_g$ and $\bar x=\sum_g n_g\bar x_g/N$. Expanding deviations around each group mean gives

$$\sum_i(x_i-\bar x)^2=\sum_g(n_g-1)s_g^2+\sum_gn_g(\bar x_g-\bar x)^2.$$

Here $\bar x=4$, the within-group term is $2(1)+2(1)=4$, and the between-group term is $3(2-4)^2+3(6-4)^2=24$. Divide the total 28 by $N-1=5$ to obtain 5.6.

This is the descriptive variance of the combined observations. It differs from pooling within-group residual variance under a common-variance model, which removes the group mean differences.

### Common mistake

Averaging the two variances gives 1 and omits the variation between group means. Also, use observation-count weights for the mean when group sizes differ.
keyTakeaways: Compute the weighted combined mean.
Convert sample variances back to within-group sums of squares.
Add the between-group mean term.
Distinguish total sample variance from pooled within-group variance.

questions.title: When must a confidence interval agree with a hypothesis test?
questions.questionMarkdown: For a normal population mean with known standard deviation, an estimate is 5 with standard error 2. Compare a two-sided 5% test of mean zero with the matched 95% z interval. Why might a differently constructed interval disagree?
questions.tldrAnswer: The z statistic is 2.5, exceeding 1.96, and the interval [1.08, 8.92] excludes zero. Agreement follows from inverting the same test; different sidedness, standard errors or methods need not agree.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The estimate is normally distributed with known standard error 2. The null is mean zero, and both procedures use the same two-sided significance level and model.

### Reasoning

The test rejects when $|\hat\mu-\mu_0|/SE>z_{0.975}\approx1.96$. Solving the corresponding non-rejection inequality for candidate values $\mu_0$ gives

$$\hat\mu-1.96SE\le\mu_0\le\hat\mu+1.96SE.$$

With the given values this is $[1.08,8.92]$, while the test statistic is $5/2=2.5$. This is a statement about matched procedures, not a claim that every reported 95% interval encodes every 5% test. A one-sided test, bootstrap interval, robust standard error or multiplicity-adjusted procedure can change the acceptance set. Boundary conventions should also match.

### Common mistake

Do not convert a confidence interval into a posterior probability for the parameter. Test-interval duality describes repeated-sampling procedures and their acceptance regions.
keyTakeaways: Calculate the z statistic and interval.
Derive the interval by inverting the test inequality.
State the matching model, sidedness and level requirements.
Avoid a posterior-probability interpretation.

questions.title: Why does a uniform offset hide an arbitrary residue?
questions.questionMarkdown: A counter outputs (X+U) modulo 5. X may follow any distribution on the residues 0 to 4, while U is independent and uniform on those residues. Prove that each output residue has probability 1/5. What fails if U depends on X?
questions.tldrAnswer: Conditioning on any X value leaves exactly one of five equally likely U values for each output. Averaging over X preserves 1/5. Dependence can destroy this, for example U=−X modulo 5 makes every output zero.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Arithmetic is modulo 5, U is independent of X, and uniformity covers every residue exactly. This is a probability statement, not a complete cryptographic security claim.

### Reasoning

For any output residue $r$, total probability gives

$$P((X+U)\bmod5=r)=\sum_{x=0}^{4}P(X=x)P(U=(r-x)\bmod5\mid X=x).$$

Independence and uniformity make each conditional term $1/5$, leaving $(1/5)\sum_xP(X=x)=1/5$. No uniformity assumption on X is needed.

If X is uniform and $U=-X\bmod5$, both marginal distributions are uniform but the sum is always zero. Thus even uniform marginals are insufficient without the relevant independence. The argument generalises to any positive integer modulus with an independent uniform offset.

### Common mistake

Do not apply the result to a die whose faces are not uniform modulo the chosen modulus, or assume that separately uniform random variables must be independent.
keyTakeaways: Condition on each possible X residue.
Use exactly one matching U value per output.
Sum to obtain a uniform output without assuming X is uniform.
Give a dependence counterexample.

questions.title: How can a median event become a binomial calculation?
questions.questionMarkdown: Five independent latency measurements are uniform on [0,10]. What is the probability that their sample median exceeds 7? Derive it by counting measurements above the threshold.
questions.tldrAnswer: The median exceeds 7 exactly when at least three measurements do. That count is Binomial(5, 0.3), giving probability 0.16308.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The five measurements are identically distributed and independent. The distribution is continuous, so ties at 7 have probability zero.

### Reasoning

For one measurement, $P(X>7)=3/10$. Let $K$ count values exceeding 7. The third ordered observation exceeds 7 if and only if at least three of the five observations exceed 7. Therefore

$$P(\mathrm{median}>7)=\sum_{k=3}^{5}\binom5k(0.3)^k(0.7)^{5-k}.$$

The three terms are 0.1323, 0.02835 and 0.00243, totalling 0.16308. More generally, for odd sample size $2m+1$ and continuous CDF F, the same event uses a binomial tail with success probability $1-F(t)$ and cutoff $m+1$. Dependence between measurements would invalidate the binomial count model.

### Common mistake

The median is not itself uniform simply because each observation is. Its distribution concentrates around the population centre as sample size grows under these assumptions.
keyTakeaways: Translate the median event into at least three exceedances.
Use an exceedance probability of 0.3.
Calculate the binomial tail as 0.16308.
State independence and distinguish the median distribution.

questions.title: How do overlapping pair conditions change a sampling probability?
questions.questionMarkdown: Six devices consist of two red devices from supplier A, two blue devices from A, one red device from B and one blue device from B. Choose two distinct devices uniformly without replacement. What is the probability that they share a colour or share a supplier?
questions.tldrAnswer: There are 15 equally likely unordered pairs. Six share a colour, seven share a supplier and two share both, giving (6+7−2)/15=11/15.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Every distinct pair of physical devices is equally likely. The event uses inclusive or, so pairs sharing both attributes qualify once.

### Reasoning

The denominator is $\binom62=15$. There are three red and three blue devices, giving $2\binom32=6$ same-colour pairs. Supplier A has four and B has two, giving $\binom42+\binom22=7$ same-supplier pairs.

Pairs sharing both attributes must lie inside one colour-supplier cell. Only the two A cells contain pairs, so the intersection count is $\binom22+\binom22=2$. Inclusion-exclusion gives 11 favourable pairs and probability $11/15$.

An ordered calculation is also valid if both numerator and denominator count orders consistently; each distinct unordered pair has two orders. Devices with the same attributes remain different sample units.

### Common mistake

Do not count only attribute combinations as equally likely outcomes. Their numbers of physical device pairs differ, and adding the two event counts without subtracting the overlap double-counts pairs.
keyTakeaways: Count 15 unordered physical pairs.
Calculate six same-colour and seven same-supplier pairs.
Subtract the two pairs satisfying both conditions.
Explain consistent ordering and inclusive or.

questions.title: How likely is any collision among several hash assignments?
questions.questionMarkdown: Five independent records are assigned uniformly to ten buckets. What is the probability that at least two records share a bucket? Explain why the answer is not simply 1/10.
questions.tldrAnswer: The no-collision probability is 1×0.9×0.8×0.7×0.6=0.3024, so the chance of at least one collision is 0.6976. The value 1/10 applies only to one specified pair.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Bucket assignments are independent and uniform. This toy model does not describe a fixed hash function on adversarially selected inputs without additional assumptions.

### Reasoning

Condition on the earlier assignments being distinct. The first record is unrestricted; the second must avoid one occupied bucket; the third must avoid two, and so on. Thus

$$P(\text{all distinct})=\prod_{j=0}^{4}\frac{10-j}{10}=0.3024.$$

Taking the complement gives 0.6976. Summing the collision probabilities over the ten pairs gives an expected number of colliding pairs equal to one, not a probability of any collision. Pair-collision events overlap because three records can share a bucket. For more than ten records, a collision is certain by the pigeonhole principle.

### Common mistake

A single-pair probability ignores the many opportunities for a collision. A union bound can be useful, but adding event probabilities does not generally give their exact union probability.
keyTakeaways: Build the no-collision product sequentially.
Take its complement to obtain 0.6976.
Distinguish a specified pair from any pair.
Explain overlaps and the pigeonhole limit.

questions.title: Why does the method of cutting an interval matter?
questions.questionMarkdown: Two independent points are selected uniformly along a cable of unit length, and it is cut at both points. What is the probability that the three pieces can form a nondegenerate triangle? Explain the sample space you use.
questions.tldrAnswer: The probability is 1/4. The ordered cut points have constant density on 0<u<v<1; valid triangles require all three gaps to be less than 1/2.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Both cut positions are drawn independently from the original whole cable. This differs from cutting once and then selecting a resulting segment for another cut.

### Reasoning

Let U and V be the ordered cut positions. Their joint density is 2 on the triangle $0<u<v<1$, whose area is $1/2$. The piece lengths are $u$, $v-u$ and $1-v$, summing to one. A nondegenerate triangle requires each piece to be smaller than one half.

Thus $u<1/2$, $v>1/2$ and $v<u+1/2$. The feasible area is

$$\int_0^{1/2}\left[(u+1/2)-1/2\right]du=\frac18.$$

Multiplying by density 2 gives probability $1/4$. The piece lengths are dependent because they sum to one; they are not three independent uniform draws. Equality cases have probability zero under this continuous sampling law.

### Common mistake

The words random cutting do not specify a probability model. Sequentially choosing a segment and cutting within it can induce a different distribution of final lengths.
keyTakeaways: Specify independent uniform cut positions on the whole interval.
Express the three dependent gap lengths.
Translate triangle inequalities into each gap below 1/2.
Integrate the feasible region to obtain 1/4.

questions.title: Can two random-chord simulators both be correct?
questions.questionMarkdown: One simulator chooses two independent uniform points on a circle and joins them. Another chooses a point uniformly inside the disc and uses it as the midpoint of a chord perpendicular to its radius. For a circle of radius R, compare the probability that the chord is longer than √3 R. In a third experiment, pair four independent uniform circumference points into two chords. What is the probability that the chords intersect inside the circle?
questions.tldrAnswer: The endpoint simulator gives 1/3; the uniform-disc-midpoint simulator gives 1/4. They define different distributions over chords, so random chord alone does not determine a unique answer.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The endpoint angles are independent uniform angles. The second simulator samples midpoint area uniformly, not midpoint radius uniformly; the centre point has probability zero and its orientation can be chosen arbitrarily.

### Reasoning

For the first construction, rotational symmetry fixes one endpoint. The angular difference $\theta$ is uniform on $[0,2\pi)$, and chord length is $2R|\sin(\theta/2)|$. It exceeds $\sqrt3R$ when $2\pi/3<\theta<4\pi/3$, occupying one third of the angular range.

For a midpoint at distance r from the centre, chord length is $2\sqrt{R^2-r^2}$. The same threshold is equivalent to $r<R/2$. A uniform point in the disc lies there with probability $\pi(R/2)^2/(\pi R^2)=1/4$.

Both are valid sampling procedures. Sampling radius uniformly would be a third procedure and would give 1/2, illustrating why the measure must be explicit.

### Common mistake

Uniform area does not mean uniform radius. A histogram from one simulator cannot disprove a result based on a different sampling law.

### Intersecting two chords

For four distinct independent uniform endpoints, condition on their circular order. Of the three possible pairings of four ordered points, exactly the pairing with alternating endpoints crosses inside the circle. Exchangeability makes the three pairings equally likely for the two labelled chords, so the intersection probability is 1/3. Coincident endpoints have probability zero. This result uses the independent-uniform-endpoint construction; other ways of sampling two chords need not have the same crossing probability.
keyTakeaways: Specify the two distinct sampling measures.
Derive the endpoint angular interval and probability 1/3.
Use the midpoint-distance criterion and area ratio 1/4.
Distinguish sampling laws and derive the 1/3 crossing probability for two chords from four independent uniform endpoints.

questions.title: How can unequal coin outcomes produce a fair bit?
questions.questionMarkdown: A device emits independent H or T values with a fixed unknown probability p of H, where 0<p<1. Read non-overlapping pairs, emit 0 for HT and 1 for TH, and discard HH or TT. Prove fairness and calculate the expected number of input flips per output bit.
questions.tldrAnswer: HT and TH each have probability p(1−p), so the accepted outcomes are equally likely. Acceptance probability is 2p(1−p); each attempt uses two flips, giving expected cost 1/[p(1−p)] flips.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Flips are independent with the same fixed probability p throughout. Pairs do not overlap, and the procedure repeats until an accepted pair appears.

### Reasoning

Within one pair, $P(HT)=p(1-p)=P(TH)$. Conditional on acceptance, either output has probability $1/2$. Independent disjoint pairs also give independent acceptance attempts.

The number of pairs until acceptance is geometric with success probability $a=2p(1-p)$, so its expectation is $1/a$. Multiplying by two flips gives $2/a=1/[p(1-p)]$. At $p=1/2$ this is four flips; the expected cost grows without bound as p approaches zero or one.

If the first and second flip have different biases, the two unequal-pair probabilities need not match. Dependence can also undermine this derivation and independence of emitted bits, so the assumptions must be justified for a real device.

### Common mistake

Discarding equal pairs does not repair every defective random source. In particular, a stationary marginal bias by itself is weaker than the independent-identically-distributed assumption used here.
keyTakeaways: Show equality of HT and TH probabilities.
Condition on acceptance to prove fairness.
Derive acceptance rate and expected flip cost.
Identify changing bias or dependence as limitations.

questions.title: How do sample moments determine a beta model?
questions.questionMarkdown: You model independent fractions with a Beta(α,β) distribution. The sample mean is 0.4 and the second raw sample moment is 0.20. Derive method-of-moments estimates of α and β. Must these also be the maximum-likelihood estimates?
questions.tldrAnswer: The moment variance is 0.20−0.4²=0.04. Matching beta mean and variance gives α+β=5, hence α=2 and β=3. Maximum likelihood uses the full likelihood and need not give the same values.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Fractions lie strictly between zero and one and are modelled as iid beta observations with positive parameters. Raw sample moments use denominator n, not the unbiased variance denominator n−1.

### Reasoning

Let $k=\alpha+\beta$. For a beta distribution, $\mu=\alpha/k$ and $v=\mu(1-\mu)/(k+1)$. Matching $\mu$ to $m=0.4$ and $v$ to $0.20-m^2=0.04$ gives

$$\hat k=\frac{m(1-m)}{v}-1=5,\quad \hat\alpha=m\hat k=2,\quad \hat\beta=(1-m)\hat k=3.$$

Method of moments equates selected theoretical moments to empirical ones. Maximum likelihood instead maximises the joint density; for beta data its equations involve averages of log X and log(1−X), information not determined by these two raw moments. Thus equality of the estimates is not guaranteed.

Check feasibility: a positive beta solution requires $0<m<1$ and $0<v<m(1-m)$. Degenerate or boundary data may not yield finite positive estimates.

### Common mistake

Do not substitute an n−1 variance silently into a raw-moment derivation or assume that matching moments validates the distributional model. Assess the model against the observed shape and purpose.
keyTakeaways: Compute the moment variance as 0.04.
Solve for α+β, α and β.
Distinguish moment equations from likelihood equations.
State moment conventions and feasibility conditions.

questions.title: How do you intersect lists without losing encounter order?
questions.questionMarkdown: Two event lists are [8, 3, 8, 5, 2] and [2, 8, 9]. Return each shared value once, in the order of its first appearance in the first list. Explain why converting a set intersection to a list does not meet the contract.
questions.tldrAnswer: Scan the first list with a membership set for the second and a set of values already emitted. The required result is [8, 2]; set iteration does not promise the requested order.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Values are hashable integers and equality has its usual meaning. Output multiplicity is one per shared value, not the minimum frequency in the two inputs.

### Reasoning

```python
def ordered_intersection(left, right):
    allowed = set(right)
    emitted = set()
    result = []
    for value in left:
        if value in allowed and value not in emitted:
            result.append(value)
            emitted.add(value)
    return result

assert ordered_intersection([8, 3, 8, 5, 2], [2, 8, 9]) == [8, 2]
```

The scan defines the order explicitly. The membership sets decide eligibility and prevent duplicate output. Under ordinary expected constant-time hash operations, work is O(n+m) and extra storage is O(m+k), where k is the number emitted. Empty inputs produce an empty list. Unhashable values require a different representation or a comparison-based approach.

### Common mistake

A set models distinct membership, not a stable presentation order or multiset counts. Do not rely on a particular observed iteration order across runs or versions.
keyTakeaways: Return [8, 2] with no repeated output.
Preserve first-list encounter order explicitly.
State hashability and expected complexity.
Distinguish set membership from multiset intersection.

questions.title: What does the first repeated value mean in a stream?
questions.questionMarkdown: For [7, 4, 9, 4, 7, 4], find the value whose second occurrence is seen first, then list every repeated value once in second-occurrence order. Explain how this differs from selecting the earliest-position value that eventually repeats.
questions.tldrAnswer: The first repeat encountered is 4 and the repeated-value list is [4, 7]. The earliest original position that eventually repeats belongs to 7, which is a different contract.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Inputs are hashable values. First repeat means the first encounter of a value already seen while scanning from left to right.

### Reasoning

```python
def repeated_values(values):
    seen = set()
    reported = set()
    result = []
    for value in values:
        if value in seen and value not in reported:
            result.append(value)
            reported.add(value)
        seen.add(value)
    return result

repeats = repeated_values([7, 4, 9, 4, 7, 4])
assert repeats == [4, 7]
first_repeat = repeats[0] if repeats else None
```

For only the first repeat, return immediately when a value is already in seen. For all repeated values, reported prevents later occurrences from appearing again. Expected work is linear under ordinary hashing and storage grows with distinct values. For strings, the same scan operates on Unicode code points, not necessarily user-perceived grapheme clusters.

### Common mistake

Searching for the first original position with a future duplicate requires a different procedure, such as counts followed by a scan. Also, None as a missing-result sentinel is ambiguous if None itself is a valid input value.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish first second-occurrence from earliest original position.
Return 4 and [4, 7] for the example.
Use separate seen and reported state.
Explain complexity and the missing-result contract.

questions.title: Why can the largest product need the smallest integers?
questions.questionMarkdown: Choose three distinct positions from [-12, -5, 1, 4, 6] to maximise their product. Give a general algorithm for at least three integers and account for negative values and zeros.
questions.tldrAnswer: The maximum is 360 from −12×−5×6. After sorting, compare the three largest values with the two smallest values times the largest.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The input contains at least three Python integers. Positions must differ, but equal numeric values at different positions may all be selected.

### Reasoning

```python
def max_product_three(values):
    if len(values) < 3:
        raise ValueError("Need at least three integers")
    a = sorted(values)
    return max(a[-1] * a[-2] * a[-3],
               a[0] * a[1] * a[-1])

assert max_product_three([-12, -5, 1, 4, 6]) == 360
```

A positive maximum can arise from three positive values or two negative values with a positive one. The best pair of negatives has the largest magnitudes, at the low end of sorted order. If no positive product is possible, zeros or the least-negative triple are still covered by the two candidates. Sorting costs O(n log n) comparisons; retaining only the three largest and two smallest values allows a linear scan with constant auxiliary slots.

### Common mistake

Choosing the largest three numbers alone misses the contribution of two negative numbers. Converting to a set is also wrong because different positions with equal values remain usable.
keyTakeaways: Calculate the product 360.
Compare the two extreme-value candidates.
Explain negative, zero and repeated-value cases.
State input-size checks and algorithmic cost.

questions.title: Should an all-negative maximum subarray return zero?
questions.questionMarkdown: Find the maximum sum of a nonempty contiguous segment of [4, −6, 3, 5, −2]. Give a linear-time algorithm and explain the required result for [−8, −3, −5]. How does allowing an empty segment change the contract?
questions.tldrAnswer: The first maximum is 8 from [3, 5]. A nonempty all-negative input returns its largest element, −3. Allowing an empty segment instead permits zero.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Inputs are finite nonempty lists of integers, and the required segment is contiguous and nonempty. The function returns the sum rather than the segment indices.

### Reasoning

```python
def max_segment_sum(values):
    if not values:
        raise ValueError("Need a nonempty list")
    ending = best = values[0]
    for value in values[1:]:
        ending = max(value, ending + value)
        best = max(best, ending)
    return best

assert max_segment_sum([4, -6, 3, 5, -2]) == 8
assert max_segment_sum([-8, -3, -5]) == -3
```

At each position, the best segment ending there either starts at that value or extends the previous best ending segment. The invariant gives an O(n)-time scan and O(1) state, aside from the slice allocation in this readable implementation; an iterator avoids that allocation. If empty segments are allowed, zero is an additional candidate and empty input can return zero.

### Common mistake

Initialising best to zero silently changes a nonempty problem into an optional-empty one. A subsequence can skip positions, while a contiguous segment cannot.
keyTakeaways: State whether empty segments are allowed.
Derive the start-or-extend recurrence.
Return 8 and −3 for the two examples.
Distinguish contiguous segments and account for implementation space.

questions.title: Which Python container matches each data requirement?
questions.questionMarkdown: Choose containers for an editable ordered task list, a fixed coordinate record, distinct account IDs and a numeric matrix used in elementwise calculations. Explain why a tuple containing a list is neither deeply immutable nor hashable.
questions.tldrAnswer: Use a list, tuple, set and NumPy array respectively. A tuple prevents replacing its references, but a contained list can still change and makes that tuple unhashable.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The matrix has an appropriate numeric dtype. Fixed coordinate record means a fixed sequence of values, not a promise that every nested object is immutable.

### Reasoning

Lists preserve order and allow element replacement and resizing. Tuples preserve order with a fixed set of references. Sets represent distinct hashable members without a sequence-order contract. A NumPy array supplies multidimensional shape, dtype and array operations; object-dtype arrays have different performance and storage behaviour from ordinary numeric arrays.

```python
record = ([2, 4], "draft")
record[0].append(6)
assert record[0] == [2, 4, 6]
# hash(record) raises TypeError because the contained list is unhashable.
```

A tuple of hashable coordinates can be a dictionary key, whereas this nested-list tuple cannot. Container choice should follow mutability, membership, shape and computation needs rather than a universal ranking of speed.

### Common mistake

List multiplication repeats a sequence; NumPy numeric-array multiplication is elementwise. Do not assume that every object called an array has identical semantics or that a tuple freezes its nested objects.
keyTakeaways: Match the four requirements to appropriate containers.
Separate tuple-reference immutability from deep immutability.
Explain the hashability requirement.
Distinguish sequence operations from numeric array operations.

questions.title: Does Series subtraction compare labels or positions?
questions.questionMarkdown: Series a has values [1, 4] indexed by [x, y]. Series b has values [4, 1] indexed by [y, x]. Compare their Euclidean distance by matching labels with their distance by raw positions. How should code make the choice explicit?
questions.tldrAnswer: Label-matched distance is zero; positional distance is √18. pandas aligns labels during Series arithmetic, while converting directly to arrays removes labels and uses positions.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Indexes are unique, both Series contain exactly the same coordinate labels, and all values are finite numeric observations. Missing coordinates require an explicit policy.

### Reasoning

```python
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

a = pd.Series([1.0, 4.0], index=["x", "y"])
b = pd.Series([4.0, 1.0], index=["y", "x"])
if not a.index.is_unique or not b.index.is_unique:
    raise ValueError("Coordinate labels must be unique")
if set(a.index) != set(b.index):
    raise ValueError("Coordinate labels must match")
label_distance = np.linalg.norm(a.to_numpy() - b.reindex(a.index).to_numpy())
positional_distance = np.linalg.norm(a.to_numpy() - b.to_numpy())
assert label_distance == 0
assert np.isclose(positional_distance, np.sqrt(18))
```

The vectors refer to the same labelled coordinates but in different orders. For positional comparison, shape equality is necessary but does not prove semantic alignment. Check finiteness before calculation; silently dropping NaNs can compare only a subset of dimensions.

### Common mistake

A concise expression can be mathematically wrong for the intended coordinates even when it executes successfully. Do not rely on pandas reductions skipping missing values as a missing-coordinate policy.
keyTakeaways: Calculate zero label distance and √18 positional distance.
Explain pandas label alignment.
Check unique matching labels or deliberate positional shape.
Handle missing and nonfinite values explicitly.

questions.title: Why generate combinations without building a huge list?
questions.questionMarkdown: You must evaluate every group of three distinct sensor IDs from range(1, 9). Produce the groups once without treating different orders as different groups. How many groups exist, and what does using an iterator save?
questions.tldrAnswer: itertools.combinations produces 56 three-element tuples. Iteration avoids retaining all output groups at once, but cannot remove the work required to evaluate all 56, or all combinations in a larger problem.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

IDs are unique, input order is stable, and selection is without replacement. The general task may have much larger n and k.

### Reasoning

```python
from itertools import combinations
from math import comb

groups = combinations(range(1, 9), 3)
assert next(groups) == (1, 2, 3)
assert comb(8, 3) == 56
```

There are n!/[k!(n−k)!] groups. combinations follows input-position order and does not emit permutations such as both (1,2,3) and (3,2,1). It stores a pool of input values and iteration state, so it is lazy over outputs rather than a constant-memory consumer of an arbitrary infinite input. Materialising all results needs storage proportional to the number of groups times group size. k=0 gives one empty tuple; k>n gives no groups.

### Common mistake

Iterators reduce retained output memory, not combinatorial growth in total requested work. Repeated input values can produce equal-looking tuples because uniqueness is by input position.
keyTakeaways: Use combinations rather than permutations.
Calculate 56 selections.
Distinguish output laziness from input pooling and total work.
State boundary cases and input-position uniqueness.

questions.title: What makes a normal-sampling experiment reproducible?
questions.questionMarkdown: Generate 2,000 normal samples with mean 3 and standard deviation 1.5 for a repeatable experiment, then plot a density histogram. Explain why the sample mean need not equal 3 and why histogram heights need not sum to one.
questions.tldrAnswer: Use an explicitly seeded local generator and record the software setup. A finite sample fluctuates; a density histogram has total area one, so heights are weighted by bin widths.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The generator is used in a fixed sequence of calls. Exact bit-for-bit reproducibility requires recording relevant library, generator and execution details rather than assuming a seed alone guarantees it across versions.

### Reasoning

```python
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(27)
samples = rng.normal(loc=3.0, scale=1.5, size=2000)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.hist(samples, bins=30, density=True)
ax.set_xlabel("Value")
ax.set_ylabel("Density")
```

The scale argument is standard deviation, not variance. Recreating the same generator under the same setup and repeating the same calls reproduces the sequence; advancing its state changes later draws. Sampling variability means the empirical mean and standard deviation generally differ from the population parameters. Density normalisation makes the sum of height×bin-width equal one, whereas an ordinary count histogram totals observations.

### Common mistake

Do not reseed inside every loop iteration when independent successive draws are intended. A density can exceed one for narrow distributions without violating probability rules.
keyTakeaways: Use a local seeded generator with scale 1.5.
Explain generator state and reproducibility limits.
Distinguish population parameters from sample summaries.
Explain histogram area rather than height-sum normalisation.

questions.title: When should pandas apply receive a row instead of a scalar?
questions.questionMarkdown: A numeric DataFrame has columns sensor_a and sensor_b. You need to square every entry and separately compute the range within each row. Compare DataFrame.map, DataFrame.apply and vectorised operations.
questions.tldrAnswer: map passes individual values, while apply(axis=1) passes rows and apply(axis=0) passes columns. Prefer direct vectorised expressions such as df**2 and row-wise reductions when they express the task.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Use pandas with DataFrame.map available, numeric columns only and no missing values for the example. Missing-value behaviour must be decided separately.

### Reasoning

```python
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"sensor_a": [2, 7], "sensor_b": [5, 3]})
squared = df ** 2
row_range = df.max(axis=1) - df.min(axis=1)
via_map = df.map(lambda value: value * value)
via_apply = df.apply(lambda row: row.max() - row.min(), axis=1)
assert squared.equals(via_map)
assert row_range.tolist() == [3, 4]
assert row_range.equals(via_apply)
```

map is appropriate when the function consumes one scalar. apply can express a function consuming a whole row or column; its output shape depends on what the function returns. Built-in arithmetic and reductions usually express simple numeric work more clearly and can avoid repeated Python callbacks. Older examples may call applymap; DataFrame.map is its replacement in current pandas.

### Common mistake

Leaving apply at its default axis=0 applies the function to columns, not rows. Do not assume every apply call is vectorised merely because it returns a pandas object.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish scalar map from row or column apply.
Set axis=1 for row functions.
Use vectorised squaring and range reductions.
Identify obsolete applymap examples and missing-value assumptions.

questions.title: What must a recursive factorial function reject?
questions.questionMarkdown: Write a recursive factorial function accepting nonnegative Python integers, with zero mapping to one. Reject negative inputs and booleans explicitly. Why is this implementation unsuitable for arbitrarily large n?
questions.tldrAnswer: Validate the domain, use n<2 as the base case, and recurse with n−1. Python recursion depth and integer computation costs make recursion a poor choice for large inputs; math.factorial is preferable.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The contract accepts only the built-in int type, deliberately rejecting bool and other integer-like types. It is an educational implementation for modest n.

### Reasoning

```python
def factorial_recursive(n):
    if type(n) is not int:
        raise TypeError("Expected a Python integer")
    if n < 0:
        raise ValueError("Expected a nonnegative integer")
    if n < 2:
        return 1
    return n * factorial_recursive(n - 1)

assert factorial_recursive(0) == 1
assert factorial_recursive(6) == 720
```

The recurrence follows n!=n×(n−1)! with 0!=1. Each recursive call moves towards the base case. It uses O(n) call frames, and Python enforces a recursion limit. Integer multiplication is not constant-cost as the result grows, so counting calls alone is not a full bit-complexity analysis. An iterative implementation removes the recursive stack, while math.factorial provides the standard library operation.

### Common mistake

A negative-input sentinel can be confused with a valid domain value in other APIs; exceptions make this contract explicit. Raising the recursion limit is not a general solution to memory or stack risks.
keyTakeaways: Validate type and nonnegative domain.
Return one for zero and one.
Use a decreasing recursive argument.
Explain stack depth and standard-library alternatives.

questions.title: Why does memoisation make an increasing-grid path tractable?
questions.questionMarkdown: From any cell in a rectangular grid, move up, down, left or right only to a strictly larger value. Find the maximum number of cells in a path. Explain why caching by starting cell is valid and what happens for equal neighbouring values.
questions.tldrAnswer: Strict increase makes the move graph acyclic. Cache the longest path starting at each cell, which is one plus the maximum cached result among larger neighbours. Equal values create no edge.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The grid is rectangular and unchanged during the calculation. Values are finite comparable numbers. The path length counts cells, and an empty grid has result zero.

### Reasoning

```python
from functools import cache

def longest_increasing_path(grid):
    if not grid:
        return 0
    rows, cols = len(grid), len(grid[0])
    if any(len(row) != cols for row in grid):
        raise ValueError("Expected a rectangular grid")
    if cols == 0:
        return 0

    @cache
    def visit(r, c):
        best = 1
        for dr, dc in ((1, 0), (-1, 0), (0, 1), (0, -1)):
            nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
            if (0 <= nr < rows and 0 <= nc < cols
                    and grid[nr][nc] > grid[r][c]):
                best = max(best, 1 + visit(nr, nc))
        return best

    return max(visit(r, c) for r in range(rows) for c in range(cols))

assert longest_increasing_path([[1, 2], [4, 3]]) == 4
```

A strict increase cannot return to an earlier value, so no cycle exists and the future optimum depends only on the current cell. Each cell is solved once and has at most four outgoing edges: O(rows×cols) time and cache space, assuming constant-cost comparisons. A long path can exceed Python recursion depth; a topological dynamic programme avoids that call stack.

### Common mistake

Do not restrict movement to right and down unless the contract says so. Allowing non-decreasing moves introduces equal-value cycles and invalidates this recurrence without further rules.
keyTakeaways: Use all four neighbours and strict comparison.
Explain acyclicity and the cached recurrence.
Analyse one state per cell and bounded degree.
Identify recursion depth and non-decreasing-cycle risks.

questions.title: What does Flask provide for a model prediction endpoint?
questions.questionMarkdown: A team wraps a trained model in a Flask POST /predict route. Explain what Flask handles and what the team must still implement before serving real requests. Why should the model not be loaded anew for every request?
questions.tldrAnswer: Flask provides request routing and HTTP response handling. Input validation, model lifecycle, concurrency, resource limits and deployment remain application responsibilities. Load the model through a controlled process lifecycle rather than repeatedly per request.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The model is already trained and the endpoint accepts a documented JSON schema. This question concerns application boundaries rather than a specific hosting provider.

### Reasoning

A route maps an HTTP method and path to application code; Flask exposes request data and helps form responses. Validate content type, required fields, numeric ranges, array dimensions and request size before calling the model. Return defined errors for invalid requests and keep internal exception details out of public responses.

Loading a large model on every request adds latency and repeated allocation. Initialise it during an appropriate worker lifecycle, considering process count, memory duplication and whether inference is thread-safe. Use a production WSGI server or supported deployment arrangement, with logging, timeouts and capacity controls. The Flask development server and interactive debugger are for development. Long-running inference may need a separate worker queue.

### Common mistake

A small framework does not automatically make an endpoint scalable or secure. HTTP routing does not enforce the model input contract or make shared mutable model state safe across concurrent requests.
keyTakeaways: Identify routing, request and response responsibilities.
Validate schema and resource limits before inference.
Plan model loading and concurrency per worker.
Distinguish development serving from production operation.

questions.title: Why can a WHERE condition remove unmatched outer-join rows?
questions.questionMarkdown: In PostgreSQL, list every customer and their paid orders, keeping customers with no paid orders. Use customers(id, name) and orders(id, customer_id, status). Explain where the paid condition belongs and how a RIGHT JOIN could express the same result.
questions.tldrAnswer: Put the paid-order condition in the LEFT JOIN ON clause. A WHERE condition on the nullable order side removes unmatched rows. Swapping table sides expresses the same preservation with RIGHT JOIN.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Customer and order IDs are primary keys, customer_id references customers, and a customer can have several orders. One result row per matching paid order is intended.

### Reasoning

```sql
SELECT c.id AS customer_id, c.name, o.id AS order_id
FROM customers AS c
LEFT JOIN orders AS o
  ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid'
ORDER BY c.id, o.id;
```

An unmatched customer receives a row with NULL order columns. Moving o.status = 'paid' into WHERE rejects that row because the comparison evaluates to unknown, not true. The equivalent join is orders AS o RIGHT JOIN customers AS c ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.status = 'paid', with the same explicit projection. A RIGHT JOIN is not inherently more powerful or faster. Multiple qualifying orders produce multiple rows for their customer.

### Common mistake

Even WHERE o.status = 'paid' OR o.id IS NULL can lose a customer whose only existing orders are unpaid, because the join found matches and never produced an unmatched row. Filter the match condition itself.
keyTakeaways: Preserve every customer with a left outer join.
Place the paid filter in ON.
Explain NULL rejection and the unpaid-only case.
Rewrite using RIGHT JOIN with the same projection.

questions.title: Do primary, unique and foreign keys enforce the same rule?
questions.questionMarkdown: Design PostgreSQL constraints for accounts(id, email) and purchases(id, account_id). IDs must identify rows, known emails must not repeat, and every non-null account_id must refer to an account. What happens to multiple NULL emails under a default UNIQUE constraint?
questions.tldrAnswer: Primary keys enforce unique non-null identities; UNIQUE prevents repeated known emails but permits multiple NULLs by default in PostgreSQL; a foreign key enforces references for non-null account IDs.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Use ordinary PostgreSQL equality for email, which is case-sensitive unless the type or index is configured otherwise. A nullable account_id is allowed in this stated contract.

### Reasoning

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  email text UNIQUE
);
CREATE TABLE purchases (
  id bigint PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id bigint REFERENCES accounts(id)
);
```

A primary key may be composite, but a table has one designated primary-key constraint. A table can have several unique constraints. PostgreSQL treats NULLs as distinct by default for uniqueness; UNIQUE NULLS NOT DISTINCT can instead permit at most one NULL for a single nullable column. A foreign key can reference an eligible unique key, not only a primary key. Add NOT NULL to account_id if every purchase must have an account, and define deletion behaviour deliberately.

### Common mistake

A foreign key does not make account_id unique: many purchases can reference one account. A UNIQUE email constraint also does not automatically make email mandatory or case-insensitive.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish identity, uniqueness and referential integrity.
Explain default multiple-NULL uniqueness.
Allow many purchases per referenced account.
State optional NOT NULL and email-comparison requirements.

questions.title: Why is an inclusive timestamp range easy to get wrong?
questions.questionMarkdown: Select events during November 2026 from events(id, occurred_at), where occurred_at is a UTC timestamp with time zone. Compare BETWEEN with a half-open interval and explain how IN differs. What does NULL do in these predicates?
questions.tldrAnswer: Use occurred_at >= the start of November and < the start of December. BETWEEN includes both endpoints; IN checks listed values. Ordinary comparisons involving NULL usually yield unknown, which WHERE excludes.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The reporting month is defined in UTC and occurred_at has PostgreSQL timestamptz type. Application-local calendar months require boundaries in the appropriate time zone instead.

### Reasoning

```sql
SELECT id, occurred_at
FROM events
WHERE occurred_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-11-01 00:00:00+00'
  AND occurred_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-12-01 00:00:00+00';
```

BETWEEN a AND b means >=a AND <=b, so using the next month boundary includes its first instant. Choosing an artificial last fractional second is fragile. IN (a,b) instead tests equality with either listed value, not every value between them. BETWEEN works for ordered types, not just numbers. A NULL timestamp is excluded here; use IS NULL if missing timestamps are a separate required group. A nonmatching IN list containing NULL yields unknown rather than false.

### Common mistake

Do not use = NULL, and be especially careful with NOT IN when its list or subquery may contain NULL. Half-open boundaries also avoid overlapping adjacent monthly windows.
keyTakeaways: Use UTC half-open month boundaries.
Explain inclusive BETWEEN versus discrete IN membership.
Explain WHERE handling of unknown.
Identify = NULL and nullable NOT IN traps.

questions.title: How do you count returning users without counting new users?
questions.questionMarkdown: Using PostgreSQL activity(user_id, occurred_at), count users active in April 2026 who had no activity in March but did have activity before March. Timestamps are UTC. Return one count even if a user has many April events.
questions.tldrAnswer: Select distinct April users, require an earlier-history EXISTS and a correlated March NOT EXISTS. The earlier-history requirement excludes brand-new April users.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

user_id and occurred_at are non-null; occurred_at is timestamptz. Reactivated explicitly means active now, absent in the previous calendar month, and active before that month.

### Reasoning

```sql
WITH april_users AS (
  SELECT DISTINCT user_id
  FROM activity
  WHERE occurred_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:00:00+00'
    AND occurred_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-05-01 00:00:00+00'
)
SELECT COUNT(*) AS reactivated_users
FROM april_users AS a
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM activity AS m
  WHERE m.user_id = a.user_id
    AND m.occurred_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-03-01 00:00:00+00'
    AND m.occurred_at <  TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-04-01 00:00:00+00'
)
AND EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM activity AS old
  WHERE old.user_id = a.user_id
    AND old.occurred_at < TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-03-01 00:00:00+00'
);
```

The distinct CTE fixes the counting unit as users. Each subquery is correlated to that same user. Half-open intervals handle boundary timestamps without overlap. An index beginning with user_id and occurred_at can help the existence checks, while the best overall plan depends on data size and distribution. Test users with repeated events, only new activity, previous-month activity and exact boundary timestamps.

### Common mistake

An uncorrelated NOT EXISTS tests whether anyone was active in March. Counting April events inflates active users, and omitting earlier history classifies new users as returning.
keyTakeaways: Define the reactivation population and exclude new users.
Deduplicate April users.
Correlate both existence checks by user ID.
Use correct half-open UTC month boundaries.

questions.title: How should access patterns guide relational or document storage?
questions.questionMarkdown: An order system needs unique order IDs, consistent payment updates, customer-wide reports and flexible item metadata. Compare a relational schema with a document-oriented design without assuming that one database family always scales better.
questions.tldrAnswer: Choose around relationships, transaction boundaries, query patterns and operational needs. Relational constraints and joins fit shared entities; documents can group data read together, but duplication and cross-document updates need planning.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Requirements include correctness during concurrent writes, known reporting queries and metadata whose fields vary. No specific product or scale benchmark has already been established.

### Reasoning

A relational design can keep customers, orders and payments linked by keys, enforce constraints and join them for reporting. PostgreSQL also supports JSON/JSONB for flexible metadata, so variable fields do not force a separate database family. A document design can embed details commonly retrieved together, but repeated customer attributes create update and consistency questions.

Evaluate transaction scope, indexes, query latency, write conflicts, backup and recovery, and the cost of schema evolution using representative workloads. Document databases can support transactions; MongoDB, for example, supports multi-document transactions with associated constraints and cost. Conversely, using SQL does not imply a single fixed scaling strategy. Model guarantees and measured behaviour matter more than labels.

### Common mistake

Avoid absolute claims such as NoSQL has no transactions or relational databases cannot store flexible data. Embedding every relationship can make cross-entity updates and reports harder rather than simpler.
keyTakeaways: Start from access patterns and consistency requirements.
Explain normalised relationships versus embedded documents.
Recognise PostgreSQL JSON and document transactions.
Compare concrete operational and performance trade-offs.

questions.title: How do you choose the fourth event for each account reproducibly?
questions.questionMarkdown: Write a PostgreSQL query returning the fourth event per account from events(event_id, account_id, occurred_at). Some timestamps tie. Explain why ordering only by occurred_at is insufficient.
questions.tldrAnswer: Use ROW_NUMBER partitioned by account_id and ordered by occurred_at plus unique event_id, then filter row number four in an outer query. Accounts with fewer than four events produce no row.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

event_id is a unique non-null key, account_id and occurred_at are non-null, and event_id is the agreed deterministic tie-breaker rather than proof of real-world temporal order.

### Reasoning

```sql
WITH numbered AS (
  SELECT event_id, account_id, occurred_at,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (
           PARTITION BY account_id
           ORDER BY occurred_at, event_id
         ) AS position
  FROM events
)
SELECT event_id, account_id, occurred_at
FROM numbered
WHERE position = 4
ORDER BY account_id;
```

ROW_NUMBER gives each row a distinct position within its account. Equal timestamps otherwise leave the order of tied rows unspecified. The outer query filters the window result because the same SELECT level cannot generally use a window function in WHERE. A fourth event row differs from the fourth distinct timestamp, for which a rank over distinct values would answer another question.

### Common mistake

A window ORDER BY does not guarantee final presentation order; use an outer ORDER BY when needed. Do not claim that the tie-breaker recovers chronology that the recorded timestamp cannot resolve.
keyTakeaways: Partition event numbering by account.
Use a unique deterministic tie-breaker.
Filter the window result in a separate query level.
Distinguish row position, distinct timestamp rank and output order.

questions.title: How do you list related row pairs only once?
questions.questionMarkdown: In registrations(id, device_id), each row is a registration with a unique ID. Return all distinct pairs of registrations sharing the same known device, without pairing a row with itself or emitting both (a,b) and (b,a).
questions.tldrAnswer: Join two aliases of registrations on equal device_id and require a.id < b.id. The strict ID inequality removes self-pairs and chooses one orientation for each pair.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

id is a unique non-null numeric key. A NULL device_id means unknown and must not be treated as a shared device.

### Reasoning

```sql
SELECT a.id AS first_id, b.id AS second_id, a.device_id
FROM registrations AS a
JOIN registrations AS b
  ON a.device_id = b.device_id
 AND a.id < b.id
ORDER BY a.id, b.id;
```

The aliases represent two roles for rows from the same relation, not two physical tables. SQL equality does not match NULL device IDs, which fits the stated contract. A device with k registrations creates k(k−1)/2 pairs; a large result can be inherent to the requirement. An index may help find same-device rows but cannot avoid emitting the requested number of pairs.

### Common mistake

Using a.id <> b.id removes self-pairs but still emits both directions. DISTINCT alone is not a substitute for defining the pair orientation and can conceal an unintended result shape.
keyTakeaways: Use two aliases of the same table.
Match known device IDs.
Use a strict ID ordering to remove self and reverse pairs.
Explain quadratic output size within a large group.

questions.title: Why can joining three tables inflate an order total?
questions.questionMarkdown: One order has three line items and two payments. A query joins orders, line_items and payments and then sums both item amounts and payment amounts. Explain the error and write a query returning one row per order with correct totals.
questions.tldrAnswer: The join creates six item-payment combinations, repeating each item twice and each payment three times. Aggregate each child table to one row per order before joining the totals.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Use orders(id), line_items(order_id, amount) and payments(order_id, amount). Amounts are non-null numeric values, multiple equal amounts are legitimate, and missing children should produce zero totals.

### Reasoning

```sql
WITH item_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS item_total
  FROM line_items
  GROUP BY order_id
), payment_totals AS (
  SELECT order_id, SUM(amount) AS payment_total
  FROM payments
  GROUP BY order_id
)
SELECT o.id,
       COALESCE(i.item_total, 0) AS item_total,
       COALESCE(p.payment_total, 0) AS payment_total
FROM orders AS o
LEFT JOIN item_totals AS i ON i.order_id = o.id
LEFT JOIN payment_totals AS p ON p.order_id = o.id
ORDER BY o.id;
```

Each aggregate now has at most one row per order, so joining cannot multiply those totals. Left joins preserve orders with no items or payments. The COALESCE rule is justified by the stated meaning of absent children; it should not silently replace unknown monetary values in a different schema.

### Common mistake

SUM(DISTINCT amount) is not a general repair: two legitimate line items can have equal prices. Diagnose the row cardinality and intended aggregation unit before choosing a fix.
keyTakeaways: Identify the three-by-two row multiplication.
Preaggregate each child relation by order ID.
Preserve orders with no children and define zero handling.
Explain why SUM(DISTINCT amount) can undercount.

questions.title: Which rank finds the second distinct score?
questions.questionMarkdown: A leaderboard has scores 90, 90, 75 and 60. Compare RANK, DENSE_RANK and ROW_NUMBER in descending score order. Write PostgreSQL to return everyone with the second distinct non-null score.
questions.tldrAnswer: RANK gives 1,1,3,4; DENSE_RANK gives 1,1,2,3. ROW_NUMBER assigns distinct positions, with a tie-breaker needed for reproducibility. Filter DENSE_RANK=2 to find the second distinct score.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

Use leaderboard(player_id, score), with unique non-null player IDs. Exclude NULL scores explicitly and include all players tied at the requested distinct score.

### Reasoning

```sql
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT player_id, score,
         DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY score DESC) AS score_rank
  FROM leaderboard
  WHERE score IS NOT NULL
)
SELECT player_id, score
FROM ranked
WHERE score_rank = 2
ORDER BY player_id;
```

RANK records the first row position of a peer group, so a tie consumes positions and the next rank skips them. DENSE_RANK counts peer groups without gaps. For row numbering, ORDER BY score DESC, player_id defines a deterministic order, but adding player_id to the DENSE_RANK ordering would break score ties into separate groups. If only one distinct score exists, the query returns no rows.

### Common mistake

Do not use RANK=2 for the second distinct score when the highest score is tied. Separate the value that defines peers from the key used merely to present results deterministically.
keyTakeaways: Calculate the three ranking behaviours.
Use dense rank over score only.
Handle NULLs and all tied players explicitly.
Keep peer definitions separate from output tie-breakers.
