questions.title: When is a temporary table more useful than a CTE?
questions.questionMarkdown: A PostgreSQL analysis reuses an expensive intermediate result in five separate statements and wants an index on it. Compare a common table expression with a temporary table, including lifetime and materialisation behaviour.
questions.tldrAnswer: A CTE belongs to one statement; a temporary table can be reused within its session and indexed. PostgreSQL may fold or materialise suitable CTEs depending on query structure and options, so a CTE is not automatically a persisted cached result.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The five statements run in the same database session. Temporary-table lifecycle and transaction behaviour are chosen explicitly rather than relying on a connection pool to preserve session state.

### Reasoning

```sql
CREATE TEMP TABLE recent_orders AS
SELECT id, customer_id
FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= TIMESTAMPTZ '2026-01-01 00:00:00+00';

CREATE INDEX ON recent_orders (customer_id);
ANALYZE recent_orders;
```

The table can support later statements in that session. ON COMMIT options can alter row or table lifetime; the default is normally session lifetime, not visibility to every connection. A CTE names a subquery for one statement and can improve structure. PostgreSQL can fold eligible side-effect-free CTEs into a parent query or materialise them; MATERIALIZED and NOT MATERIALIZED influence eligible cases. Inspect plans and benchmark rather than assuming either form is faster. Temporary tables also require storage and maintenance, and a connection pool may route a later statement to another session.

### Common mistake

Neither a CTE nor a temporary table is guaranteed to live only in RAM. Do not assume a CTE can be queried by name in the next statement or a session-local table is visible to other sessions.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish statement scope from session scope.
Explain indexing and reuse of a temporary table.
Qualify PostgreSQL CTE folding and materialisation.
Consider transaction options, connection pools and measured cost.

questions.title: How would you choose a Python framework for a custom neural loss?
questions.questionMarkdown: A team prototypes an image model in NumPy and now needs automatic gradients for a custom loss, accelerator training and a maintained deployment path. Compare staying with NumPy alone with using PyTorch, TensorFlow or JAX. What small experiment would justify the choice?
questions.tldrAnswer: NumPy supplies array computation but not a built-in neural automatic-differentiation system. PyTorch, TensorFlow and JAX offer differentiable tensor operations with different APIs and execution constraints. Test the actual custom operation, device and deployment requirements rather than choosing by reputation.
questions.detailedAnswerMarkdown:
### Assumptions

The loss is differentiable almost everywhere, the target hardware is known, and the team can change the prototype. This concerns training computation, not HTTP request handling or a claim that one framework is universally fastest.

### Reasoning

With NumPy alone, the team must supply derivatives or introduce another differentiation system. Array syntax by itself does not record the operations needed for reverse-mode differentiation. PyTorch autograd can record operations on tensors requiring gradients; TensorFlow uses GradientTape to watch differentiable computations; JAX provides function transformations such as grad over compatible numerical functions. Each requires operations that its differentiation machinery understands.

Implement a small version of the actual model and custom loss in the candidate framework. Check gradients against finite differences on a smooth, small example, then test supported device operations, memory use, training throughput and the intended export or serving path. Include compilation warm-up separately when comparing timings. Team familiarity, maintained dependencies and reproducible checkpoints also matter.

Converting intermediate values to ordinary NumPy arrays can leave the framework's tracked computation, losing the intended gradient connection. Custom operations may need a supported composition or an explicitly implemented derivative. JAX transformations also impose constraints on Python side effects and control flow, so familiar-looking array code is not automatically compatible.

### Common mistake

Automatic differentiation computes derivatives of the implemented computation; it does not prove that the loss, labels or gradients are the ones intended. Do not select a framework from a list of names without checking the actual operation and deployment requirements.
keyTakeaways: Distinguish NumPy array computation from automatic differentiation.
Compare PyTorch autograd, TensorFlow GradientTape and JAX function transformations.
Check custom-operation gradients and computation-boundary mistakes.
Evaluate hardware, performance and deployment using a representative prototype.
